## Summary
- The overview page's "Sensor feeds" card capped at the top 30 sensors by event count (`topN(..., 30)` in `aggregate.go`) — a low-volume or newly added sensor was only reachable through the heatmap's sensor filter (`/api/filter-values`, which ranks the full set before applying its own, separate 20-cap), never visible on this card by default. That's the asymmetry reported: sensors discoverable by filtering, not by browsing the plain card.
- `aggregate.go`: uncap the `topN` call so every expected+observed sensor reaches the snapshot.
- `overview.html`: wrap the table body in `.sensor-card__scroll`, add a visible "Showing all N sensors" count.
- `theme.css`: bound `.sensor-card__scroll` to a fixed `max-height` + `overflow-y: auto` so a long list scrolls in place instead of growing the card/page.

author: jerocq
body:
### Motivation
- Provide a small password-protected administrative dashboard API to edit and manage per-client system instructions and upload large catalog PDFs outside GitHub. 
- Integrate a Supabase-hosted password-only proxy for the dashboard to avoid exposing platform JWTs and to isolate client access. 
- Add Tanaka-specific system instruction and a placeholder catalog PDF so the bot can be managed from the dashboard and serve a deterministic public catalog URL. 

### Description
- Add `dashboard_api.py` with an authenticated FastAPI router exposing `/api/generate-si-changes`, `/api/format-and-save-si`, `/api/current-si`, `/api/si-history`, `/api/upload-catalog`, and `/api/current-catalog`, plus `GeminiAdapter`, `GitHubAdapter`, and `CatalogStorageAdapter` abstractions and rate-limited admin auth using `X-Dashboard-API-Key`.
- Add a Supabase Edge Function proxy at `supabase/functions/dashboard-api/index.ts` and `supabase/config.toml` to authenticate via per-client passwords and forward requests to the backend while enforcing client isolation.
- Update `config.py` to add dashboard-related settings and helpers (`GEMINI_DASHBOARD_MODEL(S)`, GitHub/Railway metadata fallbacks, Supabase catalog helpers, CORS and timeout configuration) and introduce model normalization and fallback list parsing.
- Update `bot.py` to load the Tanaka file catalog, override the `catalogo_pdf` entry to the deterministic Supabase public URL at runtime, and to source the `SYSTEM_INSTRUCTION` literal from `src/clients/tanaka/system_instruction.txt` when present.
- Wire the dashboard into the running app by including the new router, adding CORS middleware, and mounting `public` static files in `main.py`.
- Add `public/catalogos/tanaka_catalogo.pdf` placeholder and `src/clients/tanaka/system_instruction.txt` system instruction content for Tanaka, pin some `requirements.txt` versions, and add `python-multipart` for file uploads.
- Add a comprehensive set of unit tests for the new dashboard features and config behavior (`tests/test_dashboard_api.py`, `tests/test_dashboard_proxy_contract.py`, `tests/test_tanaka_dashboard_files.py`, plus updates to existing tests such as `tests/test_config.py`, `tests/test_business_catalog_selection.py`, and `tests/test_system_prompt_preserved.py`).

### Testing
- Ran the unit test suite including `tests/test_dashboard_api.py`, `tests/test_dashboard_proxy_contract.py`, `tests/test_tanaka_dashboard_files.py`, `tests/test_config.py`, `tests/test_business_catalog_selection.py`, and `tests/test_system_prompt_preserved.py` as part of automated CI and the tests passed. 
- Exercised dashboard endpoints in tests to validate Gemini retries, GitHub commit/update flows, resumable Supabase uploads, PDF validation, client isolation, and error mapping for provider errors and oversized uploads. 
- Verified config parsing behavior in tests for Railway Git metadata fallbacks, dashboard model normalization, and default dashboard timeouts.

author: estevanhernandez-stack-ed
body:
Wave 3 of the Settings + navigation glow campaign. Closes **F-009**, **F-012**, **F-010**, **F-011**. Partially closes **F-001**.

## The band

Six identically-weighted buttons — Settings / About / History / Diagnostics / Games / Plugins — collapse to two: **Settings**, and **Tools ▾**.

The split is F-001's test, not taste. Settings is the only one of the six that writes `settings.json` or `discord.dat`. The other five are verb-shaped and episodic: you go there, do a thing, and leave. That's what makes them tools, and it's why History and Diagnostics were never preferences despite sitting at Settings' exact visual weight on the main band.

The gear glyph is gone (F-012) — one of six peers wore an icon for no distinction the other five lacked.

## The popup has a border, deliberately

`NavyBrush == BgBrush` in all three built-in themes, and in any user theme that leaves them equal. A menu filled with Navy and no border is **invisible** against the window behind it — the same failure flatline exposed in the Settings cards. `BorderThickness="1"` on `DividerBrush` is what makes it survive.

Verified, not assumed: captured with the menu open under flatline, and it reads.

A `ContextMenu` rather than a `ui:DropDownButton`, because a ContextMenu hung off the button inherits the window's DataContext through `PlacementTarget` — so the five items bind to the same commands the buttons used, with no re-plumbing.

## The ad copy

Goal 4's two clearest instances, both deleted:

- **F-010** — the header's Store-listing pitch, read on every launch by someone who already has eight accounts on screen. The first-run tour and the empty state already carry it to the only user who needs it.
- **F-011** — `"Multi-launcher for Windows. A 626 Labs product."` sat in a status bar where every other cell reports live state. It sold the app to someone already running it. It's the actual subject of the About window, which is where it still lives. Column left in place so the neighbours keep their positions.

## A conflict in the register, resolved

F-009's fix direction says *"rename Games → Library in the menu."* That is **stale**. F-006 shipped in wave 1 and swept "Library" out of every user-visible string, including the window this menu item opens. Following F-009 literally would undo a merged wave.

The menu says **Games**.

## Residue on F-001 — named, not hidden

F-001's fix direction also lists **Stop all**, **Open log folder**, and the **Welcome tour** as Tools items. Those three have no view-model command — the tray raises events handled in `App.xaml.cs` instead. Building three new commands inside a wave that's already introducing a new mechanism trades reviewability for tidiness.

F-001 stays **open** with exactly those three named. F-018 (Multi-Instance state on the status bar) is untouched.

## Verification

`dotnet test ROROROblox.slnx` — **1268 unit + 18 integration passed, 0 failed.**

Runtime: the toolbar reports exactly two buttons; the menu opens with all five destinations; and invoking About *from the menu* opens the About window — which is the proof that the ContextMenu's DataContext inheritance actually carries the command bindings, rather than the items merely looking enabled (a null `Command` doesn't disable a `MenuItem`).

author: mitsuru
body:
## Summary

Adds five `pub(crate)` methods to `ObjectHandle` — `unparse_object`, `unparse_object_qdf`, `unparse_stream_body`, `unparse_stream_body_qdf`, `unparse_trailer` — porting qpdf 11.9.0's `QPDFWriter::unparseObject`/`writeTrailer` (not `QPDFObjectHandle::unparse`, already ported separately). This is additive-only infrastructure for `flpdf-egzr.3.2.5` (writer group consumer migration, not part of this PR) — no existing consumer file is touched, and every new method carries `#[allow(dead_code)]`.

- Resolves a three-way null-suppression conflict onto `ObjectHandle::try_is_null` (promoted out of dead-code; mirrors `QPDFObjectHandle::dereference`→`QPDFObject::resolve`), applied to `unparse_object`/`unparse_object_qdf`/`unparse_stream_body`/`unparse_stream_body_qdf`. `unparse_trailer` deliberately does not suppress, matching `writeTrailer`'s own unconditional key loop.
- Replaces flpdf's legacy `write_pdf_with_id_writer`/`write_pdf_trailer` two-function split with one `unparse_trailer(xref_stream: bool, ...)`, matching qpdf's real `writeXRefStream`→`writeTrailer(xref_stream=true)` boundary and forcing `/ID`/`/Encrypt` last in both modes (the legacy split's plain-lexicographic behavior for the xref-stream case is `flpdf-wt2w`'s tracked root cause; this closes it once `flpdf-egzr.3.2.5` adopts the new primitive).
- `unparse_stream_body_qdf` was added in a follow-up commit after a final full-branch review found the original four-primitive design had silently missed a fifth legacy shape (`write_pdf_stream_qdf`, `object.rs:1036`, live callsite at `writer.rs:4437`).
- None of the five primitives goes through the existing `unparse_resolved()`/`materialize()`-to-`Object` bridge — each walks `ObjectHandle`'s own graph directly, delegating scalar formatting to `object.rs`'s existing helpers.

Design and implementation plan: `docs/plans/2026-08-05-objecthandle-writer-emission-api-design.md`, `docs/plans/2026-08-05-objecthandle-writer-emission-api.md`.

Tracks `flpdf-egzr.3.2.13`. Related: `flpdf-umye` (legacy `write_pdf_stream` null-suppression gap, deliberately out of scope here — closes via `flpdf-egzr.3.2.5`'s consumer migration), `flpdf-wt2w` (xref-stream byte-parity bug, same).

## Test plan

- [x] `cargo test -p flpdf` — full suite green (3380 lib + 75 doctests)
- [x] `cargo test -p flpdf --features qpdf-zlib-compat` — byte-identical corpus unchanged (3425 passed)
- [x] `cargo llvm-cov` + `scripts/patch-coverage.sh --base origin/main` — 100% changed-line coverage (916 changed, 0 uncovered)
- [x] `cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings` — clean
- [x] `cargo fmt --check` — clean
- [x] `git diff --name-only` scoped to `object_handle.rs`, `object.rs` (one visibility promotion), and docs — no consumer files touched
- [x] Every primitive independently spec-compliance-reviewed and code-quality-reviewed, with mutation-testing-verified fixes where gaps were found

author: ulsklyc
body:
## Summary

Nur `PATCH /:id/status` legte beim Erledigen die Folgeinstanz einer wiederkehrenden Aufgabe an. `PUT /:id` akzeptiert ebenfalls `status='done'` - das Bearbeiten-Formular hat im Edit-Modus ein Status-Dropdown und schickt `body.status` mit - erzeugte aber keine Folgeinstanz. Wer eine wöchentliche Aufgabe über den Bearbeiten-Dialog auf "Erledigt" setzte, beendete die Serie lautlos. Die Rücknahme war seit v1.75.2 in beiden Pfaden behandelt (#650); die Erzeugung war die fehlende Hälfte.

Verwandt: #650 (dort wurde die Rücknahme gefixt, der Issue ist bereits geschlossen).

## Changes

**Die Lücke selbst**
- Der Spawn-Block aus PATCH steckt jetzt in `spawnRecurrenceFollowup()`, direkt neben `discardRecurrenceFollowup()`. Beide Pfade rufen ihn beim Übergang nach `done` auf.
- `PUT` übergibt die frisch gelesene Zeile: eine im selben Speichern geänderte Wiederholungsregel, Fälligkeit oder Verankerung gilt schon für die Folgeinstanz.

**Aus dem Review dazugekommen**
- **Atomarität:** PATCH und PUT umschließen UPDATE, Punkte, Outbound-Marker und die Serien-Bewegung (Spawn oder Discard) mit einer Transaktion. Vorher konnte ein gescheiterter Spawn die Aufgabe erledigt und ohne Nachfolger zurücklassen - derselbe stille Serienabbruch, nur verschoben von "nie versucht" zu "versucht und verloren". `pushToCalDAV` bleibt außerhalb und hinter der Antwort.
- **`start_date`:** der Spawn-INSERT führte es nie mit, die nächste Instanz verlor ihren Vorlauf. Bestandsfehler, den der PUT-Weg neu erreichbar macht. Der Abstand zwischen Start und Fälligkeit reist jetzt mit.

**Merge von v1.80.0**
- main hat mit #658 denselben Block angefasst (Anker ab Erledigungstag, Haushaltszone). Beides ist in `spawnRecurrenceFollowup()` übernommen: `todayInHouseholdZone()` + `nextDueAfterCompletion(...)`, und `recurrence_from_completion` reist in der Folgeinstanz mit. Die beiden Änderungen greifen ineinander - weil PUT die frische Zeile übergibt, gilt der Anker jetzt auch beim Abhaken über den Dialog.

**Tests** (`test/test-tasks-recurrence.js`, 38 gesamt)
- Erzeugung über PUT inkl. Zuweisungen und `recurrence_origin_id`, kein Nachlegen bei doppeltem Speichern, Rücknahme per PUT, Subtask-Guard.
- Die frische Zeile als Spawn-Eingabe: geänderte Regel gilt sofort, abgeschaltete Wiederholung erzeugt nichts, im selben Zug gesetzter Anker greift.
- Atomarität über einen SQLite-Trigger, der gezielt den Spawn-INSERT scheitern lässt - je einer für PATCH und PUT.
- Vorlauf: bleibt erhalten, komponiert mit dem Anker, und die Folgeinstanz wartet auf ihren Starttag (Standardliste vs. `include_future`).

## Checklist

- [x] `npm test` passes (Exit 0)
- [x] Follows [CONTRIBUTING.md](../CONTRIBUTING.md) conventions
- [x] No new frontend dependencies (vanilla JS, no frameworks)
- [x] UI strings use `t('key')` (no hardcoded text) - keine UI-Strings berührt, reine Backend-Änderung
- [x] CHANGELOG.md updated (if user-facing change)

author: karl-bullock
body:
Closes #8, by taking that issue's second option: declare 1.x unsupported and refuse loudly, rather than building out half-support for it.

## Why refusing beats fixing

The alternative in #8 is to derive a `DB_DRIVER` from the target version and thread it through `install.yml`, `write_config_php` and the sync `sed`, then version-gate the 2.0-only packages in the hard-require list. That is four coupled changes across the whole entrypoint, permanently maintained, so that someone can start a **new** forum on a version that is near end of life. The bench broker already refuses 1.x for the same reason.

Refusing costs 25 lines and removes the failure mode entirely.

## What it does

When `TARGET_FLARUM_VERSION` names a major below 2, the boot stops immediately with an explanation:

```
[!] FATAL: TARGET_FLARUM_VERSION='^1.8' asks for Flarum 1.x, which this image does not support.
       Flarum 1.x cannot install or boot here (linkrobins/flarum-docker#8), and 1.8 is near end of life.
       Use Flarum 2.x (e.g. TARGET_FLARUM_VERSION=^2.0), or unset it to install the version baked into this image.
```

That fires before the database wait, so a misconfigured deploy fails in about a second instead of getting three different errors in sequence, each needing its own workaround to reach the next one. The comment above the guard lists all three breaks so the next reader knows why the variable is restricted rather than rediscovering it on a bench.

`.env.example` now says 2.x only, and explains that leaving the variable unset is the recommended path.

## Version parsing

The first run of digits in the constraint decides. Verified across the forms composer accepts:

| constraint | result |
| --- | --- |
| `^1.8`, `1.8.*`, `~1.8.0`, `>=1.8 <2.0`, `dev-1.8` | refused |
| `^2.0`, `2.0.0-rc.5`, `>=2.0 <3.0` | allowed |
| `dev-main` (no digits) | allowed |
| unset | allowed, uses the baked skeleton |

A constraint with no digits is deliberately left alone rather than guessed at: a branch alias could point anywhere, and blocking it would be worse than letting it through.

## Testing

`bash -n` clean. Run in a real container built on `ghcr.io/linkrobins/flarum-docker:latest` with this entrypoint:

- `TARGET_FLARUM_VERSION=^1.8` exits **1** with the message above, before touching the database.
- `TARGET_FLARUM_VERSION=^2.0` passes the guard and proceeds normally (reaches the MariaDB wait).
- Unset passes the guard and installs from the baked skeleton, which is the path exercised end to end in #9's verification.

## Note

Independent of this PR, #8's third finding stands and is **not** fixed here: the sync `sed` rewrites the driver on **every** boot, which is a footgun in its own right. With 1.x refused it can no longer break a 1.8 forum, so it stops being urgent, but narrowing it to first boot, or replacing it with the same `php -r` read/modify/write already used for the websocket block, would still be an improvement. Happy to do that separately if you want it.

author: pushery
body:
### Fixed

- **The payload-version select now shows the stored version on the first paint, not the first
  option.** The control was bound with `wire:model` alone, which sets the choice once Alpine has
  run — so the server render carried no `selected`, and an endpoint pinned to `v2` rendered as
  though it inherited. That is the state a reader acts on before hydration, and the only state a
  reader without JavaScript ever sees.

- **The six shipped tables now name their own scroll region.** Each table sits inside a focusable,
  horizontally scrolling container, and the container took its accessible name from WireKit's
  generic fallback — so a screen-reader user tabbing through the dashboard met several identically
  named regions. They now carry a translated, table-specific name in all seven locales, which also
  makes the name independent of which locales WireKit itself happens to ship. Two of the six had no
  table name at all and gained one.

### Changed

- **The bundled Boost skill now states the UI prerequisites.** Switching on the dashboard or the
  self-service portal needs `livewire/livewire` and `pushery/wirekit`, neither of which is a hard
  dependency — so an agent following the skill turned a layer on and met `Unable to locate a class
  or view for component [wirekit::card]` at render rather than a clear message at boot. The layer
  table's dependency notes now name both packages, the install line, and the publish-and-restyle
  route for a host on another UI kit.

- **The two publishable delete dialogs now say why they set their own cancel label, and when it
  would be safe to stop.** WireKit ships translations of its own from 2.26 on, which reads like an
  invitation to drop the override — but it ships `en` and `de`, and these screens ship seven
  locales. Taking the invitation would return `es`, `fr`, `it`, `nl` and `pt` to English with

## Summary

Adds the dormant, provider-scoped Podman command/preflight/start-stop boundary and proves it against a real rootless Podman 5 service with Docker disabled. The provider remains absent from the production registry: this PR does not activate or advertise Podman support.

Stacked on #8261. Part of #7744.

## Related Issue

Part of #7744.

## Changes

- Adds an immutable operation-scoped container-engine command contract and a Podman adapter pinned to one qualified Unix-socket authority.
- Adds Linux amd64/arm64 rootless Podman 5 preflight, subordinate UID/GID and cgroups v2 validation, and exact labeled-container start/stop semantics.
- Adds an inert Podman runtime bundle with only host doctor and direct CPU lifecycle capabilities; managed bootstrap, snapshots, recovery, cleanup, GPU, local inference, and production selection remain explicitly unsupported for later slices.
- Adds unit coverage across OpenClaw, Hermes, and Deep Agents Code while keeping the production registry limited to qualified providers.

author: yajinni
body:
## Summary

Automatically move repository setup changes into a dedicated pull request instead of leaving the configured base branch dirty after package and component installation.

## Behavior

- preflight the working tree before installing repository components
- allow only package-managed setup files in the automatic commit
- refuse to mix unrelated user changes into the setup PR
- create `ai/install-paseo-automation` from the configured base branch
- stage and commit only the issue template, `paseo.json`, package manifest, and recognized lockfiles that actually changed
- push the setup branch and open a PR into the configured base branch
- return the local workspace to the base branch after submission
- keep Issues Processing disabled while the setup PR is open or not yet synchronized locally
- poll the setup PR in the background and fast-forward the clean local base branch after merge
- recover installations created by older versions when the expected files are already left uncommitted
- show setup-PR progress and failures in the Components section

## Safety

- never commits files outside the explicit setup allowlist
- stops before installation when unrelated working-tree changes are present
- never pushes directly to the configured base branch
- preserves GitHub lifecycle labels and the machine-local Paseo workspace outside the setup commit
- records setup-PR state under Git-local Paseo state rather than in the repository

## Validation

- unit coverage for porcelain parsing, allowlisting, unrelated-change rejection, automatic PR submission, base-branch restoration, and post-merge synchronization
- existing Node, Windows command-shim, syntax, and packed-install CI

author: rchari1
body:
Selecting **Piccolissimo + Altissimo** is supposed to mean one thing: every solve runs Altissimo, in Harmoniqs Cloud, without anyone deciding anything. We wired that quickly for the hackathon and four gaps were left between the promise and the code. This closes them and adds the tests that would have caught each one.

## 1. Nothing actually selected Altissimo

The solve template shipped `SOLVER = :ipopt`. Choosing the paid cloud tier changed the entitlement, the routing, and the UI — but not the backend. A "High-Performance" run could solve on IPOPT and be **indistinguishable** in the artifacts: same run dir, same frames, same converged badge.

The template is now **staged at session prep** with `SOLVER` substituted from the solver mode, so the backend follows the selected tier instead of being an authoring decision the agent can get wrong. The placeholder lives inside a string literal (`SOLVER = let s = "{{SOLVER}}" …`), so an unstaged template still parses and degrades to a local IPOPT solve rather than dying on a syntax error.

## 2. Altissimo produced no telemetry at all on the shipped stack

This is why cloud runs came back with an empty Run Inspector. Two independent causes, both silent:

- Piccolissimo 0.2.0's `solve!(prob, ::AltissimoOptions; kwargs...)` forwards a **hardcoded whitelist** to `Altissimo.optimize!`. `callback` is not on it, so the callback we hang telemetry on never fires.
- `AltissimoOptions.verbose` defaults to `false`, so the iteration table never printed either.

Neither path existed, so a run reported `iterations = 0` and looked like it had converged. Now: `verbose = true` (load-bearing, not chatter — it is plumbed to `verbose_outer`/`verbose_inner`), plus a stdout bridge that translates Altissimo's own table rows into `AMICODE_ITER`. Numbering is sequential over rows because the table's `iter` column is `·` for every inner step and only becomes an integer on the final outer iteration — trusting that column yields a single point at the end.

Verified locally: **154 streamed iterations**, objective 48 → 7.8e-3, with the callback never firing once. Where a newer Piccolissimo *does* forward the callback it supersedes the bridge (it also carries frames), so there is exactly one numbering scheme per run.

Also still in: the DirectTrajOpt 0.9.7 `_solve` dispatch bridge, without which every Altissimo solve is a silent no-op that reports success.

## 3. The default launch failed instead of going to the cloud

A plain `amico-run script.jl` under the HP tier exited 64 with a message telling the agent to retry with `--executor remote`. That round-trip surfaced to users as a failed run.

It is now **promoted** to remote — selecting the cloud tier *is* the routing decision. An explicit `--executor local` is still refused, because silently inverting a flag someone typed is worse than an error. And a promotion with no cloud connection refuses with *"Connect Harmoniqs Cloud in the Connections panel"* rather than failing deep in `RemoteExecutor` with a `~/.amico/cloud.json` path the user has never heard of.

## 4. The UI never said where a run ran

A cloud run and a local run produced an identical Inspector pane, so "did that actually use the cloud I'm paying for?" was unanswerable from the UI. The topbar now reads `<runId> · Harmoniqs Cloud` for remote runs.

Keyed on `remote.json` (written by `RemoteExecutor` and nothing else) rather than a new `run.toml` field — `run.schema.json` is `additionalProperties: false`, which is why the remote executor put `task_id` in that sidecar to begin with.

## Guidance corrections

Four claims in the agent guidance no longer matched the code and are now accurate: the local-launch refusal (it promotes), the "`AMICODE_ITER` not yet available on the cloud bundle" note (it is), and the quoted `SOLVER = :altissimo` line (the guidance now says the line arrives already set, so the agent doesn't "fix" it).

Two **real** limits are now stated plainly instead of being papered over: the cooperative Stop needs the solver callback the cloud bundle's Piccolissimo does not forward, and re-rollout verification is skipped for cloud runs.

## Tests

- Promotion proven by a `--julia` that writes a sentinel file if it ever runs — it doesn't, and `AMICODE_FINISHED` comes from FakeCloud.
- Explicit `--executor local` still exits 64; the no-`--spec` path is covered (the gate never runs there).
- Disconnected promotion refuses and names the Connections panel.
- Template staging: hp → `altissimo`, piccolo → `ipopt`, agent and grants point at the same staged file, and the **shipped** template is asserted to keep its placeholder inside a string.
- The cloud location label is proven end-to-end in `remote_statemachine.test.ts`: a real `RemoteExecutor.submit` writes the `remote.json` the label reads.

941 amico-run tests and the extension suite pass. The two `slow/*_e2e` tests need a live model provider and fail identically on `main`.

author: tesseractaz
body:
## The correction

v1.70.0 attributed the on-peak grid draw to `smartBackupMode: 2` on the Smart Home Panel. **That was wrong.** The real cause is **"Charge Now" — a PER-DPU setting** in the EcoFlow app, enabled on individual Delta Pro Ultra units.

The evidence is unambiguous. When Charge Now was switched off:

```
grid import      16.6 kW  ->  0 W
smartBackupMode        2  ->  2      (unchanged)
backupReserveSoc      10  ->  10     (unchanged)
timeTask.isEnabled false  ->  false  (unchanged)
```

Every field in the SHP2 strategy blob was byte-identical across the transition. The setting is not on the panel — which also explains the ~16 kW magnitude: several Cores each pulling their own AC charge simultaneously, not one panel-level decision.

## What changes

- **Attribution corrected** in the module docs, DOCS.md §7.9, and — most importantly — the operator-facing alert text, which previously sent the reader to a panel setting that had nothing to do with it.
- **The alert now names which Cores are drawing.** With a per-unit setting, "which Core" is the actionable part. Attribution uses each DPU's `acInWatts` — the same field `aggregateFleetFlow` sums into `acIn`, so parts reconcile with the total. Cores under 500 W are standby and not named.

```
Drawing   Core 1 (7.2 kW), Core 3 (4.4 kW)
```

## The design point this vindicates

Nothing in the SHP2 strategy, and no DPU field this add-on projects, exposes Charge Now. It is **invisible in telemetry** — which is exactly why the detector infers from power flow rather than reading a mode flag. A flag-reading implementation was never buildable.

## Verification

- `tsc` clean (server src + test config), **1891 / 1891 tests pass**
- `scripts/mutate-peak-grid-draw.mjs` — **15 / 15 mutants killed**, including two new attribution mutants: reversing the sort (naming the least guilty Core first) and listing idle Cores as culprits.

author: jasonwarta
body:
**Draft** — follow-up to the merged Aurora Skills dataset. Adds the Q2→feedback→Q3 loop, rubric **v0.9** alignment, and **false-positive discrimination traps**. Scoring is owned by `team-assess`, not this dataset.

## The loop (data-side only — no scores here)

`team-assess` scores Q2 → recommendations → the team enacts them in Q3 → `team-assess` scores Q3. This dataset provides the **data and the loop map**, not the scores:
- `assessments/q2-anticipated-recommendations.md` — the recommendations the Q2 dysfunctions should surface + the Q3 artifacts that answer each (score-free).
- `assessments/five-dysfunctions-signal-map.json` — every seeded signal → rubric v0.9 dimension + observable OBM facet + verbatim act, before vs after.
- What's asserted: objective data metrics (talk-time, reopen counts, survey values). What's **not** asserted: any 1–5 dysfunction score.

## Discrimination traps (false positives)

The set is not all clean signals — labeled traps a shallow scorer misreads (`ground_truth.json → discrimination_traps`):
- **artificial_harmony** — a user-facing cut decided with zero debate (looks decisive; is Fear of Conflict).
- **heated_but_healthy** — interrupt-heavy debate that resolves with repair (looks toxic; is healthy). Splits the interruption signal into dominance vs healthy.
- **reopen_with_new_information** — a reopen justified by a district dropping out (looks like relitigation; is healthy revisiting).
- **Greg Olsen** — a genuinely disengaged contractor (silent + absent + empty agreement + status-as-activity), the contrast to Naomi's silent-but-engaged.

## Q3 expanded + dominance nuance

- Q3 grows 7 → 15 meetings; each Q2 recommendation is enacted across multiple artifacts.
- Per-meeting `led_by` / `dominant_is_lead` / `dominance_expected`: a lead running a small session reads as expected, not a red flag; headline dominance is over substantial (≥5) meetings.

## Also

- `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-05-simulated-team-data-workflow.md` — reusable workflow spec.
- `claude-impact-lab-logo.png` at repo root (typo corrected from source `imapct`).

## Integrity

Seeded metrics computed from authored `content` turns only; all 33 meetings ≥15 min; deterministic regen via `generate.py`.

The Organizational Instrument is frozen at v1.1. Eleven scored items across three dimensions, two of which set your quadrant. Options weight one, two and three. A dimension reads high only when its mean is strictly above 2.0, and the cases that sit on the boundary have a stated rule rather than a judgment call.

author: z0u
body:
Closes #73.

Three batches in the order the issue lays out, each its own commit with the full `./go check` run after it, so a regression is attributable to one batch.

| Batch | Commit | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Patch bumps + lint-staged | `a695bb3` | green |
| 2. ruff + scipy-stubs | `2eabd62` | green |
| 3. jax + numpy + huggingface-hub | `716af03` | green, **but the numerics move — see below** |

Batch 3 is last and self-contained, so batches 1 and 2 can land without it.

## The memo-key question

**Package versions do not feed the memo key, and a JAX bump does change the numbers.** Both halves were checked, and the briefed framing holds.

Static half: `_is_project_file` excludes site-packages, so no library source ever reaches the manifest, and `task_key_parts` builds identity from the fn's module-qualified name plus an input fingerprint. Checked directly on a task that imports jax — no `jax`, `jaxlib`, or version string appears anywhere in the key or in the validity evidence (`code_fp`, `deps`, `version`).

Empirical half: 150 steps of the real `train_step` on nGPT d64-L4, fixed seed, fixed batches, three single-use L4 containers per version, `us-east`, with the same `XLA_FLAGS` that `[tool.mini] env` ships.

| jax / jaxlib | distinct digests | digest | final loss |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0.10.1 | 1 of 3 | `e4b7c106…` | 5.531451225280762 |
| 0.11.0 | 1 of 3 | `884ee00c…` | 5.531452655792236 |

So 0.11 is exactly as reproducible as 0.10 — it just lands about one part in 4×10⁶ away. That is the same magnitude as the nondeterminism the `XLA_FLAGS` were introduced to remove, which is the part worth sitting with: the flags buy reproducibility *within* a pinned environment, not across one.

The consequence is the unhelpful direction of the two. A spuriously invalidated key would be harmless — just a re-run. Instead the key is stable while the result underneath it is not: a DONE record written under 0.10.1 keeps serving its old number after the upgrade, and a task re-run for any unrelated reason quietly writes a different one under the key that already meant the old.

Nothing is done about that here beyond writing it down (`eng/determinism.md`, alongside the existing reasoning for why `XLA_FLAGS` stay out of the fingerprint) and a backlog entry with three options: fold pinned numerics packages into the evidence, warn when a record's `compute_env` numerics differ from the current environment (cheap, detection-only, probably the right first move), or keep it manual via `version=`. **Worth an explicit decision before batch 3 merges** — the honest choices are to accept that records straddle two regimes and say so where the numbers are published, or to bump `version=` on the affected tasks.

Caveat the doc already flags: determinism is a per-device-class property, so this is an L4 result and says nothing about other GPUs. Both measurements used the same probe, so the digests are comparable to each other but not to the `6d18d792…` in `eng/determinism.md`, which came from a differently-parameterised probe that was never checked in.

## Batch notes

**lint-staged 15 → 17** needed the manifest edit the issue predicted; `npm update` could not move it past `^15`. The hook still fires and both ruff tasks run (verified on a throwaway commit). Its dependency tree shrank a lot — hence the large `package-lock.json` diff.

**ty 0.0.65** resolves `eqx.filter_jit`-wrapped signatures more precisely than 0.0.63, surfacing six real annotation diagnostics: `sample_batches` yields numpy, `eval_step` declared jax `Array`. Correct at runtime — jit converts on the way in — but the annotation was narrower than the contract, so the boundary widens to `ArrayLike` and narrows once inside. Bisected to ty alone, with stubs held fixed.

**ruff 0.16** began formatting fenced code blocks inside Markdown, reaching 11 docs and reading them as runnable code rather than illustration — most visibly collapsing the multi-line method chain that `style-py` exists to *teach*, because the one-liner fits in 120 columns. `*.md` is now excluded from ruff, restoring 0.15 behaviour. No Python source moved under the new formatter, so the upgrade is otherwise a no-op for us.

**huggingface-hub 1.26** got the end-to-end exercise the issue asked for: the network-gated `test_hf_store.py` suite passes against the real bucket (7 passed, 1 skipped), covering CAS round-trips, refs, and the publish tier. It retires `HfFolder`, which we never used.

**numpy 2.5** stubs made two `savez_compressed` suppressions in the M1 notebooks unnecessary, and ty fails on an unused ignore, so they go. That shifts those two tasks' code fingerprints; both are `publish_results` steps in frozen M1 experiments, so the cost is a cheap re-run if anyone ever drives them again.

## One thing not resolved

`tests/sca/test_training.py::test_progress_emitted_during_training` failed once under `-n auto` on a loaded container, then passed on the next three full-suite runs and on a serial re-run. Nothing in the upgraded packages touches mini's progress debouncer, and `BackgroundEmitter.close` flushes synchronously, so it reads as a pre-existing race in the test's queue-content assertion — but that is reasoning, not evidence, and I could not reproduce it to confirm. Logged in `todo-eng.md` with what is and isn't known.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

author: pathgao
body:
Marking a numbered item as a bullet left the number behind: `1. foo`
became `- 1. foo` (#451). All three list toggles put their prefix on the
line, and only the numbered one took anything off first — its
`line.replace(/^(?:[-*+]|\d+\.)\s+/, "")` is why the reverse direction,
bullet to numbered, looked correct.

A bullet, an ordered number and a task box claim the same slot at the
head of a line, so the reported case is one of a family. The two
unreported siblings that shipped with it: checklist on `1. foo` gave
`- [ ] 1. foo`, and checklist on `- foo` gave `- [ ] - foo`. Two more
sit on the removal side, where the bullet toggle's `/^[-*+]\s+/` also
matches a checklist item — bullet on `- [ ] foo` un-toggled it down to
the orphan `[ ] foo`, and the numbered toggle stripped the dash but not
the box, producing `1. [ ] foo`, a state whose own un-toggle then yields
`[ ] foo` as well. A mixed selection hit the same wall: bullet over
`- a` and `1. b` gave `- - a` and `- 1. b`.

`shouldRemove` itself is right — removal should need every content line
to carry this tool's own marker — and once applying displaces
competitors, a mixed selection converges on one list type rather than
stacking markers. It only needed the bullet and numbered patterns to
stop claiming a checklist line as their own.

Quote is deliberately left as it was. `> - foo` is a quoted list item
and `> 1. foo` a quoted numbered one; both are legitimate Markdown, and
that nesting is exactly what pressing quote on a list item is for. So
the rule encoded here is not "strip whatever was there" but "a list
marker displaces a competing list marker; a block-level wrapper does
not".

Rather than repeat a strip regex at each call site, the three
near-identical toggles in `Editor.svelte` (`toggleLinePrefix`,
`toggleHeading`, `toggleNumberedList`) collapse into one table in
`utils/editorToolbar.ts`, keyed by the toolbar ids the actions already
register: every entry says which marker it owns, how it renders, and
what it competes with (`null` for quote; headings against headings).
That is also what makes the transform reachable from `scripts/` —
`Editor.svelte` cannot be imported by the test runner, so a matrix of
28 input/output pairs would otherwise have been unwritable. The
extraction is deliberately minimal: only the line-marker toggling moved,
and the heading rows reproduce the old behaviour exactly, `# - foo`
included — a heading is not a list toggle, so it displaces nothing but
headings.

Seven matrix rows and the mixed-selection case fail against the code
they replace.

Trade-off: turning a checklist item into a bullet or a numbered item now
drops the box, checked state included, instead of stranding it. The
three list types are alternatives in one slot, so keeping `[x]` would
mean minting a fourth form that the checklist toggle does not recognise.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>


---

## Transitions

| input | bullet | numbered | checklist |
|---|---|---|---|
| `1. foo` | `- foo` *(was `- 1. foo`)* — #451 | — | `- [ ] foo` *(was `- [ ] 1. foo`)* |
| `- foo` | `foo` | `1. foo` | `- [ ] foo` *(was `- [ ] - foo`)* |
| `- [ ] foo` | `- foo` *(was `[ ] foo`)* | `1. foo` *(was `1. [ ] foo`)* | `foo` |
| `- [x] foo` | `- foo` *(was `[x] foo`)* | `1. foo` | `foo` |
| `> foo`, `# foo` | unchanged | unchanged | unchanged |

## Verification

    npm test        631 / 631   (598 before; +33)
    npm run check   638 files, 0 errors, 0 warnings
    cargo test      154 / 154
    npm audit       0 vulnerabilities

Reverting the fix and keeping the tests turns **8 red** — the seven matrix rows
above plus mixed selection — and leaves all five quote rows and all five heading
rows green, which is the evidence that neither was touched.

Also exercised by hand in a local macOS build: `- [ ] foo` → `- foo` → `foo` →
`- foo` → `foo` across four clicks of the bullet button.

## Not covered

None of the toggles has ever handled leading indentation (`  - nested`), a
space-less marker (`>tight`), or `1)` as an ordered delimiter. That is detection
breadth rather than marker competition, and widening it would change quote and
heading behaviour too — left alone deliberately.

author: gsdali
body:
## Summary

`AAG.buildGraph()` (`Sources/OCCTSwift/FeatureRecognition.swift`) read `Shape.faces()`, the deduplicated (`IsSame`-keyed) enumeration that keeps only the first orientation a shared face is reached in. `AAGNode.isHorizontal`/`isUpward`/`isDownward`/`isVertical`/`zLevel` are all derived from that node's normal, so which orientation survived the dedup silently decided the answer. `AAG.detectPockets()` selects floors on exactly those fields, so `Shape.detectPocketsAAG()` reported a different pocket count for the identical geometry depending only on which order two solids were compounded in.

This is #614's defect (a normal-derived value losing information across `faces()`'s dedup collapse) surviving in a fourth consumer that PR #631 did not reach, because AAG was never enumerated as one of #631's "geometry consumers".

**Fixed** by moving `buildGraph()` onto `Shape.orientedFaces()`: a face shared between two solids in a compound is now two nodes, one per owning solid, each carrying that solid's own normal, rather than one node carrying whichever normal the dedup happened to keep. `AAGNode` gains `distinctFaceIndex`, the node's position in the old `faces()` enumeration, so a caller can still tell the two sides of a shared face apart or recover the old one-node-per-distinct-face view. `buildGraph()` also skips building a graph edge between the two occurrences of one shared face: without that guard, `OCCTFacesAreAdjacent` (which compares edge sets by `IsSame`, ignoring orientation) reports every one of a shared face's own boundary edges as adjacent to itself.

## Before / after (both compound orders, same geometry)

Origin-centred 10mm box cut through z=4, recompounded in both member orders (the horizontal-cut fixture; see "the correction" below for why this fixture, not a vertical cut, is required):

| | order A | order B |
|---|---|---|
| `detectPocketsAAG().count`, before | 1 | 2 |
| `detectPocketsAAG().count`, after | 2 | 2 |
| AAG upward+horizontal node indices, before | `[2, 8]` | `[2]` |
| AAG upward+horizontal node indices, after | `[2, 8]` | `[2, 8]` |
| `buildAAG().nodes.count`, before | 11 | 11 |
| `buildAAG().nodes.count`, after | 12 | 12 |

No regression: on a plain box (nothing shared) and on #614's own vertical-cut fixture, `buildAAG()`/`detectPocketsAAG()` are unchanged before and after, since `orientedFaces()` equals `faces()` exactly whenever nothing is shared.

## The correction Cluster A's census caught

This issue's own text says the defect reproduces on "PR #631's own two-solid split fixture". Cluster A's census (#664, `Scripts/repro/cluster-a-subshape-enumeration/`) found that fixture is a **vertical** cut, whose shared wall's normal is horizontal-axis, so it never reaches `isHorizontal()`/`isUpward()` at all and does not exercise this defect. The fixture that reproduces it is a **horizontal** cut (an origin-centred 10mm box cut through z=4), which is what this PR's regression test and the census's own `main.swift` use. Re-running the census after the fix confirmed the headline numbers now agree in both orders; the committed census README is updated in place with the post-fix table and says so explicitly.

## A second, different, pre-existing defect found while verifying the fix

Verifying order-independence on the vertical-cut fixture (which #642 does not reproduce on) surfaced a different, unrelated defect: `detectPocketsAAG().count` there moved from agreeing (1/1) to disagreeing (1/2) across compound order. Confirmed by temporarily reverting `buildGraph()` alone that this asymmetry already existed **before** this fix and only cancelled out to the same total by coincidence. Root mechanism: `OCCTFacesAreAdjacent`/`OCCTEdgeGetConvexity` have no concept of solid membership, so a face occurrence's adjacency/convexity is checked against every topologically coincident neighbor, including one that belongs to a different solid than the occurrence's own orientation; doubling the shared wall's node count (this fix) made the pre-existing ambiguity fire more often. This is a different mechanism than #642 (a graph lacking solid-membership tracking, not a normal losing information across a dedup collapse), out of scope for this issue, and documented rather than fixed in `Scripts/repro/cluster-a-subshape-enumeration/README.md`'s new "Update following #642's fix" section. Recommend a follow-up issue.

## Prove-the-test-fails matrix

All 7 new tests in `Tests/OCCTModelingTests/Issue642AAGNodeIdentityTests.swift`, each broken and restored per `okf/policies/prove-the-test-fails.md`:

| Injection | Result |
|---|---|
| Revert `orientedFaces()` back to `faces()` in `buildGraph()` | 5 of 7 fail red (`detectPocketsAgreesAcrossOrder`, `upwardHorizontalCountAgreesAcrossOrder`, `nodeCountMatchesOrientedFaces`, `sharedWallNodesShareDistinctIndexAndOpposeUpward`, `sharedWallNodesAreNotMutualNeighbors`). The 2 no-regression tests (`plainBoxUnaffected`, `verticalCutFixtureUpwardHorizontalUnaffected`) correctly still pass, since neither exercises the collapse this injection targets |
| Restore `orientedFaces()`, remove only the `distinctFaceIndex` adjacency guard | Exactly 1 of 7 fails red (`sharedWallNodesAreNotMutualNeighbors`, showing the self-loop: `AAGEdge(face1Index: 2, face2Index: 10, ..., sharedEdgeCount: 4)`), the other 6 unaffected |
| Both restored | All 7 pass |

## Docs

- `SEMVER.md`: new recorded exception (silent behaviour change, no compile error), since this PR is unreleased.
- `CHANGELOG.md`: entry under "Pass 1b of the #377 duplication audit".
- `docs/reference/FeatureRecognition.md`: `AAGNode`, `AAG`, `buildAAG()`, `detectPocketsAAG()` sections updated with the node-identity change and a runnable snippet each.
- `///` doc comments + fenced `swift` snippets on `AAGNode`, `AAG`, `Shape.buildAAG()`, `Shape.detectPocketsAAG()`.

## Verification

- Clean `swift build`: 0 errors, 0 warnings in changed files, no `OCCTSWIFT_LOCAL`.
- Full `swift test`, no env overrides: **5327 tests, 0 failures** (baseline 5320 + 7 new).
- All four gate scripts exit 0 (`check-bridge-index`, `check-null-handle-guards`, `check-docs-defaults`, `count-operations`), plus the three `--self-test`s.
- Census re-run (`swift run ClusterACensus`); table matches the updated README exactly.
- Zero em-dashes in all added/changed text.

## Out of scope (per the task)

- `edges()`'s own collapse is #638's call, not touched here.
- `nbEdges`/`nbFaces`/`nbVertices` vs their docs is #651's call, not touched here.
- The newly-found cross-solid adjacency defect on the vertical-cut fixture is documented, not fixed, and recommended as a follow-up issue.

Closes #642

author: basilechretien
body:
Three harnesses aimed at failure shapes this project has repeated, rather than at
hypothetical ones.

## An exemption has to prove itself

The recurring defect here is not a wrong regex. It is an escape hatch whose first version
*believed its own claim*:

- `composed` exempted a table cell without checking the exemption described it, so an entry
  declaring an empty template exempted whatever the cell actually said.
- `Verbatim`'s docstring asserted a script could not build one. It was an ordinary
  importable dataclass.
- `file_sha256` scoping was a way to review one file and pass, until `review-uncovered` was
  invented alongside it.
- Composed `parts` were folded into one project-wide allowlist, so a phantom entry in an
  empty table whitelisted its strings in a different fragment.

Every one was found by a reviewer or by opening a file, never by a test.

`tests/data/exemptions.yaml` lists all fourteen places the toolkit agrees not to look, what
each stops checking, and the test that claims it falsely and expects to be caught. The build
fails if an entry has no such test, if the named test does not exist, or if it does not
pass.

It checks **both directions**, and the second is the one that rots: each exemption's
spelling is looked for in the source, so granting one in code and leaving it off the list
fails too. A list that only grows when somebody remembers is the same "not checked looks
like checked" this repository keeps finding.

It earned its place on the first run by finding that the **code-list exemption had no abuse
test at all**. Written in this PR.

## Assert on the artefact, not on what should have produced it

Both annotated-copy defects had passing tests asserting an intermediate. The highlight never
rendered — the test checked the character styles were *defined* in `styles.xml`, which
stayed true while OOXML discarded them, since a run carries one `w:rStyle` and pandoc's Link
writer had already taken it. And the copy had no tables, because only value bindings were
substituted.

`tests/test_artifact.py` unzips what was built and asserts what a reader would see:
highlights present and coloured, tables and figure there, no placeholder surviving to the
page, the source digest and paragraph identifiers travelling inside the file.

## The example is the spec

`code_list()` existed for a day with nothing in `example/` using it — the one API added to
make a reporting requirement satisfiable, absent from the artefact that demonstrates the
toolkit. Now checked.

## Test plan

- [x] `pytest -q` — 856 passed, 2 skipped (R and Zotero present locally)
- [x] `ruff check src tests`
- [x] Exemption inventory verified to fail when an abuse test is renamed away
- [ ] CI green on this PR before merge

First PR under the worktree-and-PR workflow, rather than pushing to `main`.

author: egorfedorov
body:
Closes the last two items of epic #41 — section D, the new capabilities.

## Self-learning tool costs (#38)

MCP and Agent costs were constants someone picked once: `mcp__*` ≈ 200 tokens in, `Agent` ≈ 500. Real results vary by orders of magnitude — a "list all issues" query and a one-row lookup are the same tool name and nowhere near the same cost. On MCP-heavy sessions **the budget meter was guessing at its own biggest line item.**

PostToolUse already measured the real `tool_response` size; it just threw it away. Now it remembers.

- **EMA (α=0.25), not a flat mean** — a tool that genuinely gets more expensive is tracked, not averaged away. `max` and `total` kept alongside for the report.
- **Holds off until 3 samples** so one freak 200K response can't become "the estimate".
- **Only guessed tools.** `Read`/`Edit`/`Write` compute their estimate from real arguments; an average would be strictly worse.
- Table capped at 200 tools (least-observed pruned), writes file-locked, a failed learn never fails the hook.
- New `/cco-tools` sorts by total spend — usually the honest answer to "where does my context actually go".

Verified end to end: `200` (constant) → `44,688` (learned) after 3 observations, and correctly `null` at 1–2 samples.

## Team pattern sharing (#37)

Patterns were locked to one machine, so a teammate's fresh clone started blind and re-learned the same lessons by wasting the same tokens.

```bash
/cco-patterns export     # → .cco/patterns.digest.json — commit it
/cco-patterns import     # teammate, day one
```

**The privacy boundary is the feature**, so it got the most attention:

- Digest carries **relative paths and counts only** — no file contents, no absolute paths, no home directory.
- Entries that can't be expressed relative to the project root are **dropped and counted**, not best-effort-sanitized.
- A path merely sharing a prefix with the root (`/p/proj-secret` vs `/p/proj`) is correctly treated as **outside**.
- `auditDigest()` runs before writing **and on import** — the file came from somewhere else. A digest with absolute paths, traversal, or string values where only counts belong is **rejected, not cleaned**.

**Imported data never touches local counts.** It lives in `proj.imported`, a separate prior. `confidence` means "how many sessions *I* observed this in" — folding in someone else's sessions would make the user's own numbers a lie. The prior is consulted only where there's no local observation (the fresh-clone case), and merges take the stronger signal, so importing twice is a no-op.

Wired to a real consumer so it isn't inert: on a first read with no local history, the tracker surfaces the shared verdict, explicitly labelled as shared.

## Verification

- **274 tests pass**, up from 238 — weighted toward the privacy boundary and the imported-never-overrides-local invariant.
- Real export on this repo: 42 files, 69 outside-root entries correctly dropped, digest audited clean (`grep` for `/Users/`, `/home/`, username → 0 hits).
- Full import round-trip against a simulated fresh clone.
- This repo now ships its own `.cco/patterns.digest.json` as a live example.

author: ochola-eddyphil
body:
Refs #227

Exact-main run 30963791293 exposed two concrete problems in the otherwise stable tiered CI design: the product database job exhausted its 10-minute timeout during a slow fresh migration, and main qualification spent a third full schema build on the unrelated main_extended safeguards. The run ended cancelled after 15m54s even though required fresh/populated parity and deterministic smoke passed.

This keeps the required main contract unchanged: product database, fresh/populated upgrade parity, Lambda smoke, and deterministic benchmark smoke. It gives the product database job a 15-minute failure bound for slow storage, while removing the third extended database from main.

The embedding-rotation and role safeguards are preserved in the existing manual migration-compatibility workflow, on that workflow’s single CockroachDB server. Normal workflow and CI-contract edits still select static/unit only and cannot force database, main qualification, frontend, Lambda, or Terraform jobs on the PR path.

The required main path completes locally in 5m28s after this change; the relocated extended safeguard completes separately in the manual tier.

body: This pull request was posted by Claude Code using claude-opus-5 on behalf of David. Adds one rule to `agent_docs/api-design.md`, immediately after `rule:72`. ### Why `rule:72` says to promote settings to base classes *when 2-3+ providers support them*. That gives the threshold at which changing a shared thing is right — but on its own it reads as permission, with nothing stating the guard below the threshold. One new caller is not a threshold. The gap is not hypothetical. While working on #4221 (adding a `ContextWindowExceeded` exception), the natural-looking way to make the new exception behave correctly was to rewrite `FallbackModel`'s public `fallback_on` default so it would exclude the new type. That's a shared, public default being reshaped to accommodate a single new class — the tail wagging the dog. Nothing in the guidelines pushed back on it. The closest existing text is in the root `AGENTS.md`: > Do not refactor a shared protocol, helper, or abstraction to fix one caller unless the narrow fix is unavailable or the refactor is itself the confirmed fix but it's the tail of a bullet that opens *"for a bug fix, make the narrowest change that resolves the reported, reproduced behavior"*, so it reads as bug-fix-scoped and doesn't fire on a feature PR. This states it as its own rule, in the guide agents are told to read when designing public APIs. Worth noting the rule permits the change once it stands on its own: #4221 does end up changing that default, but as a deliberate behavior change with its own tests, docs, and follow-up issue (#7139) — not as a prop for a class hierarchy. That distinction is the point. ### One question for a maintainer `agent_docs/` looks generated — `index.md` opens with ``, and the directory was created wholesale in #4501. Every other bullet carries a `` id from that corpus. I deliberately did **not** invent an id, so this is visibly hand-added rather than masquerading as extracted. Two things I can't tell from outside: 1. Will a hand-added rule survive the next braindump run, or get dropped? 2. Is there a source-of-truth upstream of the generated markdown that this should be added to instead? Happy to move it wherever it actually belongs — including closing this and feeding the rule into the corpus, if that's the right path. - [ ] Review AI generated code

author: lifted-truck
body:
## The overload was mine, and it was 234 % of real time

The render loop made **three trig calls per oscillator per sample** — and **two of them computed a constant.** Pan depends only on `x[m]`, partial parity and width, none of which change per sample.

Measured on the isolated inner loop at 2016 oscillators (6 voices × 48 partials × 7 cloud):

| | to render 1 s of audio | real-time load |
|---|---|---|
| before | 2336 ms | **234 %** |
| after | 435 ms | **43 %** |

**5.4×.** At 234 % it simply could not keep up, which is exactly what you heard.

Then an **oscillator budget** that thins the *cloud* on the highest partials first rather than dropping partials — partial count is the brightness lever we want free to raise, and a top partial with fewer beating voices is far less audible than a missing one. Worst case goes 2016 → 636 oscillators, **76 % → 36 %** in the real engine. The cost is shown, not hidden: live oscillator count plus a flag when the budget bites.

## Why it feels static, in one measurement

With sustained K, mean R climbs to 0.96 in the first second and then **sits at 0.96 forever**:

```
static K:    0.67  0.96  0.96  0.96  0.96  0.96  0.96  0.96
```

Nothing changes after the attack. That's the whole complaint, and it points straight at the fix — the engine's distinctive mechanism (cascade) *already* reorders the spectrum, but it fires once and is over.

## Three candidates, all default off, all measured

**Lock wave — cascade made cyclic.** A travelling band of coupling ping-pongs along the partial series, so *which* partials are locked keeps changing:

```
lock wave:   0.57  0.78  0.75  0.87  0.85  0.94  0.94  0.83   (R-spread across partials)
```

**This is the headline candidate.** Cascade measured as the strongest and most distinctive control in the engine, and its only limitation was being a one-shot. Making it periodic turns the one mechanism a detuned saw bank *structurally cannot imitate* into a continuous animator. On the raster it's a diagonal that comes back.

**Per-partial drift** — SPECTRA has none at all, and SAW's drift is most of why SAW feels alive. Each partial gets its own slow rate; measured −8.4 ¢ of movement.

**R → tone** — makes the coupling audible in *timbre* rather than only in beating; a partial lifts or ducks as its cloud locks. Peak 0.496 → 0.737 (lift) / 0.366 (duck).

## Suggested starting patch

`partials 16 · K 0.75 · lock wave 100 % @ 2 s/sweep · drift 6 ¢ @ 0.4 Hz · R→tone +0.5` — that's what the screenshot patch was, and the raster shows the wave clearly.

`./verify fast` exit 0. Sine table max error 3e-7.

## Open — yours

Which of the three earn their place; brightness direction (raise partial count vs commit to dark); and whether the lock wave is a new parameter or a mode of the existing cascade.

author: lukebrooker
body:
Three gaps found while working through the Dependabot PRs. Each let a problem accumulate without anyone being told.

## `.cjs` / `.mjs` were never formatted

The `format` globs are `{ts,tsx,js,jsx,json,css,md}` — no `.cjs`/`.mjs`. But eslint **does** lint those files and applies `prettier/prettier` to them.

So they could only ever be fixed by hand. That's exactly what the prettier 3.9 bump in #82 hit: `svg-to-spot-illustration.cjs` failed lint, and `pnpm format` couldn't fix it.

Seven files sit in that gap:

```
docs/next.config.mjs
docs/postcss.config.cjs
packages/components/scripts/check-dts.mjs
packages/components/scripts/generate-package-exports.mjs
packages/components/scripts/svg-to-spot-illustration.cjs
packages/widgets/scripts/check-dts.mjs
scripts/prepare.mjs          ← root; neither linted nor formatted, left as-is
```

They're all clean today, so this is preventative — it stops the same manual fix recurring on every prettier bump.

## `format:check` wasn't in CI at all

CI ran `lint typecheck test` and `build`, never `format:check`. eslint's prettier rule only covers files eslint lints, so **markdown and JSON drifted silently** — several docs files and a CHANGELOG were already out of style on `main` before this branch.

Added as a step in `check`, deliberately not `--affected`.

## Bundle size only checked one package

CI ran `size:check` for `components` only. `widgets` has been over budget for some time with nothing reporting it:

| entry | limit | actual |
|---|---|---|
| `cart-drawer/core` | 1.6 KB | **1.96 KB** |
| `cart-drawer/react` | 8 KB | **8.96 KB** |
| `cart-drawer/vue` | 11 KB | **13.46 KB** |

I checked whether this was real growth or a measurement change from the size-limit 12→13 bump in #86 — it isn't the bump. The same overage reproduces on `main` with size-limit 12, identical numbers.

The limits were set at the initial widgets release (`b0d8b405`) and never revisited, while real features landed since: the CartExpiryDialogs rework, the full "x tickets" count pill, badge width work. So the budgets are stale rather than the code bloated.

Raised to current plus ~5–8% headroom — enough that a genuine regression still trips, not a blank cheque:

```
cart-drawer/core   1.6 KB  → 2.1 KB
cart-drawer/react  8 KB    → 9.5 KB
cart-drawer/vue    11 KB   → 14.5 KB
```

And switched CI to `pnpm -r size:check` so widgets is actually covered. (`turbo.json` has no `size:check` task, hence `pnpm -r` rather than `turbo`.)

## Verification

Build, typecheck, lint, `format:check`, `pnpm -r size:check`, all 966 tests, and `pnpm audit` pass. `ci.yml` parses and both jobs resolve.

No changeset: tooling and CI configuration only, plus size budgets. Nothing reaches published package output.

body:
Two things you spotted.

## The bar never went down

Once your stocks were capped the bar was pinned full and every hit's charge was thrown away — but spending a stock only took the pip, so the bar stayed full and the very next punch banked the stock straight back.

Spending now empties a bar that was *pinned*, while a bar you'd genuinely part-filled is left exactly where it was. Both cases are tested.

## Far less on the floor

Two in five enemies used to drop something, and the horde stock used the same table — forty of them a wave, so the street ended up carpeted.

| | drop chance |
|---|---|
| Wannabee (horde stock) | ~1 in 13 |
| Named enemy | ~1 in 5 |
| Crate | halved |
| Boss | always, floor cap or not — that's the one you worked for |

Plus a hard cap: nothing drops at all once five pickups are already lying about waiting to be walked over. Clearing a whole horde wave in a browser now leaves **four** things on the ground.

## 📝 작업 내용
- `RefreshTokenStore` 포트와 구현 2종(Redis 운영용 / 인메모리 테스트용). **엔드포인트는 없다** — 로그인·재발급·로그아웃 API 가 쓸 부품이다.
- 리프레시 토큰의 "지금 살아 있는 목록"을 서버가 따로 든다. 발급된 JWT 는 취소할 수 없어서 로그아웃해도 만료 시각까지 통하기 때문이다.
- Redis 키 2종: 개별 토큰 `refresh:{memberId}:{jti}`(TTL 자동 소멸) + 일괄 폐기용 jti Set `refresh:{memberId}`.

---

## 🖥️ 프론트엔드 연동 가이드 (API 명세)

**해당 없음** — 저장소 계층이라 엔드포인트가 없다. 프론트 영향 없음.

다만 동작에 영향을 주는 것 하나: **로그아웃하면 리프레시 토큰이 즉시 무효**가 된다. 지금까지는 서버가 취소할 방법이 없어 만료까지 통했다.

---

## 🚨 주요 에러 코드 및 예외 (Exceptions)

이 PR 자체는 예외를 던지지 않는다. 이 저장소를 쓰는 재발급 API 가 다음을 내릴 예정이다.
- `AU-004` REFRESH_TOKEN_INVALID : 목록에 없는 토큰
- `AU-005` REFRESH_TOKEN_REUSED : 재사용 탐지 → `revokeAllByMember` 로 전체 세션 폐기

---

## 💡 백엔드 리뷰 포인트 (Backend Review)

- **아키텍처 및 도메인:** 포트를 인터페이스로 둔 이유가 두 가지다. (1) 테스트가 H2 로 돌고 Redis 가 없어 인메모리 구현을 끼운다. (2) **인수인계 담당이 오프보딩 트랜잭션에서 `revokeAllByMember` 를 호출**한다 — 계약에 의존해야 그쪽 코드가 Redis 를 몰라도 된다. 시그니처 이대로 괜찮은지 봐주세요.
- **여기를 봐주세요 ① Set TTL 을 늘리기만 한다:** 계획서 초안은 매 `save` 마다 `expire(setKey, ttl)` 로 덮었는데, 그러면 짧은 토큰이 긴 토큰의 Set 수명을 깎습니다.
  ```
  기기 A: keepSignedIn=true(14일) 로그인 → Set TTL 14일
  기기 B: keepSignedIn=false(1일) 로그인 → Set TTL 1일로 축소
  1일 뒤 Set 소멸. 그런데 A 의 개별 키는 13일 남음
  → revokeAllByMember 가 지울 jti 목록을 못 찾아 A 의 토큰이 살아남음
  ```
  일괄 폐기는 재사용 탐지·오프보딩에서 쓰므로 조용히 실패하면 안 됩니다. `extendAtLeast()` 로 TTL 을 늘리기만 하게 바꿨습니다. `getExpire` 가 -1(TTL 없음)/-2(키 없음) 를 주는 경우도 새로 거는 쪽으로 처리했는데, 이 분기가 맞는지 봐주세요.
- **여기를 봐주세요 ② `KEYS`/`SCAN` 을 쓰지 않습니다:** 일괄 폐기를 하려면 그 사람의 jti 를 알아야 하는데 훑기는 운영 Redis 를 멈추게 합니다. 그래서 Set 을 따로 둡니다. 개별 키가 Set 보다 먼저 사라져 Set 에 죽은 jti 가 남을 수 있지만, `exists()` 가 개별 키를 보므로 판정에는 영향이 없습니다.
- **우려되는 부분이나 고민:**
  - `RedisRefreshTokenStore` 에 단위 테스트가 없습니다. 실 Redis 가 필요하고 저장소에 Testcontainers 가 없습니다. 계약은 인메모리로 고정했고 실제 동작은 로그인 API 이후 로컬 Redis 로 수동 검증할 계획입니다. **Testcontainers 를 도입할지 팀 의견 듣고 싶습니다.**
  - 인메모리 구현에 `@Component` 를 일부러 붙이지 않았습니다. 운영에 섞여 들어가면 인스턴스마다 목록이 갈려 한쪽에서 로그아웃한 토큰이 다른 쪽에서 통합니다.
  - 이 PR 은 #50·#51 과 **의존 관계가 없습니다.** develop 에서 바로 분기했고 단독으로 빌드 그린입니다.

---

Per-user settings now live in the Supabase user_settings table instead of env/file only. cmd/set-settings populates the row (profile + Gmail app password); the password is AES-256-GCM encrypted at rest, with the in-DB data key itself wrapped by NEXUS_SETTINGS_MASTER_KEY (double-sealed).

author: ats314
body:
Three things: ring-specific sound with the inner tracks reading hotter, a bigger arena, and the graphics that make those two say the same thing.

## The sound

Nothing about the payout differs between rings, so the only honest way to say *"inside is hotter"* is to make it **sound** hotter. Hopping inward now moves three things at once:

| | hats per bar | your voice | pad cutoff |
|---|---|---|---|
| outer | 3 | sawtooth, 784 Hz | 1490 Hz |
| mid | 7 | square, 1046 Hz | 1757 Hz |
| inner | 11 | square, 1318 Hz | 2113 Hz |

Your line **rises 9 semitones** and hardens from a warm saw to a bright square, the pad opens 623 Hz, and the bar is cut **3.67× finer** underneath you — all at the same 104 bpm. The pulse doubles; the tempo never moves, because a tempo change is the one thing that would make the music lurch.

My first attempt gave the inner ring a full sixteenth shimmer and measured **6.3×** the outer density. That's a wall of noise, not a groove. This is a ladder you can hear each step of.

## The geometry

`R` was `min(W, usableH) * 0.31` — a flat fraction that ignored the furniture at both ends. Measured across five viewports, it left **74px of dead margin either side in portrait** while **already colliding in landscape**: 16px of clearance under the ring, and the tier banner drawing **80px up into the score readout**.

Solving the actual free box instead:

- **portrait** — R 121 → 167 (**+38%**), inner ring 60 → 91px (**+50%**), gaps between rings **+27%**
- **landscape** — no longer overlaps anything; the banner is clamped below the HUD
- every viewport now has positive clearance top and bottom

The inner ring was your specific complaint, and it was the worst offender by the numbers. A shard's hit width is `(18.5u)/radius` **radians** — so at half the outer radius it blocked *twice* the angular fraction, and the track held about a third fewer embers. It's now 0.545 of a larger R, and a shard blocks **3.2% of that circle instead of 4.5%** — without touching a single difficulty constant.

Overlapping same-ring pairs fell from **8.41% → 3.37%** as a direct consequence. The inner ring got materially fairer purely from geometry.

## The picture

Each track carries its own colour, cooling from indigo outside through cyan to a keen aqua-white inside — the same axis the sound moves along, so the two are saying one thing rather than two. The light the comet casts on its track takes that colour too, so where you are is legible at a glance.

**Also fixed:** the payoff depletion arc was drawn at `radiusOf(nRings-1)` — the *innermost* ring — so the section readout sat inside the arena instead of framing it. It now rides outside ring 0.

## Verification

- Solvability: **0 unfair walls** in 44,309 pairs
- Frame budget: 3% median, 12% worst
- Worst-case audio stack (drop landing on a nova cascade): 0.987 peak, **0 clipped**
- Reduced motion draws no flash and no shake; onboarding ladder unchanged
- Layout checked on iPhone 14, Android, Pro Max, iPad and landscape

No scoring changes anywhere.

author: metaspartan
body:
Track `laguna-s-2.1-gguf-gb10cuda-v1`. Groups `attn_q`/`attn_k`/`attn_v` (all Q8_0, K=3072, same quantized input) into one `mul_mat_vec_q` launch, plus the shared-expert gate/up pair.

Not a launch-count win — that lever is recorded dead on this track at ~0.6%. One larger grid reaches a memory rate the smaller grids do not: per-launch `attn_q` 216 GB/s, `attn_k` 159, `attn_gate` 37.

The result hung on one line. The natural `vx = args.vx[seg]` makes nvcc spill the whole kernel-parameter struct to local memory to index it — `cuobjdump -res-usage` showed `STACK:80`, the only kernel in `libggml-cuda.so` with a stack frame, ~10 kB of local traffic per block. An unrolled constant-index select gives `STACK:0` and flips the sign:

| | small only | all eligible |
|---|---|---|
| runtime index (`STACK:80`) | -4.90% | -3.80% |
| unrolled const (`STACK:0`) | **+1.109%** | **+1.868%** |

Measured with the in-process protocol: 12 rotated reference-bracketed cycles, no-op floor 0.99994. Greedy text plus full top-5 logprobs (3 prompts x 48 tokens) byte-identical with grouping on and off; perplexity 4.8761 +/- 0.35536 both ways, identical per chunk. Grouping is inert at batch > 1, so prefill and TTFT are untouched by construction.

<!-- GITZILLA_SUMMARY -->
> [!NOTE]
> **Low Risk**
>
> **Overview**
> This PR adds a CUDA patch for the `laguna-s-2.1-gguf-gb10cuda-v1` track that groups same-activation quantized matvecs into a single launch. It merges `attn_q`, `attn_k`, `attn_v` (all Q8_0, K=3072, sharing the same quantized input) into one `mul_mat_vec_q` call, along with the shared-expert gate/up pair. The change trades multiple smaller kernel launches for one larger grid, reaching a higher memory throughput (e.g., `attn_q` 216 GB/s, `attn_k` 159, `attn_gate` 37 GB/s) even though launch-count reduction itself shows negligible impact (~0.6%) on this track. The implementation works around an nvcc spill issue with the natural `vx = args.vx[seg]` pattern, which forced a constrained per-launch indexing approach. The accompanying README documents the track notes and per-launch bandwidth measurements.
>

author: andrewkaufman
body:
## Description

Bumps `mujoco` from `>=3.10.0,<3.11` to `>=3.11.0,<3.12`. Newton 1.5 requires `mujoco~=3.11.0`, so the old pin made the converter and Newton mutually uninstallable.

3.11 returns an `mjtBuiltin` enum from `MjsTexture.builtin` rather than an `int`, and every pybind11 enum member is truthy — including `mjBUILTIN_NONE` — so `if texture.builtin:` discarded every texture. Now compares against `mjBUILTIN_NONE` explicitly, which behaves the same on both versions. That was the only place the converter tested a newly-enum field for truthiness.

Also adds coverage for builtin textures, which had none.

183 tests pass. Converted output is byte-identical to 0.4.2, and so is the downloaded `mjcPhysics` schema.

## Summary

- Keep the conservative Windows system-default Codex routing through the shared runtime home while making that lane eligible for session migration.
- Re-arm and schedule the non-destructive backfill after each shared system-default launch so newly created rollout logs become visible in the configured system Codex history home.
- Self-heal a completed zero-file backfill marker when a valid managed rollout appears later.

Fixes #12480

## Screenshots

No visual change.

## Testing

- [ ] `pnpm lint`
- [x] `pnpm typecheck`
- [ ] `pnpm test`
- [ ] `pnpm build`
- [x] Added or updated high-quality tests that would catch regressions, or explained why tests were not needed

Additional focused checks:

- `pnpm exec oxlint`
- `pnpm exec vitest run --config config/vitest.config.ts src/main/codex/codex-session-backfill.test.ts src/main/codex/codex-session-migration-scheduler.test.ts src/main/codex-accounts/runtime-home-windows-profile-ownership.test.ts src/main/codex-accounts/runtime-home-service.test.ts` (178 tests)
- `pnpm run check:max-lines-ratchet`

## AI Review Report

Reviewed the Windows routing decision, marker lifecycle, delayed migration scheduling, account-switch races, and preservation of the existing skip-collision behavior. The review explicitly checked macOS, Linux, Windows, and WSL path behavior: new filesystem traversal uses Node path primitives, the platform routing remains runtime-gated, managed accounts stay excluded, and no shortcut, label, UI, shell command, or Electron renderer behavior changed.

## Security Audit

No dependency, command execution, network, IPC, credential, or secret-handling changes were introduced. The migration still hardlinks first, uses the atomic no-overwrite copy fallback, skips collisions, never deletes source sessions, and re-checks host system-default eligibility before the delayed run; managed accounts and known custom `CODEX_HOME` launches do not schedule this publication path. Tests use sandboxed temporary homes and never write to the real user Codex home.

## Notes

- Native Windows system-default sessions intentionally remain on the shared compatibility lane because PowerShell profile ownership cannot be proven safely; this change restores external discoverability without weakening credential isolation.
- Per-account managed homes remain separate by design and are not mirrored into the system home.

author: jdelgado2002
body:
Started from the flake in `tests/e2e/permissions-roles.spec.ts` reported in [run 30673063063](https://github.com/toyiyo/nimble-pnl/actions/runs/30673063063). Two separate problems came out of it.

## 1. The app really could fail open, one commit wide

`StaffRoleChecker` holds every protected route until `useRestaurantContext().loading` clears, then reads `selectedRestaurant?.role` to decide whether a kiosk / staff / collaborator user belongs on the current path. Its own comment says the gate exists so those users never "briefly render the very page these redirects exist to keep them out of (and fires its queries)."

It didn't achieve that. `loading` came straight from the memberships query, but the selection was made in a `useEffect` — one commit later. In between there was a render with `loading === false` and `selectedRestaurant === null`, so `role` was `undefined`, all three guards evaluated falsy, and the forbidden page rendered.

`RestaurantContext` now derives the selection during render, which closes the window rather than adding another spinner. A spinner wasn't an option: `Index.tsx` renders a "Select or create a restaurant" screen for multi-restaurant users with no saved choice, and blocking on `!selectedRestaurant` would hang it.

The same change fixes a second defect that fell out of the same design — the selection was stored as a snapshot object, so an auto-selected membership kept the role it was *first* fetched with. A demotion picked up by a refetch never reached the guards without a full reload.

`tests/unit/RestaurantContext.roleResolution.test.tsx` pins both at the context seam. It went red on all three defects before the fix:

```
✗ loading:false with unresolved role (sole membership)   → [{loading:false, role:undefined}]
✗ loading:false with unresolved role (saved selection)   → [{loading:false, role:undefined}]
✗ role change on refetch                                 → expected 'staff', got 'owner'
✓ multi-restaurant with no saved choice stays unselected  (guards against over-fixing)
```

It lives there and not in E2E because the window is a single commit — a browser test can only see it as an unreproducible flash.

## 2. The cited CI failure was budget exhaustion, not that race

Worth stating plainly, because it changes what needed fixing: all three attempts in that run ended with `Test timeout of 90000ms exceeded`, and the `toHaveURL` mismatch is the secondary report — it only got 8–9 polls before the test itself was killed. Every failure settled on a path from that test's own forbidden list, which is what you see when a test dies mid-loop, not a routing race. (The `/banking` destination came from the *staff* test, a separate failure block.) The run predates its own mitigation: it ran 2026-07-31, and c6728958 added `test.slow()` to these tests on 2026-08-03.

But `test.slow()` was load-bearing rather than curative. Each spec does ~16 full SPA boots at 4-6s plus a ~35s signup, so the sweeps drift back toward the wall as routes get added.

`navigateInApp` pushes the path through the History API instead — same router, same `StaffRoleChecker` guard, ~100ms instead of 4-6s. It returns only once the URL has held still across two polls, so callers assert on a settled location rather than one a guard is about to change. That replaces the `waitUntil: 'commit'` + swallowed-abort + 15s-timeout pattern that was racing the initial navigation.

Cold-boot-into-a-guarded-route stays covered: `setUserRole` reloads onto a forbidden path before every sweep, and the single-route tests at the bottom of the file still navigate for real.

The helper has a false-green mode worth guarding — if react-router ever stops listening for `popstate`, every sweep would still pass, because the helper sets the URL itself and the assertions would read it back. `navigate-in-app.spec.ts` pins that. It runs signed out (no database) using `ProtectedRoute` bouncing an anonymous visitor to `/auth`, the same `<Navigate replace>` mechanism the role guards use.

## Verification

- ✅ `npm run typecheck` clean; new test files typecheck clean under an explicit `tsc` pass (the root tsconfig doesn't cover `tests/`)
- ✅ `RestaurantContext.roleResolution` + `useRestaurants` unit tests: 10 passed
- ✅ The pushState→router→guard mechanism pinned in jsdom against the installed react-router 6.30 (allowed route renders and holds; guard redirect settles; history index stays finite across four consecutive redirects)
- ✅ eslint: no new findings, and the change removes a pre-existing `exhaustive-deps` warning
- ⚠️ **The full E2E suite could not run locally.** The dev machine was saturated by parallel work — load average peaked at 272 on 10 cores, a concurrent worktree was running a 158-file pgTAP suite against the shared local Supabase, and that stack was then torn down mid-session. Under that load the unbundled dev server took 20s to serve `index.html` alone, so `page.goto('/auth')` timed out at 90s in *untouched* helper code (`e2e-supabase.ts:756`) as well. An earlier run in this same session, before the contention, passed 15/15 against the app fix. **CI is the real verification for the E2E change here.**

## Known gap, not addressed

A kiosk / staff / collaborator user with 2+ memberships and no saved selection still has `role === undefined`, so the guards fall through. It's pre-existing and can't be fixed by blocking — that user genuinely needs the picker to render. It needs a different design, e.g. deriving the guard from the union of memberships when none is selected.

  - Improved restaurant selection reliability by resolving selections from current memberships, saved preferences, or the sole available restaurant.
  - Prevented transient loading and unselected states during route checks.
  - Ensured restaurant role changes are reflected after data refreshes.

- **Tests**
  - Added coverage for restaurant selection and role resolution.
