author: deenuu1
body:
## What the model was being told, and could not do

`answer_subagent` was offered to every delegating agent's model. It replies to a question
a delegate asked, and no delegate on this platform can ask one:

- The library injects its `ask_parent` tool only into agents it built itself, and every
  delegate here arrives pre-built as `SubAgentConfig["agent"]` from `_config_for` — so
  `SubAgentToolset.task` passes `inject_ask_parent=False` for a pinned delegate and an
  inline specialist alike, and `_compile_subagent` returns early for a config carrying
  `agent` without appending the toolset.
- For the two dynamic entry points the library *would* inject it, and `_autonomously`
  sets `can_ask_questions: False`, which it honours by not appending the toolset at all.

`TaskStatus.WAITING_FOR_ANSWER` is therefore unreachable and the tool's only possible
answer is "that delegation is not waiting for an answer" — from a description the model
reads on every turn, which is the strongest prompt surface in this product.

## The fix, and what the other one would have bought

**Filtered out of the offered set, and still declared** — `UNREACHABLE_TOOLS`, applied in
`Delegation.get_toolset`. Those are two different failures and only one of them is loud: a
tool offered and unusable costs context and invites a call that can only fail, while a tool
absent from `tools=` can be neither gated by the approval policy nor renamed by a binding.
The library adds it unconditionally, so the offered set is the only place the decision can
be made. It is the same shape `create_agent` and `delegate` had while they were declared
and unwired.

**Making asking work is #184, and it would not have closed this.** Which channel answers a
question is decided by the mode, and the two halves are different products:

| | Who answers | Reaches `answer_subagent` |
|---|---|---|
| `sync` | a **person**, through `ask_callback` / `ctx.deps.ask_user` | no |
| `async` | the **parent's own model**, through a future the task manager holds | yes |

So opening it for `sync` — the valuable half, and the one the issue names — buys a
delegate that can ask the person already waiting on the parent, and leaves this tool
exactly as unreachable as it was. Only the background half makes it reachable, and that is
the half whose reasoning still holds after revisiting it: the delegate blocks for up to
`ask_timeout_seconds` holding a fan-out slot while nothing obliges the parent to call
`check_task`, and `wrap_run` cancels every background task when the turn ends — money spent
on a question nobody was asked. On top of which `inject_ask_parent=False` is hardcoded for
the compiled path, so reaching a pinned delegate or an inline specialist at all is an
upstream change to `subagents-pydantic-ai`, as #174 is.

**What the product gives up, plainly:** no delegate can ask anything — not a person, not
its parent. A specialist works autonomously and says so if it could not. That was already
true; this change stops telling the model otherwise.

## What a delegating agent's model is offered after this

`task`, `check_task`, `wait_tasks`, `list_active_tasks`, `send_message_to_subagent`,
`soft_cancel_task`, `hard_cancel_task` — plus `create_agent` and `delegate` under
`allow_dynamic`. Seven of the ten declared, or nine.

## How the drift test stays meaningful

`tests/test_capability_registry.py` builds the delegation capability at its widest and
compares declared against offered in both directions. It now knows about one exemption,
explicitly:

- `DECLARED_AND_NOT_OFFERED` names `answer_subagent` — **spelt out in the test rather than
  imported** from the capability (an imported set makes the check a tautology), and
  **subtracted rather than skipping the capability** (skipping is what put `subagents`
  outside the check entirely before, so an undeclared tool could appear beside the exempt
  one and nothing would notice).
- A new test refuses an entry that no longer names a declared tool, or names nothing.
  Without it, an exemption outliving its reason widens the check silently — which is the
  failure mode of the `UNWIRED_TOOLS` table this one replaces. The other direction needs no
  test: a tool that becomes genuinely offered while still listed fails the comparison.
- The rename test now also proves a binding cannot smuggle it back. The filter keys on the
  stable id, inside the wrapper that renames, so `answer_subagent_as_this_agent_calls_it`
  is not offered either.

And the consequence is asserted where the configuration is: `test_subagents_capability.py`
pins the exact seven-tool set a delegating agent's model reads, and that the tool is still
declared. `test_answering_a_delegate_finds_nothing_to_answer` is gone — asserting the
library's refusal message for a tool no model can call was a test for somebody else's code.

## Rebased onto `main`, and what that took

This was branched from `feat/subagents`, which has since squash-merged as `f618e8c` after
gaining four more commits. Replaying these two onto `main` collapses the diff from ~18,800
lines to **311 across 8 files**, and four of the merged commits' changes land in files this
one also touches. All of them survive:

- `cancel_in_flight()` swept in `wrap_run`'s `finally`, and the corrected docstring saying
  the library's grace period *expires* rather than concludes;
- `_DELEGATE_MODE_NOTE` and `_override_note`, marking a delegate whose `preferred_mode`
  differs from the capability's beside its own name in the instructions;
- in `docs/reference/capabilities.md`, the paragraphs on `max_depth` binding in both
  directions and on a sync delegation parking and resuming in place.

Two conflicts, both about the same sentence being replaced rather than kept twice: the
`answer_subagent` declaration's note that the deployment cannot keep the tool's promise is
what this change makes obsolete, so it gives way to the pointer at `UNREACHABLE_TOOLS`, and
the test asserting the library's refusal message goes with the tool it called. The one
edit the rebase itself needed is in the docs: main's new "a sync delegation can stop to ask
a person" paragraph now sits directly above this one, so its opener says *no delegate can
ask a question of its own* and names the difference — parking for an approval is a gated
tool being reviewed, not a specialist asking anything.

## Verified

`make check` — every CI job except `e2e`: `make lint`, `make test` with the 100% statement
and branch gate on the platform layer, `make test-frontend-cov`, `build-frontend`,
`docs-build --strict`, and the audit. Run against a database of its own
(`POSTGRES_DB=agenticos_test_rb193`), which is what #216 now makes routine — the deadlocked
integration teardown reported here before the rebase was two runs sharing `agenticos_test`,
and it does not reproduce.

## Docs

`docs/reference/capabilities.md` — the tool line, a note under the "what ships" table that
the declared column is not always the offered set, the count corrected from eight to seven,
and a paragraph beside "a background delegation cannot stop to ask a person", which is the
same question on the same surface. `backend/app/agents/capabilities/subagents/README.md`
carries the reasoning and corrects its own earlier claim that the drift check had nothing
left to be told about — that held for a tool declared and *unwired*, not for one declared
and deliberately unoffered.

## Found along the way, deliberately not fixed

**#185** — the six background-task tools are offered to an agent configured `mode="sync"`
whose delegates override nothing, which can never have a background delegation to use them
on. Same failure as this one, under a condition that has to be computed per run rather than
stated once (`auto` resolves per delegation), so narrowing it wrongly removes a tool an
agent needs mid-turn. Pre-existing; found reviewing this.

**#184** — the feature above.

Closes #182

author: gaspergrom
body:
## Summary

- podman, buildah, and skopeo moved from `github.com/containers` into a dedicated org, `github.com/podman-container-tools`, which also introduced repos not yet tracked (`container-libs`, `image_build`, `podman-machine-os`, `automation`)
- The Insights `podman-container-tools` project page still shows the old org's repos because the source-of-truth data (`insightsProjects.github` + `public.repositories`, CDC'd to Tinybird via Sequin) was never updated
- Adds a one-off manual correction script (`backend/src/bin/scripts/insightsProjects/fix-podman-container-tools-repos.ts`), following the existing pattern in `backend/src/bin/scripts/insightsProjects/` (`cleanup-duplicate-repos-projects.ts`, `cleanup-duplicate-insights-projects.ts`), that:
  1. Updates the project's `github` org field to the new org URL
  2. Renames the 3 existing repo rows from the old org URLs to the new org URLs, resetting their git processing state so the git worker re-onboards them
  3. Inserts the 4 previously-untracked repos under the new org

No API/service-layer change exists for renaming a repo's URL or org, so this follows the repo's established convention of a manual one-off script run against prod, rather than going through the HTTP admin API.

## Deploy / run notes

- Not wired into any migration or automated pipeline — run manually against prod:
  ```
  LOG_LEVEL=debug SERVICE=script ./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/bin/scripts/insightsProjects/fix-podman-container-tools-repos.ts --dryRun
  LOG_LEVEL=debug SERVICE=script ./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/bin/scripts/insightsProjects/fix-podman-container-tools-repos.ts
  ```
- Idempotent — safe to re-run (renames are keyed off the old URL, inserts are skipped if the URL already exists)
- After this runs in prod, Sequin CDC propagates the change to Tinybird automatically — no separate Tinybird change needed

## Follow-up (not code, out of scope for this PR)

Per DE-1017's standard DQ ticket process, once this is live in prod someone needs to manually, on GitHub:
- Remove the `needs-triage` label from `linuxfoundation/insights#2056`
- Close `linuxfoundation/insights#2056`

## Test plan

- [ ] Run the script with `--dryRun` against a local/staging DB and confirm the logged before/after values are correct
- [ ] Run the script for real against prod
- [ ] Confirm `insights.linuxfoundation.org/project/podman-container-tools`'s repository selector shows the new org's repos, including `container-libs`
- [ ] Confirm the git worker re-onboards the 3 renamed repos (state `pending` → processed)

author: kihahu
body: ## Summary - An interrupted store migration (e.g. the fast-node "Upgrading IAVL storage" step killed mid-flight) can leave the root multistore's `s/latest` version ahead of a lagging store. - The stock `rollback` command (wired via `server.AddCommands` → `server.NewRollbackCmd`) constructs the app with `loadLatest=true`, so it panics in `LoadLatestVersion` before it can ever call `RollbackToVersion`. This leaves an affected node unrecoverable via any built-in tool. - Adds `allorad debug-store {inspect, check-tip, force-rollback}`: - `inspect` — read-only dump of `s/latest` and per-store commit-info at the tip and tip-1. - `check-tip` — builds the app with `loadLatest=false` (so store construction succeeds regardless of tip consistency) and attempts to load all stores at the latest version, without writing anything. - `force-rollback --to N` — same load-and-validate probe at a target version; only writes (deletes versions above target, rewrites `s/latest`) when passed `--yes`. - Uses the app's real declared store keys (via `app.NewAlloraApp(..., loadLatest=false, ...)` and its `CommitMultiStore()`) rather than inferring stores from on-disk commit-info, so it stays correct if store types/keys change in the future. ## Alternative considered Hardening the existing `rollback` command itself (constructing the app with `loadLatest=false` and auto-detecting/loading `latest-1` when the tip is inconsistent) would be a cleaner long-term fix and could make this command unnecessary. Open to that direction instead if maintainers prefer it — happy to discuss. ## Test plan - [x] `go build ./...` - [x] `golangci-lint run ./cmd/allorad/...` — no issues - [x] `allorad debug-store --help` / subcommand `--help` output reviewed - [x] `allorad debug-store inspect --home ` runs without panicking on a home with no application state - [ ] Exercise `check-tip` / `force-rollback` against a real interrupted-migration data dir (not available in this environment) before relying on it in a live incident --- ## Summary by cubic Adds `allorad debug-store` commands to inspect and safely recover a multistore after an interrupted migration, avoiding the `rollback` panic by loading the app with `loadLatest=false`. Enables dry-run validation and a gated rollback to a target version. - **New Features** - `allorad debug-store inspect` — show `s/latest` and per-store commit-info at tip and tip-1. - `allorad debug-store check-tip` — build with `loadLatest=false` and attempt to load all stores at the latest version (read-only). - `allorad debug-store force-rollback --to N [--yes]` — validate target version loads; with `--yes`, delete versions above N and set `s/latest=N`. - Uses the app’s real store keys via `CommitMultiStore()` for correctness across store changes. Written for commit 3a997962f165289730dc0719bbcee0b8409b2550. Summary will update on new commits.

author: dvcolomban
body:
## What

Once `startHttpAndWs`'s owned `httpServer` is past its bind, it has zero error listeners for the rest of its life — a later runtime error (a transient `EMFILE` while accepting a connection, say) still crashes the process, and there's no way for a caller to defend against it: `StartedServer` doesn't expose the underlying server, unlike the shared-server path where the caller already owns that object.

Adds `onServerError?: (error: Error) => void`, attached only after the bind has already succeeded — so it doesn't touch bind-time crash/hang semantics at all, just gives the server's remaining lifetime an escape hatch.

## Why not just expose httpServer

Considered it, but handing out the raw object would let a caller call `.close()` on it directly, bypassing the wrapper's own `close()` and leaking the WS transport — basically the same class of bug #163 fixes, through a different door. A narrow callback matches the shape the file already uses (`onReady`, `onPeerConnect`, `rpcOptions.onFunctionError`/`onGeneralError`) without that risk.

## Why it's gated on `ownsHttpServer`

Deliberate, and the JSDoc leads with it: passing `onServerError` alongside `server` does nothing.

A `net.Server` with zero `'error'` listeners crashes the process; with one, it doesn't. Attaching to a caller-supplied server would flip that server's failure mode process-wide for as long as the devframe is mounted — on a Next or Vite host that's the host's own server, and its crash semantics aren't devframe's to change. `close()` also deliberately leaves a caller-owned server running, so the listener would outlive the devframe and keep firing; making that symmetric would need a `close()`-time detach on top. And on that path the caller already holds the object, so `server.on('error', handler)` is one line on their side — the owned path having no such handle is the entire gap here. Matches how `listen`, `destroyUnmatched`, `close` and `separateWsPort` are already gated in this file.

## Note for maintainers — no test here, on purpose

`StartedServer` deliberately doesn't expose the raw server (that's the whole point of this over just exposing it), so there's no way to trigger a genuine post-bind error through the public API without adding a test-only seam. The wiring itself is a one-line pass-through of Node's own documented `'error'` event, so I'm leaving it to review rather than inventing something fragile to cover it.

I also considered forwarding bind-time errors to the same callback, so it'd be one place to observe every server error instead of two — but dropped it. That's only safe once #163's promise-settlement fix is also in: attaching any listener during the bind window changes whether Node treats a failed bind as fatal, and without #163 that trades a loud crash for a silent hang for anyone who opts in early. Independent of #163 (this PR doesn't depend on it, and applies cleanly to `main` either way), so not worth that risk here.

## Tests

`pnpm lint && pnpm knip && pnpm test && pnpm typecheck && pnpm build` — all green (1054 tests, unchanged — see above for why there's no new one).

author: limonte
body:
Part of #15.

> [!WARNING]
> **Do not merge yet if verification hasn't been confirmed.** The token in this PR came from the DNS flow and may need swapping — see below. Comment the HTML-tag token and I'll amend this branch in place, so no extra deploy is wasted.

## What

```html
<meta name="google-site-verification" content="m0A3okYBxSPb9KF0JKVbxAX6tmXBWS25WmaApwPK_1w">
```

## Why the token may be wrong

Verifying `csv-viewer-online.github.io` needs a **URL prefix** property, not a **Domain** property:

- Domain properties verify **only** via DNS TXT record
- GitHub owns the `github.io` zone, so no TXT record can be added for this host
- A meta tag is never consulted for a Domain property, whatever it contains

The token committed here is the DNS TXT value. Google issues **method-specific** tokens, so the HTML-tag method will most likely hand out a different string.

**Steps to finish:**
1. In Search Console, add a **URL prefix** property for `https://csv-viewer-online.github.io/`
2. Choose the **HTML tag** method
3. If the token differs from the one above, post it here and I'll update this branch
4. Merge, wait for Pages to deploy, then press **Verify**

## Verified

```
{ "present": true,
  "content": "m0A3okYBxSPb9KF0JKVbxAX6tmXBWS25WmaApwPK_1w",
  "inHead": true,
  "count": 1,
  "canonicalStillThere": true }

present in raw HTML source: true
token in raw source       : true
no page errors
```

- `count: 1` — duplicate verification tags are a common failure, since Google only reads the first
- Confirmed present in the **raw HTML source**, not JS-injected, so the crawler will actually see it
- The canonical from #22 is untouched

## Note for later

Removing this tag un-verifies the site and silently drops your access to the data, so it needs to stay put.

Once Google is verified, Bing Webmaster Tools can **import** the property directly from Search Console — no second tag required.

> [!NOTE]
> Merging deploys to production, since Pages publishes from `main`.

author: xinha-sh
body:
Follow-up to #94, found by running the merged bridge against real thread data before releasing.

## The gap

#94 recovers any worktree git still has on record. A worktree that was deleted **and pruned** is gone from git entirely — and on a real machine that's most of the back catalogue. 17 of 53 Spaces were long-dead worktrees of a single project, each sitting as its own row:

```
salty-hibiscus      ~/.superset/worktrees/d0f7efc8-…/salty-hibiscus
canary-tungsten     ~/.superset/worktrees/d0f7efc8-…/canary-tungsten
intermediate-diplodocus  …
succulent-dime      …            (14 more)
```

That workspace directory resolves to `pounce-mono` — its live sibling `v2` is a registered worktree — but each pruned entry still landed on its own.

## The fix

Tools that batch worktrees put them side by side under one parent: superset gives a workspace its own directory, Claude Code uses `.claude/worktrees/`, and both hold worktrees of a single project. So when git can't speak for a directory, its neighbours can — a directory whose siblings are known worktrees of one repo is a worktree of that repo.

Guarded so it only ever *stands in for* git, never overrides it:

- **Requires positive evidence** — at least one sibling already resolved through git.
- **Abstains on disagreement** — if resolved siblings name two different projects, it guesses nothing.
- **Never touches a real checkout** — a directory git answered for is excluded, so a worktree parked beside real repos can't swallow them.

## Result on real data

| | Spaces |
|---|---|
| before #94 | 53, incl. 4 identical `"Workspace"` rows |
| after #94 | 53, no duplicates but 17 stray rows |
| after this | **36** |

17 rows fold into the project they belong to. One workspace (`efb16a56-…`, a copy with no `.git` and no sibling ever resolved) is left alone rather than guessed at — correct abstention.

3 new tests cover the pruned-sibling case and both misfire guards. 165 bridge tests pass.

author: tolian82
keizer619
body:
## Purpose

The **Run** button was `variant="ghost"`, so it rendered as plain text in the editor toolbar with no fill or border.

This became a real usability problem while embedding the playground on the upcoming `ballerina.io/nutcracker` landing page: in informal testing, people **did not realise the embedded playground was runnable at all** — several read the whole editor as a static screenshot or GIF. The `Run` control simply did not look like a control.

## Goals

Make Run read unambiguously as the primary action, using the Ballerina brand teal so it is consistent with `ballerina.io` — without making the toolbar loud.

## Approach

Rather than hardcoding a colour in the component, this follows the existing design-system pattern:

1. **`styles.css`** — adds a `--brand` token to both `:root` and `.dark`, mapped through `@theme inline` as `--color-brand`.

   Worth noting: the theme previously had **no brand colour at all** (`--primary` is neutral `oklch(0.205 0 0)`), so this introduces the brand as a proper token that other actions can reuse.

2. **`button.tsx`** — adds a reusable `brand` variant:
   `border-brand text-brand hover:bg-brand/10 focus-visible:ring-brand/40`

3. **`editor.tsx`** — Run uses `variant="brand"` and gains `px-4` for presence. **Stop deliberately stays `ghost`**, so a running program is not signalled with a "go" colour.

### Before

Text-only — no border, no fill. Easy to miss entirely.

![Run button before](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ballerina-nutcracker/playground/assets/pr-105-screenshots/pr-105/run-button-before.png)

### After

Teal border and label, with a faint teal tint on hover.

![Run button after](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ballerina-nutcracker/playground/assets/pr-105-screenshots/pr-105/run-button-after.png)

In context:

![Editor with the updated Run button](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ballerina-nutcracker/playground/assets/pr-105-screenshots/pr-105/editor-after.png)

An earlier revision of this PR used a solid teal fill. That was too heavy for this minimal, monochrome UI, so it was changed to the outlined treatment. Square corners are kept so the button matches the surrounding `rounded-none` design language.

> Screenshots are hosted on the `assets/pr-105-screenshots` branch to keep binaries out of this diff. That branch can be deleted once this PR is merged.

### Notes for the reviewer

- **Colour format.** The rest of `styles.css` uses `oklch`, but converting `#20b6b0` lands on `rgb(31,182,176)` — off by 1/255. The literal brand hex is used so the colour is exact and self-documenting. Happy to switch to `oklch(0.703 0.116 190.6)` if format consistency is preferred.
- **Contrast, for transparency.** `#20b6b0` against white measures **2.51:1** — below the 3:1 WCAG 1.4.11 asks for UI component boundaries, and below 4.5:1 for text. Note this is unchanged by using an outline instead of a fill: contrast is a ratio between the two colours, so swapping foreground and background does not affect it. It matches how `ballerina.io` uses this teal today, so it was kept for brand consistency; a darker teal would be needed to reach AA if you would rather prioritise that.

## Release note

The Run button in the playground editor is now outlined in the Ballerina brand teal, making it clearly identifiable as the primary action.

## Documentation

N/A — visual change to an existing control, no documented behaviour changes.

## Automation tests

- Unit tests: none added — this is a styling change. The existing `data-testid="run-button"` hook is unchanged, so current tests and e2e selectors continue to work.
- Integration tests: N/A

## Security checks

- Followed secure coding standards in http://wso2.com/technical-reports/wso2-secure-engineering-guidelines? yes
- Ran FindSecurityBugs plugin and verified report? N/A (frontend styling change)
- Confirmed that this PR doesn't commit any keys, passwords, tokens, usernames, or other secrets? yes

## Samples

N/A

author: lionsr
body:
Migrates the eleven wave-4 Section-IV closure/wrap cases off the 0.7 grid and free tiers onto the kernel language, per the §12.7 wide-operator idiom: the boundary operators L, R, and X are stock-pill **wide atoms** with lobe legs at top-face stations, closed through the kernel side cups; invisible `skin=none` junctions carry uncovered stretches to the cups and turn cut virtual ends upward, exactly as the author panels draw them. Every case was vision-verified against its author panel at 200dpi and countersigned on a genuine second 400dpi pass.

## Per-case verdicts

| Case | Verdict | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `rmp-iv-ground-space-1d` | cosmetic-gap (K1) | Traced word returns through corner junctions with the author's **square X box** on the return — the old K3 (small ring glyph, tight placement) is resolved. Residue: recorded corner arcs ink as straight diagonals (shared-renderer limitation, same as the accepted boundary-algebra family). |
| `rmp-iv-intersection-lhs-one` | faithful | A–B and the uncovered stretch close through pill L's side cups; lobe leg at station 3. |
| `rmp-iv-intersection-rhs-one` | faithful | Mirror: uncovered stretch, B–C, lobe leg at station 1. |
| `rmp-iv-intersection-lhs-two` | faithful | Both cut virtual ends now **turn upward** (junction + top station), retiring the 0.7 sideways-openings residue. |
| `rmp-iv-intersection-rhs-two` | faithful | Mirror of lhs-two; upturned pair matches Rtensor2. |
| `rmp-iv-intersection-lhs-three` | faithful | Source order A, B, cut pair, lobe reproduced; ends upturned. |
| `rmp-iv-intersection-rhs-three` | faithful | Both outer ends close through R's cups; cut interior ends upturned between B and C, retiring the 0.7 facing-break (`\tnskip`) spelling. |
| `rmp-iv-intersection-lhs-four` | faithful | The free identity wire is now the source's **open U** between two junctions, retiring the 0.7 horizontal-wire equivalence. |
| `rmp-iv-intersection-rhs-four` | faithful | See R-operator note below. |
| `rmp-iv-intersection-lhs-five` | faithful | Three-index boundary at the stations of the lhs-four panel; near-lobe stub upward for the source's horizontal lobe stub (equivalent open-leg presentation, noted). |
| `rmp-iv-intersection-rhs-five` | faithful | See adjudication below. |

## rhs-five adjudication (requested re-audit)

The verdict asked that the "mirrored open C–X contraction" be re-audited against Rtensor5 before acceptance. Finding: the 0.7 layout **was** topologically equivalent — same C–X bond, same three open legs (C physical, X physical, C's west virtual) — but it embedded X's physical leg east of the contraction where the author places it at the far west, with the bond wrapping around C's east into the bar. The kernel respell restores the source embedding directly: X's leg at station 1 (far west), C closing east through the cup, and C's cut end left sideways-west exactly as the author draws it. The mirror residue is gone; promoted to `faithful`.

## rhs-four R-operator respell (#5363 census note)

The 0.7 case spelled R as a free-tier `\tnput[pill]` with hand-tuned angle ports and millimetre placements. Per the signed §14 judgment (LANGUAGE-1.0), that operator is a `wide=` **box atom**, not a pill: it is now `skin=box, wide=7` with the escaped leg at `90@1` feeding S, drop junctions closing B's and C's outer bonds into the top face, and the cut ends upturned between B and C. This retires the family's last free-tier body and its 18 owned layout dimensions. The other Section-IV carriers are genuine pill demand and keep `skin=pill` (per the same issue's demand list).

## Bookkeeping

- Dimension census: **401 → 383** sites (composition/layout 177 → 159; route/string unchanged at 224); ceilings in `scripts/tenkzlib/dimensions.py` and the provenance pins tightened to the recompute.
- M4: **22.48 → 22.88** (kernel cases name the atoms, junctions, and typed ports the retired tiers implied); `tests/tenkz/census-baseline.json` regenerated from the meters.

author: cmartinez9
body:
## Intent

Complete phase 6 of loom-clone (decode + WebGL2 compositor, screen-only preview holding frame budget at 4K) by restoring the strict acceptance gate that an earlier CI auto-fix round weakened, and by making the WebGL context-loss detection durable.

THIS RUN'S SPECIFIC PURPOSE. A previous run of this same branch reached green CI, but only because its own CI auto-fix round had relaxed the acceptance criterion. Firstmate refused to merge it. This run re-validates the branch with the strict criterion restored. The head commit a67295f is the revert; every commit under it is the phase 6 work plus the earlier pipeline fixes, all of which are preserved deliberately.

WHAT THE REVERT DID AND WHY. Architecture report section 8's phase 6 gate is: scrub and play a 4K fixture with NO FRAME OVER 16 MS at a 1440p viewport, and the live VideoFrame count never exceeds the ring cap. Commit 1e389b8 replaced that with a p99 assertion, a one-in-a-hundred over-budget allowance, and a new 3x stall ceiling of 50 ms. It was justified by a CI run reporting a 19 ms frame. The NEXT auto-fix round then proved that run came off a broken instrument: the runner's WebGL context was lost mid-run, Compositor.readPixels was silently returning stale pixels, and the report was partly fabricated (renderer 'unknown', play samples decoding as -1 out of an upside-down stale buffer). Firstmate's decision: a measurement from an instrument since proven unreliable cannot justify permanently weakening an acceptance criterion - fix the instrument, re-measure, then decide, in that order. So a67295f restores expect(maxMs).toBeLessThanOrEqual(FRAME_BUDGET_MS) and expect(overBudget).toBe(0) for both scrub and play, and removes STALL_MS and the toleratedOverBudget helper. p99Ms deliberately REMAINS in the printed report - it is what distinguishes a regression from one descheduled frame when this does fail - but it is a diagnostic, not the bound. AGENTS.md's gate note was rewritten to record the strict bound and this reasoning, replacing the note that documented the allowance.

STANDING CONSTRAINT, AND IT APPLIES TO THIS RUN'S OWN AUTO-FIX ROUNDS. Do NOT weaken, widen, add tolerance to, or add a retry around any acceptance assertion in test/phase6-gate.test.ts. Specifically prohibited: raising FRAME_BUDGET_MS above one 60 Hz refresh; allowing overBudget > 0; switching an assertion from maxMs to a percentile; excluding frames from the measured window; lowering the play.count or scrub.count minimums; widening the relaunch condition. A genuine optimisation that makes the frame faster is fine. An environment control that removes a real, identified source of noise and is justified by a measurement is fine. If CI shows a genuine frame over 16 ms on the now-trustworthy instrument, REPORT THE HONEST NUMBERS AND STOP - that is a fresh decision for firstmate, not something to absorb by adjusting the threshold.

THE CONTEXT-LOSS WORK, KEPT AND MADE DURABLE. Firstmate asked that this stop being a diagnostic that happened to be added while chasing something else, because it is the most valuable find of the whole exercise. Compositor.readPixels throws on a lost context instead of returning the caller's stale buffer, and there is a contextLost getter. Two new tests pin it: packages/compositor/test/context-loss.test.ts asserts readPixels throws rather than handing back stale bytes, and includes a CONTROL proving the fake GL context really does model a lost context as a silent no-op so the assertions cannot pass vacuously; test/relaunch-policy.test.ts fences GATE_ATTEMPTS = 2 by extracting the trigger into a named predicate shouldRelaunch and enumerating every bad-run shape (over budget, short of frames, leaked frame, over the ring cap, black frames while settling, a control that did not fire, mostly misses, not ok, errored) and requiring that none of them earns a second launch. This matters beyond the gate: phase 8's exporter reads every frame back through ONE scratch buffer, so a silent stale return would encode fabricated output indistinguishable from real output, and section 4.5's golden-frame test comparing preview against export could compare two copies of the same stale buffer and pass.

EVERYTHING ELSE ON THE BRANCH IS INTENTIONAL AND SHOULD BE LEFT ALONE. packages/decode is the ONE decode path (section 4.2): DemuxIndex with hold-last-frame VFR frame selection compared in integer timescale ticks (frame selection is on section 4.5's must-be-identical list, so there is exactly one implementation); FrameRing as the single owner of every frame, capped at section 4.2's 20 per source, with a FrameLedger that throws on the FIRST frame past the cap per section 10.2; SourceReader with cancelable priming, keyframe seeks, discard-before-target, one coalesced range request per keyframe run, and a matching close on every exit including error and cancellation. packages/compositor is the ONE compositor (section 4.1) with render-into-FBO and present-blits-to-canvas, pure geometry functions so the section 4.5 split is exhaustively checkable, and no allocation in render. The preview loop lives in apps/renderer/src/preview because section 1.3 keeps both packages framework-free. resolved-state.ts is the throwaway struct section 8 says phase 7 will delete. VideoDecoder.flush is deliberately absent from VideoDecoderLike because Chromium requires a keyframe after every flush. prime() rides along with an in-flight request rather than superseding it, and re-seeks only when the ring has moved past t or the decoder has gone idle. The fixture media file is an H.264 elementary stream with a truthful .h264 extension, which is sound because section 2.4 makes the index the only thing a reader needs.

The branch was rebased by the pipeline onto the new main, which now contains phase 1 (capture spine, PR #3) and phase 5 (cursor sampler, PR #4); the AGENTS.md and README.md conflicts from that were resolved preserving both phases' content. PR #2 is open for this branch.

Verified locally before this run: npm run verify clean - typecheck, lint, format:check all pass, 353 tests across 31 files, and the phase 6 gate green on the STRICT assertions (scrub max 0.20 ms, play max 0.30 ms, over-budget 0 in both phases, peak live 18/20, 0 live at end, all 12 scrub targets and all 6 play samples showing the correct frame).

## What Changed

- Adds `packages/decode` — the one decode path (`DemuxIndex` with hold-last-frame VFR selection in integer timescale ticks, `FrameRing` as the single `VideoFrame` owner capped at 20 with a `FrameLedger` that throws on the first frame past the cap, and `SourceReader` with cancelable priming, keyframe seeks and one coalesced range request per keyframe run) — and `packages/compositor`, the one WebGL2 compositor (render into an FBO, present blits to the canvas, pure geometry functions, no allocation in `render`). Both are fenced as pure in `eslint.config.mjs`: no `node:`, no `electron`, no I/O, reaching the world only through a `ByteRangeReader`, a `DecoderFactory` and the GL context they are handed. `apps/renderer/src/preview` wires them into a `PreviewLoop` with per-frame metrics; no shipping window drives it yet.
- Adds the phase 6 gate under `test/` and folds `test/**/*.test.ts` into `npm test`: it builds a harness with esbuild, launches Electron, encodes a 4K VFR fixture whose frame number is painted into every frame, and plays it through the shipping `PreviewLoop` at a 1440p viewport, reading frame numbers back out of the framebuffer so a blank screen cannot pass. The bound is §8's as written — the single worst frame under 16 ms and zero over-budget frames in both scrub and play, with `p99Ms` kept in the printed report as a diagnostic only.
- Makes lost-WebGL-context detection durable rather than incidental: `Compositor.readPixels` now throws instead of silently returning the caller's stale buffer, alongside a `contextLost` getter. `packages/compositor/test/context-loss.test.ts` pins that (with a control pr

author: caothu2k1
body:
Closes #3046.

## What

#2853 gave the C++ binding the Service and Action patterns. The server side
was complete; the client side was only usable from a node that can afford to
stop and wait. This adds the three pieces #3046 asked for, all additive — no
existing signature changes.

### 1. Non-blocking correlated receive

| Rust | C++ |
|------|-----|
| `EventStream::try_recv_service_response` | `try_recv_service_response(...)` |
| `EventStream::try_recv_action_result` | `try_recv_action_result(...)` |

Returns `Ok(None)` / `DoraPatternStatus::NotReady` instead of waiting.
Buffering, restart detection, correlation **and the deadline** are all
handled as in the blocking form; only the waiting is gone.

The framework owns the timeout. The first poll carrying one registers a
deadline against the correlation id, and a later poll past it returns
`Timeout` exactly once — the registration is dropped as it expires, and also
on a match or terminal error. A caller passes the same timeout every
iteration and reacts to `Timeout` like any other outcome; it does not sweep
deadlines itself. Rust takes `Option<Duration>`; C++ spells "no deadline" as
`timeout_ms == 0`.

Decisions worth a look:

- **The clock starts at the first deadline-carrying poll, not at send time.**
  `EventStream` does not see the send, and threading registration through
  `DoraNode` would couple the two for no practical gain — a client polls in
  the same iteration it sends.
- **The first deadline registered for an id wins.** Otherwise a caller
  recomputing a relative timeout each iteration would push its own deadline
  forward forever and never expire.
- **A reply that arrived before the deadline always wins over it**, whether it
  was already buffered or still unread on the stream — the deadline is
  consulted only after everything available has been examined. So `Timeout`
  means the reply had genuinely not arrived, not that the caller polled late.
- `cancel_correlation` (Rust **and** C++) drops a registration for a request
  that will never be polled again — a peer died, the operator cancelled, the
  reply stopped mattering. Without it that entry lives until the stream is
  dropped, which on a node running for days is an unbounded slow leak. It is
  a no-op for an unknown id, so a cancel racing a reply is harmless.
- **`timeout_ms == 0` means "no deadline", not "return immediately."** That
  is right here — a poll never blocks, so there is nothing to time out — but
  it inverts the usual convention for a timeout argument, so both docs now
  say so explicitly. Flagging it in case a different spelling is preferred.
- For actions the timeout bounds the *whole goal*, not the gap between
  feedback messages.

`NotReady` follows the convention `try_next_event` already established for
plain events, and stays distinct from `Timeout`: "not yet" and "too late"
are different answers, and only the second is terminal.

### 2. Caller-supplied `request_id`

| Rust | C++ |
|------|-----|
| `DoraNode::send_service_request_with_id` | `send_service_request_with_id(...)` |

`send_service_request` mints a fresh id per call, so it cannot express one
logical request fanned out to several nodes. It now delegates to the new
variant and its warning points at it. Existing behaviour is unchanged.

### 3. Correlation without a single fixed server

New `ExpectedServers` enum — `One(&NodeId)` / `AnyOf(&[NodeId])` / `Any` —
plus `recv_service_response_from`, `recv_action_result_from` and the `_from`
polls. In C++ these take a `Vec<String>`; empty means "any".

The existing `recv_service_response(request_id, &NodeId, timeout)` delegates
to `ExpectedServers::One`, so nothing breaks.

Two semantics worth checking in review:

- **The server set governs only restart detection.** Which reply matches is
  decided by `request_id` alone, so a fan-out reply is correlated even from a
  node the caller never listed. There is a test pinning this.
- **`AnyOf` reports a restart of any listed node**, naming that node (taken
  from the event, not the caller's expectation). For a first-reply-wins
  fan-out that is a notification rather than a verdict — the other candidates
  may still answer — so the caller can simply wait again. Buffered events,
  the correlation **and its deadline** survive across calls.
- **What counts as `One` is decided by candidate count, not spelling.** The
  C++ single-server polls wrap their lone id in a slice, and a one-element
  `Vec` passed to a `_from` variant is the same thing — both resolve to
  `One`, so their restart releases the deadline. Routing them through a
  one-element `AnyOf` (as an earlier revision did) kept the entry alive and
  leaked it on the give-up path.
- **A restart therefore affects the deadline differently per variant.** For
  `One` it is terminal: the request is orphaned and its deadline is dropped
  with it. For `AnyOf` the deadline keeps running on its *original* clock. An
  earlier revision dropped it in both cases, which meant a caller following
  the documented "just wait again" advice re-registered a fresh deadline
  every poll — so a flapping node could hold the correlation open forever and
  `Timeout` would never fire. Caught in review; both branches are now pinned
  by tests.

## One thing that came out of building the example

The polls and the caller's own `next_event` read the **same** stream, so
whichever runs first consumes what is there. A poll correlates the reply it
wants and buffers everything else, so polling first loses nothing. The
reverse is not true: a reply handed to `next_event` is gone, and no later
poll can see it.

My first version of the example got this wrong and silently timed out every
request. That ordering rule is now documented in `docs/patterns.md`, the C++
README, and prominently in the example itself. It may be worth a maintainer's
eye — it is inherent to polling a single shared stream rather than something
this PR introduces, but it is a sharp edge.

## Why the deadline part is here

The first revision of this PR punted timeouts to the caller. Re-reading
#3046's acceptance criteria — *"timeout and server-restart handling for those
requests come from the framework rather than from caller-side bookkeeping"* —
that only got half way: restarts came from the framework, deadlines did not,
and the issue explicitly expected to be able to delete its deadline sweep.
The example proves the difference — `polling-client.cc` no longer does any
clock arithmetic.

## `DoraEventType::NodeRestarted`

`Event::NodeRestarted` had no C++ variant and no accessor, so it fell through
`event_type`'s catch-all and arrived as `Unknown` — delivered but
unidentifiable. Added the variant plus `event_as_node_restarted`, following
`NodeFailed` / `Reload`, whose own doc comment gives this same reason.

This bears on the `ServerRestarted` contract. The correlation reports it for a
restart that lands *while a wait or poll is running*, since it owns the stream
then — verified by driving a blocking `recv_service_response` against a restart
on the stream. A restart landing between calls belongs to the node's own loop,
and that route used to drop it silently, leaving the next request to wait out
its full deadline against a server the node had already been told about. The
bridge doc and README now scope which restarts go where.

## Two confirmed issues left open for a maintainer's call

Both reproduced, both raised in the PR discussion rather than fixed here.

**A `NodeRestarted` reaches only the first-polled correlation.** Less severe
since `DoraEventType::NodeRestarted` landed: the restart now reaches the node's
own loop, so a client can cancel and resend the others itself (the C++ README
shows the loop). The framework still does not do it for you.

Originally: With N requests
in flight to one server, one gets `ServerRestarted` and the other N-1 wait out
their deadlines; the restart is buffered and never re-classified. Fixing it
means new per-correlation state and making registration

body:
## Hvad og hvorfor

B2b. `/metode/` bliver til `/om-data/` og overtager hele indholdet inklusive de genererede dækningstabeller (mulighed A, besluttet af Alexander 05.08). `/metode/` 301-redirecter, så ingen canonical URL brydes tavst.

Mail-gaten er grøn: `kontakt@hulensdata.dk` modtager mails via ImprovMX på Netlify DNS, og Google Search Console har godkendt domæneverificeringen. Siden publicerer derfor nu en kanal, der faktisk virker.

Nul nye data. Ingen Supabase-write. Ingen CSS-ændringer.

## Ændringer

**Ny sektion 06 "Ansvar"** med tre blokke — ret en oplysning, gør indsigelse, sådan henviser du til arkivet — plus en kolofon med kontaktadressen. Bygget udelukkende af eksisterende klasser (`profile-section`, `section-heading`, `method-definition-grid`, `unofficial-note`). Ingen ny CSS og ingen nye komponenter; `PRODUCT.md` kræver aftale før begge dele.

**Header:** eyebrow `Om data · snapshot …`, H1 `Om arkivets data`, ny dek. `<title>` og nav-label er det korte `Om data`.

**Sektion 01–05 er bevaret ordret.** Eneste undtagelse: sektion 05's afsluttende note stod som `unofficial-note` og indledtes med "Hulens Data er uofficielt og uafhængigt" — den halvdel er nu redundant, fordi kolofonen bærer uafhængighedserklæringen. Resten står videre som `context-note`.

## Fire hårdkodede referencer ud over ruten selv

Disse er hele risikoen i ændringen:

- **`tools/lib/site.mjs` `PUBLIC_DIRS`** — fodrer `check:links`, `check:seo`, `check:a11y` og `check:expected-routes`. Uden denne rettelse var den nye side usynlig for fire verify-trin, som ville have rapporteret grønt uden nogensinde at have læst siden. Fanget af `check:expected-routes`, ikke af de tre andre.
- `tools/validate-build.mjs` — både `requireFile` (`BUILD_METHOD_PAGE` → `BUILD_ABOUT_PAGE`) og routeundtagelsen for trykte sider.
- `tools/check-seo.mjs` — breadcrumb-undtagelsen.
- `tools/test-validation-guards.mjs` — fixturelisten.
- `js/layout.js` — `NAV_PAGES` **og** gruppe-rangeringen i ⌘K. En gruppe uden rangering giver `indexOf === -1` og ville sortere Om data øverst i alle søgeresultater.

`.gitignore` får `om-data/`; `metode/`-linjen bliver stående, så gammelt lokalt output ikke kan committes.

## Verifikation

- `npm run verify` grøn, alle 15 trin, exit 0.
- Sitemap uændret 364 URL'er, indeholder `/om-data/`, nul `metode`-forekomster. Canonical `https://hulensdata.dk/om-data/`.
- 369 ruter kontrolleret, 5 opfyldt via permanent redirect (var 4).
- Søgeindeks 393 opslag; alle syv grupper har en rangeringsplads; nul `/metode/`-URL'er. Nøgleordet `metode` er beholdt, så ⌘K stadig finder siden på det gamle ord.
- Målt i browser ved 1280 px: H1 én linjeboks på 543 af 554 px målekasse, intet tekst- eller sideoverløb. Ved 375 px: grid falder til én kolonne, H1 brydes til to linjer, `scrollWidth === clientWidth === 375`.
- Alle seks `profile-nav`-ankre rammer et eksisterende id.
- Impeccable-detektor: fire advarsler, alle præeksisterende (Fraunces-fonten samt accentkanterne på `style.css:427/480/716`, allerede noteret i changeloggen ved PR #9). Nul nye fund. Antallet af `unofficial-note`-elementer på siden er uændret ét.

## Begrænsninger

- **Redirecten kan ikke testes lokalt.** `python3 -m http.server` behandler ikke `_redirects`. `/metode/` → 301 skal måles på production efter deploy.
- CSS-klasserne hedder fortsat `method-*`. Bevidst: PR #9 konsoliderede netop stylesheetet til 741 linjer, og en omdøbning ville give en stor diff uden virkning.
- Forsidens sektion beholder `id="metode"` og kickeren "Metode og kilder". Den beskriver metoden og påstår ingen rute; ingen links peger på ankeret.

## Reviewpunkter

1. Kolofonens formulering — navnløs redaktionel form efter Alexanders beslutning; hans navn indgår bevidst ikke.
2. Om sektion 05's nedtoning fra `unofficial-note` til `context-note` er den rigtige vægtning nu, hvor siden slutter på kolofonen.
3. Om `metode` bør blive i søgeordene på længere sigt.

author: cgtqwmwkhp-rgb
body:
# Change Ledger

## Summary

**A statutory obligation activated through the UI reminded nobody.** Not "reminded the
wrong person" — nobody.

Compliance Schedule was enabled in production this morning. A requirement was activated
through the catalogue, and I ran the sweep in dry-run mode against the production worker to
see what it would deliver. It reported:

```json
{ "tenants_swept": 1, "requirements_scanned": 1, "in_band": 1,
  "notifications_created": 0, "recipients_unresolved": 1 }
```

The sweep found the obligation, correctly classified it as inside a reminder band, and had
no one to tell. Two independent causes, both confirmed by reading the code rather than
inferred:

1. **The page never sent an owner.** `activateCatalogue` in the client accepts `owner_id`
   (`frontend/src/api/complianceScheduleClient.ts:132-140`), the API accepts it on both
   create and update (`src/api/routes/compliance_schedule.py:136,216`), and the response
   carries it. The Activate button sent only `next_due_date`. So every requirement created
   through the interface is unowned, in every environment.
2. **The fallback had nobody to fall back to.** `recipient_user_ids`
   (`src/domain/services/compliance_schedule_notifications.py:133-163`) escalates an
   unowned obligation to the tenant's admin-role holders, deliberately for every band. In
   production `user_roles` has zero rows, so that list is empty.

This PR fixes cause 1. Cause 2 is a production permissions question and is being handled
separately; either fix alone restores the reminder, and both are worth having.

## Impact Map

- `frontend/src/utils/auth.ts` — new `getCurrentUserId()`, alongside the other token
  accessors. Reads `sub`, which is set to `user.id` at issue
  (`src/domain/services/auth_service.py:42-49`) but serialised as a string.
- `frontend/src/pages/ComplianceSchedule.tsx` — sends `owner_id` on activate, and renders
  ownership on each row.
- `frontend/src/pages/complianceScheduleHelpers.ts` — new pure `ownershipOf()`.
- `frontend/src/i18n/locales/en.json` — three keys.
- Three test files: one new, two extended.

Ownership is rendered from `owner_id`, which is already in the list response, and the id
already in the token. **No users lookup.** `usersApi.search`/`list` exist and would give
real names, but coupling the register to them would add a request that can fail and a
permission the page does not currently need, on a screen whose whole recent history is
failing quietly. That trade is named in Gate 4 as the follow-up, not smuggled in.

## Compatibility

No API, schema, contract or flag change. `owner_id` was already an accepted, optional field
on the activate endpoint; this sends a value where it previously sent none.

Behaviour change, stated plainly: requirements activated from now on are owned by the person
who activated them, where previously they were unowned. That is the point of the change, but
it does mean ownership is now asserted by a default rather than chosen. It is visible on the
row and changeable through the existing update endpoint. Requirements already in a register
are untouched.

When the user cannot be identified, `owner_id` is **omitted** rather than sent as `null` or
`0`, so the request is identical to today's.

## Acceptance Criteria

- **AC-01** Activating a template sends the activating user's id as `owner_id`.
- **AC-02** When the current user cannot be identified, no `owner_id` is sent at all —
  not `null`, not `0`.
- **AC-03** Each row states whether the obligation is owned by you, by someone else, or is
  unassigned.
- **AC-04** An unowned obligation is visibly unassigned rather than blank, because that is
  the state in which reminders depend on a fallback that may resolve to nobody.
- **AC-05** `getCurrentUserId()` returns null rather than `NaN` or a fabricated id for a
  missing, malformed, or non-numeric `sub`.

## Testing Evidence

Ran and observed:

- **12 new tests pass** (3 page, 5 helper, 6 auth wired into the two existing suites).
- **Negative-tested** by reverting the page to merged `main`: **2 failed, 1 passed.** The
  two that fail are AC-01 and AC-03/04. Being straight about the third: AC-02 also passes
  against the old code, because the old code sent no `owner_id` either. It does not
  discriminate against the pre-fix behaviour; it guards a *future* regression where someone
  sends `null` or `0` for an unknown user. I would rather say that than imply 3/3.
- **Full frontend suite: 338 files, 2178 tests, 0 failures.** No existing test weakened; the
  two existing suites were only appended to.
- **`tsc --noEmit` exit 0, `eslint` exit 0** across all six changed files.
- **Production dry run** as quoted in the Summary — measured against the live worker, not
  a fixture.

Not verified: the Playwright spec `compliance-schedule-cuj.spec.ts` fails on my machine —
but it fails **identically on unmodified `origin/main`**, which I checked by stashing, so it
is a local environment problem and not this change. CI's End-to-End Tests job passed on
#1576 with that spec present, so I am relying on CI for it rather than claiming I ran it.
The spec asserts with `toContainText`, and the text I added to each row does not contain any
string it asserts the absence of.

## Critical Journeys

- **CUJ-01** Someone activates a statutory obligation and a reminder actually reaches a
  person before it falls due.
- **CUJ-02** Someone scanning the register can see which obligations have an owner and which
  do not, rather than discovering it when a reminder fails to arrive.
- **CUJ-03** Completion, filtering, navigation and the register's error handling are
  unchanged.

## Observability

No new logging here, but the counter that exposed this already exists and did its job:
`recipients_unresolved` is what turned "the sweep ran fine" into "the sweep told nobody".
Worth stating for whoever reads next: a run with `notifications_created: 0` and
`recipients_unresolved > 0` is a silent failure, not a quiet success, and it is the single
counter to watch after this lands.

## Release Plan

Merge and deploy normally. The frontend ships as a Static Web App, independently of the API.
No migration, no flag, no sequencing. Existing unowned requirements are unaffected and will
still depend on the admin fallback.

## Rollback Plan

Revert the commit. Requirements activated in the meantime keep their owner, which is
harmless — the field was always supported. Reverting restores the state where new
activations are unowned.

## Evidence Pack

- Production dry run, task `bca42030-b038-4642-8006-1ab47ef6de9c`, 08:49Z 5 Aug:
  `recipients_unresolved: 1`, `notifications_created: 0`.
- Production `user_roles`: 0 rows. `abac_user_roles`: 0 rows. One role, `admin`, held by
  nobody.
- `recipient_user_ids` docstring already anticipated this: "An unowned statutory obligation
  going overdue with nobody told is precisely the failure this module exists to prevent."
  The mechanism it relies on to prevent it is absent in production.
- By contrast, staging delivered 12 notifications from the same sweep at 08:15Z today —
  because its requirements were seeded with explicit owners and it has real admin-role
  holders. That difference is exactly why this was invisible until production.

## Gate Checklist

- **Gate 1** Root cause, not symptom. The symptom is zero notifications; the cause is that
  nothing ever set an owner. Fixed at the point of creation rather than by widening the
  fallback.
- **Gate 2** No test weakened. Two existing suites appended to, one file added, nothing
  modified or removed.
- **Gate 3** Negative-tested, and honestly reported as 2 of 3 discriminating.
- **Gate 4** Scope held. Left for a decision rather than fixed uninvited: a real owner
  picker with name resolution on the requirement detail (this PR shows "someone else"
  rather than a name); the same ownership display on the detail page; and
  `frontend/src/pages/Actions.tsx:292-300`, which duplicates the token-id logic inline

author: prajith-max9
body:
Interaction polish only — no navigation, visual redesign, features or architecture touched. Audited everything first; four of seven items were already done.

## Audit: already existed vs. genuinely added

| # | Item | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Tab content transition | **Missing** — `.view` had `animation-name: none`. Added. |
| 2 | Modal/panel entrance | **Missing** — settings, graph settings, dump box, palette box, photo viewer and all three backdrops had no animation. Added. |
| 3 | Optimistic save | **Skipped deliberately** — see below. |
| 4 | AI busy states | **Already existed** — Ask (`ASKING…` + disabled + "Reading your notes…"), Synthesize (`SYNTHESIZING…`), Digest (`DIGESTING…`), Brain Dump ("Splitting into notes…"). No change. |
| 5 | Smooth height changes | **Partial** — `collapseThen()` existed but only for resurface/echo dismissal. AI results snapped in. Added an entrance for those. |
| 6 | Scroll preservation | **Genuinely broken** — measured 348 → 0. Fixed. |
| 7 | Keyboard/focus | **Already sensible** — palette autofocuses, save refocuses the composer, edit focuses the textarea, and entering a tab does *not* autofocus (which would pop the keyboard unexpectedly). No change. |

Reduced-motion was already a global `*` override, so every rule added here inherits it — verified, not assumed.

## Item 3 — skipped, with reasoning

`saveStore` is a **synchronous** `localStorage.setItem` — measured at 0.40ms for a 30-note store. The composer already closes in the same tick as the write. There is no wait to hide and no perceived speed to gain; the only thing an optimistic path could introduce is a window where the UI has moved on and the S-1 storage-full guarantee hasn't caught up. Taking that risk for zero gain is a bad trade, so I took the brief's explicit option to skip and report. **`verify-s1.js` re-run and passing.**

## Two implementation notes worth reading

**The view fade is opacity-only, not translate.** `#synth-bar` is `position: fixed` *inside* `#view-ideas`. A transform on `.view` would make it a containing block for the full 180ms and throw the bar across the screen on every tab switch. A fade reads as the transition without buying that bug — asserted in the suite.

**Scroll restoration can't be set once.** A view's height settles over several frames as swapped fonts reflow text, so an early `scrollTo` is clamped against a still-short document; and setting `location.hash` makes the browser adjust scroll itself a frame or two later, silently undoing an offset that had already landed. The restore re-asserts each frame for a short bounded window.

## ⚠️ Flagging a product decision, not deciding it

**`#tabs` is `position: relative`, not sticky.** Reaching the tab bar means scrolling to the top first — so by the time a tab is *tapped*, the offset is already 0 and there is nothing to preserve. Restoration therefore works on the paths that don't need the tab bar (back gesture, programmatic navigation — verified restoring exactly), and is a no-op for tab taps.

Making tab taps preserve scroll needs one of: tracking scroll continuously per view (so returning restores where you were *reading*, even though you deliberately scrolled to the top to leave — arguably wrong), or making the tab bar sticky (a navigation/layout change, explicitly out of scope). **Not deciding this unilaterally — tell me which you want, if either.**

## Test plan

New `verify-smooth.js`, 24 checks on a 390×780 phone viewport: every entrance animation present and in the 150–220ms band, the opacity-only rationale asserted, AI busy state observable mid-flight against a held-open mock, scroll restoration on both real paths, tab taps unchanged, fresh loads starting at top, `openNote` still winning over restoration, and reduced-motion collapsing all of it.

17 suites green, S-1 explicitly included.

author: nguyencanhqk
body:
## Vấn đề

Owner báo 2026-08-05: *"FE không tự deploy kể cả đã merge"*. Đo lại: pipeline **có** chạy và bản live **đúng** là master — nhưng nó **âm thầm mất deploy 2 lần** hôm 04/08 và không có gì báo đỏ.

`concurrency.cancel-in-progress: true` (group theo `github.ref`, có ở **cả 4** workflow) gặp luồng chuẩn của dự án — `merge PR → gen-status → commit → push`, hai commit cách nhau ~2 phút trên cùng `master` ⇒ **cùng group**:

- run của **commit merge** (đang build/deploy 3 app) → **`cancelled`**
- run của **commit STATUS** (docs-only) → `Detect changed apps` thấy không app nào đổi ⇒ Build/Deploy **`skipped`** ⇒ kết thúc **`success`** trong ~26s

`cancelled` và `skipped` **đều không phải failure**, nên `gh run list` nhìn qua thì "xong hết".

**Đo được trên 25 run master gần nhất:**

| Run | Commit | Kết quả |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `30875769114` | merge S7-CHAT-FE-1 (#334) | `cancelled` — deploy **không chạy** |
| `30880774978` | merge S7-CHAT-FE-2 (#336, trang `/chat`) | `cancelled` — deploy **không chạy** |

⇒ Trang `/chat` chỉ thực sự lên Pages ở merge **kế tiếp** (FE-3), hơn 1,5 giờ sau. Cùng lỗi này từng nuốt S5-FND-THEME-AA-1 (#289) hôm 25/07 — theme mới nằm trên master còn 3 app live vẫn màu cũ.

## Bản vá

**1. `cancel-in-progress` chỉ áp cho nhánh PR** (`apps-frontend` · `ci` · `api` · `security`).

Trên master/main hai run nối đuôi nhau — chậm hơn vài phút nhưng không mất bản. Ba file không-deploy vẫn nên sửa: thứ đang mất ở đó là **bằng chứng cổng** (RLS/integration, secret-scan) của commit **đã nằm trên master**; run thay thế nó là docs-only, xanh trong 26 giây.

**2. Bước `Verify bundle live == bundle vừa deploy`** trong job deploy — so tên bundle trong `dist/index.html` với bundle mà alias production **đang phục vụ**, retry 8×15s, lệch ⇒ **ĐỎ** kèm tên cả hai bản.

`wrangler` exit 0 không chứng minh gì: deploy nhầm nhánh preview, sai tên project, alias không cập nhật — tất cả đều để lại exit 0 + bundle **cũ** trên domain. Dùng `<project>.pages.dev` chứ không custom domain, để "đỏ vì DNS/cache" không trỏ sai chỗ điều tra.

**Không đổi:** trigger, path-filter, ma trận app, gate `DEPLOY_FE_ENABLED`, secrets/environment.

## Nghiệm thu

YAML cả 4 file parse sạch (`js-yaml`), `cancel-in-progress` resolve đúng biểu thức. Hiệu lực thật chỉ có **sau khi vào master** — push event dùng bản workflow trên nhánh mặc định. Cách chứng minh sau merge: merge một PR chạm FE rồi push STATUS ngay sau như thường lệ, run của commit merge phải chạy **tới cùng** thay vì `cancelled`.

author: juanmaguitar
body:
Adds automated review on top of the existing unit suite, split into two layers that are deliberately kept apart.

| Layer | Covers | Tool |
|---|---|---|
| Deterministic | Style, formatting, unused vars, JSDoc, React hooks | ESLint + `@wordpress/eslint-plugin` |
| Judgement | Architecture, security, performance, cross-platform | Claude via `claude-code-action` |

The split is the point. When style and process nits share space with substantive findings, authors skip the nits and the real findings get buried with them. Handing style to a linter keeps the agent's output on things a linter cannot decide.

## Why this repo needs it

This is a public repo aimed at Contributor Day newcomers, and it carries invariants that are not visible in a diff — child processes run on Electron's bundled Node rather than the host's, Git goes through `isomorphic-git` with no binary to shell out to, `electron-store` is the only persistence layer, servers bind to loopback so a contributor's `admin`/`admin` WordPress is not served to the conference wifi. Those are exactly what a first-time contributor breaks, and exactly what a well-primed automated first pass catches cheaply.

## What is in each commit

**ESLint.** `@wordpress/eslint-plugin`, so this project follows the same JS standards as `wordpress-develop` and `gutenberg`. Plus `.editorconfig` ported from `wordpress-develop`.

Prettier is deliberately absent. `configs.recommended` layers it on top of `recommended-with-formatting`, but only when the package is installed — and it arrives transitively under the plugin, so switching it off had to be explicit. Indentation here is genuinely mixed (tabs in `src/*.js` and `test/`, four spaces in `src/renderer/index.jsx` and `scripts/azure-sign.cjs`), and enabling Prettier reported **2937 problems, 2863 of them pure formatting**. `curly` is off for the same reason: it fires on 142 single-line guards that are the house style.

What remains is **85 real findings** of inherited debt, none of them formatting. `test/` is already clean.

CI lints **only the files a PR touches**. `eslint .` would fail every PR over code its author never opened; scoping to the diff holds new code to the standard from day one while the backlog is cleared separately — the same trade `gutenberg` makes with its lint suppression files.

**Agent review.** `.github/ai-review-rules.md` is the asset; the runner is replaceable. Two callers read that one file — the CI workflow and a `/self-review` skill — so the standard CI applies is the same one an author can apply *before* opening a PR.

Reporting rules: severity and scope on every finding so `[follow-up]` is distinguishable from ignored, style notes collapsed out of the body, and reconciliation against the previous run instead of re-asserting from a fresh read.

## Safety

- **Never approves, requests changes, or merges.** The tool allowlist grants no path to any of those. Not a required check.
- **Fork PRs are skipped, not failed.** They receive no secrets. Covering them safely needs a separate `pull_request_target` workflow that reads the diff without ever executing the PR's code — checking out untrusted code alongside these credentials would hand the repository away.
- **The credentials guard is a step, not a job-level `if`**, because the `secrets` context is unavailable there. Without it, every fork PR would carry a failing check, which only teaches people to ignore CI.
- Neither workflow ever executes a PR's code (`npm ci --ignore-scripts`).

## Testing

Verified locally:

- `npm test` → 113/113 pass; the dependency install moved no production dependency and no existing devDependency (`electron` still 43.2.0)
- `npx eslint .` → 85 findings, the documented baseline
- Changed-files lint: generated `bundle.js` is ignored without warning noise, an injected `==` is caught, a clean file exits 0
- Both workflows parse as valid YAML; the credentials guard was exercised with and without a token

Verified on CI by this PR: the `eslint` job passes.

**Not fully verified:** the review job's integration with `claude-code-action` — that the prompt yields the right format, that inline comments land on the right lines, that `gh pr comment --edit-last` is genuinely sticky across re-runs. This PR is the first live exercise.

## Setup notes

Requires the `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` secret. Until it exists the review step skips cleanly and the job stays green.

GitHub authentication is separate from the Claude API token. By default the action authenticates as the official Claude GitHub App over OIDC, which must be installed on the repository — not something a repo maintainer can do in this org. Passing `github_token` takes priority over that exchange, so the job uses the built-in Actions token and comments arrive from `github-actions[bot]`.

A good calibration case: `src/main.js`'s `url:open` handler passes its argument straight to `shell.openExternal()` with no scheme check, so `file://` and `javascript:` get through. If a PR touches that handler and the review does not flag it, the prompt needs tuning. Worth its own issue regardless.

## Follow-ups

- Clear the 85-finding backlog so lint can widen to the whole repo and become required
- Fix the `url:open` scheme validation
- Normalise indentation, then reconsider Prettier

| #3, #5, #6, #7 | undici | moderate x4 | 7.28.0 | **7.29.0** |

Branched off `main` (not `phase2`) per the standing instruction for site dependencies. A follow-up PR merges the updated `main` back into `phase2`.

## Runtime or build-only?

**Build-only / dev-only — this is the key context for the two "high" alerts.**

Both packages are transitive through the local dev toolchain: `wrangler -> miniflare -> {sharp, undici}`. miniflare is the *local* Workers emulator; it is not part of the bundle wrangler uploads to Cloudflare. GitHub itself classifies all six as `"scope": "development"`.

Evidence, not assumption: `npm audit --omit=dev` reports **0 vulnerabilities before the change as well as after**. And no workflow deploys this worker — `deploy-site.yml` builds `site/` for Pages only; `wrangler deploy` is manual. So the exposure was a developer running the local emulator, never the deployed site.

## What was done, and why they needed different mechanisms

### sharp — reproduced the existing phase2 fix
Alert #1 was **already fixed on `phase2`** (commit 29f691e) and only stayed open because `main` never received it. I reproduced that commit's approach verbatim rather than inventing a new one, so the two branches do not disagree about the same dependency:

- `wrangler` `^4.0.0` -> `^4.114.0` (first release carrying a miniflare with sharp 0.35.2)
- `@cloudflare/workers-types` `^4.20250620.0` -> `^5.20260722.1`

The types **major** is forced, not optional: wrangler 4.114 has a `peerOptional` on `@cloudflare/workers-types ^5`, so the advisory cannot be cleared without it (this is why `npm audit fix` fails here). `tsc --noEmit` is clean and **no source edits were needed** for the v4 -> v5 bump.

### undici — required an `overrides` entry
Per the brief I checked for a parent bump first. There isn't one. **miniflare pins `undici@7.28.0` as an exact version, and every published release does** — including the newest stable `4.20260730.0` and the `5.20260730.0-alpha` that wrangler 4.118 pulls in. With no compatible parent release, `overrides` is the only mechanism:

```json
"overrides": { "undici": "^7.29.0" }
```

Caret rather than an exact pin, so future 7.x patches flow in without another PR; `^7.29.0` stays within undici's major and cannot jump to the 8.x line that would break miniflare.

### One deliberate judgement call
The lockfile is held at **wrangler 4.114.0 / miniflare 4.20260722.0** — phase2's exact resolution — rather than letting `^4.114.0` float to the current 4.118.0, because **4.118.0 depends on miniflare `5.20260730.0-alpha`**. Both routes give sharp 0.35.2, so there was no reason to take an alpha emulator to fix a dev-only advisory.

## Verification (real output)

A lockfile edit that leaves a stale nested copy is exactly the "looks fixed but isn't" pattern, so the tree was re-checked from scratch:

**`npm audit` before:** `4 high severity vulnerabilities` (sharp + undici)
**`npm audit` after:** `found 0 vulnerabilities`
**`npm audit --omit=dev`:** `found 0 vulnerabilities` — both before *and* after

```
$ rm -rf node_modules && npm ci
added 39 packages, and audited 40 packages
found 0 vulnerabilities

$ npm ls undici sharp --all
gitloom-site-api@1.0.0
└─┬ wrangler@4.114.0
  └─┬ miniflare@4.20260722.0
    ├── sharp@0.35.2
    └── undici@7.29.0

$ find node_modules -type d \( -name undici -o -name sharp \) -prune -print
node_modules/sharp
node_modules/undici        <- exactly one copy of each; no surviving nested 7.28.0
```

- `npx tsc --noEmit` -> clean (exit 0)
- `npx wrangler deploy --dry-run` -> **7.75 KiB**, D1 + env bindings intact (identical to phase2's recorded result)
- **Booted Miniflare and dispatched a fetch** -> `200`, serving over undici 7.29.0. Worth calling out: the dry-run only exercises esbuild bundling, so it would *not* have caught the override breaking the emulator. This does.
- `site/`: `npm ci`, `npm run build`, `oxlint` all green. Untouched by this PR, but `deploy-site.yml` triggers on `site/**`, so it will run on merge.

The worker has no `build`/`test` script (`deploy`, `dev`, `tail` only), hence `tsc --noEmit` + `wrangler deploy --dry-run` as the build check.

## Scope

`site/worker/package.json` + `site/worker/package-lock.json`, nothing else. No source changes. No .NET project and no `packages.lock.json` touched, so CI's `--locked-mode` is unaffected — disjoint from the open .NET PRs (#290, #292, #295). `package-lock.json` was regenerated by npm, never hand-edited.

No breaking change was forced in the worker: the one major bump (workers-types v4 -> v5) typechecks clean with zero source edits.
