body:
Three new pages targeting commercial-intent queries, plus the FAQ fix that the Kukas delisting made necessary.

## What is here

| Page | Targets |
|---|---|
| `/celebrations-in-jaipur` | villa for birthday party in Jaipur, private villa celebration, farmhouse party near Jaipur |
| `/family-getaways-near-jaipur` | family getaway near Jaipur, villa for family, weekend getaway from Delhi |
| `/book-direct` | Airbnb alternative, book villa direct, without the listing site |

Each has its own title, meta description, canonical, `BreadcrumbList` schema, a keyword-bearing H1, real H2 structure, internal links to both property pages, and a WhatsApp CTA.

## Everything is grounded in what the properties actually are

Capacity is stated plainly — 30–50 day guests on the lawns, ten sleeping over. The celebrations page says outright that it is not a banquet-scale venue, and the book-direct page says Stayra is two houses, not a catalogue, and will turn you away if the group is too big.

That is deliberate. Pages that oversell capacity rank for queries they cannot serve and bounce.

**Not built: party places / corporate parties in Jaipur.** Those searchers want 50–300 pax banquet venues. With The Kukas Villa gone, the largest capacity is 30–50 day guests, so a page chasing those terms would earn traffic that leaves immediately.

## FAQ fix

The events answer said "allowed at select properties" — which, after delisting Kukas, pointed at nothing specific. It now names Kankas House, gives the 30–50 figure, and states that Choti Haveli is not an events property.

## Also

- All three added to `sitemap.ts` (20 -> 23 URLs)
- Linked from the footer so they are not orphans

## Verification — please read

- ⚠️ **No local typecheck.** My sandbox ran out of disk mid-session and stayed broken, so this is the second PR I could not verify locally. The Vercel check is the only gate here — please confirm green before merging.
- Pages use only `next`, `next/link` and the existing `BreadcrumbSchema`, so the surface area for a build error is small, but that is reasoning rather than a test.
- After deploy: confirm the three URLs render, the sitemap shows 23, and submit them for indexing.

author: jlucaso1
body:
`AudioExtractor` 47.2% → **69.9%**; `src/` opted-in 72.52% → **73.46%**. Stacked on #146.

The pieces were pinned; the *pass* was not. This runs the standalone extraction over the game's own bundle into a cache the test owns — the fallback road every session takes when its mesh cache is warm and its audio cache is cold, or when the cold load's own pass was cancelled or could not stream a bundle.

**What it holds is that the pass produces clips *and* marks them complete.** `def.bin` is the cache's only completeness signal:
- clips written without it → re-extracts forever;
- it written without clips → every later boot skips the definition and plays silence, with nothing ever looking at it again.

And the other direction: a full cache reports nothing outstanding and opens nothing — what keeps a warm session from decoding a 110 MB bundle behind a loading screen for audio it already has. Proven by handing the second run a bundle path that *could not possibly be read*: if it opened it, it would have thrown.

410 runtime tests passing, format and `-warnaserror` clean.

author: adamtheturtle
body:
## Summary
- forward session, task, redirect, authentication, metrics, data, and cache callbacks through the Linux bounded loader
- run the child bounded session on the caller-supplied delegate queue
- add Linux regression coverage proving task completion reaches the supplied delegate

Closes #38
Follow-up to review feedback on #37.

## Validation
- `swift test`
- `swift build --build-tests`
- `swiftlint lint --strict`
- `git diff --check`

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Touches Linux networking delegate forwarding and auth/redirect handling; behavior change for custom URLSession delegates but scoped to Linux and guarded by tests.
> 
> **Overview**
> On Linux, **`URLSessionTransport`** uses **`BoundedURLSessionLoader`** for response-size limits instead of streaming bytes. That inner session used **`self`** as the only delegate and **`nil`** for the delegate queue, so callers’ **`URLSession`** delegate and queue were ignored.
> 
> The loader now takes the original **`session.delegate`** and **`session.delegateQueue`**, runs the bounded child session on that queue, and **forwards** delegate callbacks (auth, redirects, upload progress, metrics, cache, data, task completion) after its own size checks. Data is only forwarded when it passes the limit; overflow still cancels and fails as before.
> 
> A **Linux-only** test asserts **`didCompleteWithError`** reaches a supplied **`URLSessionTaskDelegate`**.
> 
> <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 2c168bcbe5ac3ce1052c8ff773b21977e1ab03fb. Bugbot is set up for automated code reviews on this repo. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).</sup>

This PR adds a new abstract hatch class, `MTEHatchRedstoneBase.java`, which stores a signal on each face allowing for directional output, as well as having behavior for directionality and invertedness, which inheritors can override or cancel. body:
Both `quick-xml` entries in `deny.toml` say the exposure comes from `azure_core`/`typespec` and that there is no newer `typespec` to move to. I think that has stopped being true, and the comment now points away from where the affected code actually is.

Checking the current lockfile:

| quick-xml | pulled by | affected by RUSTSEC-2026-0194/0195? |
|---|---|---|
| 0.41.0 | `typespec 1.1.0`, `quick-junit 0.6.1` | no — 0.41.0 is the fixed version |
| 0.37.4 | `opendal 0.54.0` | yes |
| 0.31.0 | this repo, `Cargo.toml:489` | yes |
| 0.39.2 | not in the lockfile | — |

So `typespec` has already moved to the fixed 0.41, and the version named in the comment isn't in the tree any more. What is still affected is `opendal`'s 0.37.4 and the direct `quick-xml = "0.31"` this repo declares for the `sources-windows_event_log` feature.

**The ignores are still needed** — 0.31 and 0.37.4 are genuinely affected, so removing them would turn `deny` red. This only updates the two `reason` strings so they describe the paths that are actually there. No code or dependency change.

I mention it because #25076 deliberately consolidated these entries with issue links, so it seemed like the kind of thing worth keeping accurate rather than letting it drift.

Separately, and not part of this PR: the direct `quick-xml = "0.31"` is the one path that isn't blocked on anyone upstream. Moving it to 0.41 would drop one of the two affected paths, though it crosses several breaking releases and the `serialize` usage in the windows_event_log source would need a proper look — happy to open a separate issue for that if it's useful.

Could you add `no-changelog`? There's no user-facing change here.

---

*Disclosure: I used an AI coding agent (Claude Opus 5) to help find this and check the dependency graph. I verified the lockfile paths and the advisory version ranges myself before opening this.*

body:
This pull request is a step 1 of large API update. It updates how parties (Beteiligte) and their roles are handled and displayed in the application, standardizing the data model and improving the display logic. It also refactors API response handling for fetching courts and procedures to use stricter schemas, and updates tests to match the new data structures.

**Data model and logic improvements:**

* Refactored the `Beteiligte` model to use `nachname`, `vorname`, and `bezeichnung` instead of a generic `name`, and updated the `Rolle` model to nest the role code under `rollenbezeichnung` and include `geschaeftszeichen`. New utility functions `getBeteiligteDisplayName` and `getGeschaeftszeichenByRoleCode` were added for extracting display names and business references. 

**API and schema changes:**

* Changed the API response schemas for fetching courts (`fetchGerichte`) and procedures (`fetchVerfahren`) to expect a top-level object with an `elemente` array, improving type safety and consistency. 

**Test updates:**

author: sfitzgerald-x1
body:
## Summary

C116 Phase 3 **item 9** — the last open Phase 3 item. A **harness** change, landed separately from any fidelity change per the program's own rule.

Showdown gives a Pokémon arriving on a forced replacement no residual tick: the replacement completes the *previous* turn rather than starting a new one. `19000020/50`'s entire protocol is two `|switch|` lines and `|turn|47`. The engine, asked for a full turn, faithfully runs one and over-emits — so all three A1 rows are uniformly `component_extra_in_engine` with `observed_only=[]`:

| row | engine_only |
|---|---|
| `19000020/50` | `('itemleftovers', 18)` |
| `19000059/27` | `('psn', -16)` |
| `19100181/45` | `('itemleftovers', 16), ('psn', -16), ('sandstorm', -16)` |

The engine is not computing residuals wrongly; it is being asked for a turn on a ply Showdown treats as the tail of the previous one. That confirms item 9's "harness marker" framing.

## The first attempt failed, and the PR records why

Keying on the absence of `|upkeep|` **alone** gave dev 4 → **34** and holdout 11 → **41**, opening 44 rows. `|upkeep|` is also absent whenever the battle **ends** during residuals — Showdown emits the tick, then `|faint|`, then `|win|` — so the filter stripped the engine's residuals there and manufactured divergences. It even reopened `19100002/53`, the battle-end sandstorm row **#1092 had just fixed**.

Root cause of my error: I validated the observable on the 15 rows already known to be divergent, and never on the ~15,000 **matching** boundaries where absence of `|upkeep|` is common and benign. The `|win|` clause is the fix, and the pin asserts all four clauses survive and stay ANDed.

## Scoping is the design

`19100180/24` **also** lacks `|upkeep|` — Medicham switches into Spikes and faints — but its engine-only component is `spikes`, a hazard mis-attributed to a side whose active never changed. Different cause. Filtering only **residual** sources leaves it divergent by construction, and the sweep confirms it rather than my asserting it.

## Verification Evidence

Single-variable: engine held fixed at the 61-patch stack, only the harness differs.

| window | boundaries | matched | diverged | closed | opened |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| dev | 15,224 | 15,220 → **15,222** | 4 → **2** | `19000020/50`, `19000059/27` | **none** |
| validation holdout | 15,396 | 15,385 → **15,386** | 11 → **10** | `19100181/45` | **none** |

Identity `matched + diverged == boundaries` holds on all four rows. `19100180/24` verified still divergent. Artifacts committed as `reports/artifacts/c127_a1_marker_{dev,holdout}_sweep.json`.

**Pin exercises the shipped predicate and source set via `inspect`**, not a local reimplementation — an earlier draft reimplemented the filter inline and would have passed with the real one deleted. Revert check run properly: **7/7 pass with the marker, 7/7 fail without** (2 failures, 5 errors). The first revert check was itself vacuous, because `git stash push` failed on syntax and the suite ran twice against the same file.

## Risk Assessment

The dangerous direction is suppressing a real divergence. Three guards: the filter touches only the **engine** side (a pin asserts `obs_exact_branch` is not rewritten, so under-emissions still surface); it is scoped to residual sources; and both sweeps show **nothing opened and nothing closed beyond the three A1 rows**.

A predicate-selectivity probe measured v2 firing on 248 dev boundaries, only 2 divergent. I initially treated that as a failure, which was wrong — firing is harmless where the engine emitted nothing to strip, and a boundary where it *did* would already be divergent. The sweep confirms all 246 matching firings are inert.

## Note

This PR is **self-reviewed**; independent review has been unobtainable across sixteen attempts and two model tiers. Held unmerged per the owner's instruction.

author: martialcayre-sketch
body:
## Le manque

`CLAUDE.md` présente `.claude/hooks/block-risky-commands.test.mjs` comme le banc du mur d'écriture — celui qui refuse `.env*`, `.git/`, les commandes destructives et celles qui exposent un secret.

Il n'était joué par aucun workflow :

```
$ grep -rn '\.claude/hooks' .github/workflows/
(rien)
```

Le mur n'avait donc pour filet que les exécutions locales. C'est mot pour mot le motif qui justifie le banc anti-secrets voisin (`ci.yml:113`) : **un garde redevenu muet reste vert.**

## Le changement

Une étape, juste après le banc anti-secrets :

```yaml
- name: Hooks de garde-fous (banc du mur d'écriture)
  run: node --test .claude/hooks/*.test.mjs
```

**Inconditionnelle**, pour deux raisons. Le banc n'importe que des modules `node:` — ni npm ni base, exactement comme `check_no_secrets.test.mjs` au-dessus. Et le gater sur `docs_only` serait ici plus dangereux qu'ailleurs : `.claude/hooks/**` est du code de garde-fou, jamais de la prose. Le classer un jour côté documentaire rejouerait ce que le registre des instruments a déjà coûté — un fichier qui fait autorité sur le chemin court, ses seuls contrôles gatés, `verify` vert.

**Glob plutôt que chemin en dur** : un banc de hook ajouté demain est joué sans toucher `ci.yml`, et si le fichier disparaît le glob reste littéral et `node --test` échoue. La disparition est bruyante — là où `node --test .claude/hooks/` passerait en silence.

## Vérification

| Contrôle | Résultat |
|---|---|
| Banc sur le hook intact | 27 tests, 0 échec |
| **Falsification** — copie du hook rendue muette par un `process.exit(0)` en tête | **18 échecs sur 27, sortie 1** |
| YAML | parsé, 54 étapes |
| `scripts/check_no_secrets.sh` | OK |

La falsification a tourné sur une copie en scratchpad, pas sur le hook du dépôt : le garde-fou de la session est resté actif tout du long, et `git status` ne montre que `ci.yml`.

## Ce que cette PR ne fait pas

Elle **ne raccourcit pas** le CI. La piste étudiée — faire passer `.claude/**` par le chemin `docs_only` — est abandonnée après vérification :

- `.claude/skills/**` et `.claude/agents/**` ne contiennent que des `.md`, donc ils empruntent **déjà** le chemin court via la règle `\.md$` : rien à y gagner ;
- le seul fichier que ça changerait, `.claude/settings.json`, fait autorité (il câble les hooks) et doit rester sur le chemin code.

Le rendre `docs_only` supposerait d'abord un contrôle d'intégrité inconditionnel de ce fichier — disproportionné pour un fichier édité rarement, et c'est une PR distincte s'il le faut un jour.

body:
## Summary

Closes #27718

- `CompileFatal::formatZendStderrLine` now emits `PHP Fatal error:` / `PHP Parse error:` with two spaces after the colon, matching Zend CLI stderr format
- All `LogicException`-based runtime fatals in VM (`ImplementsHierarchyRuntimeCheck`, `TraitCompositionConflictMessage`, `RedundantIterableUnionCheck`, `RedundantTrueFalseUnionCheck`, `DateTimeInterfaceSupport`, `ArraySpread`) emit `PHP Fatal error:` prefix
- JIT `ImplementsHierarchyJitGuard` updated to not double-prefix
- Builds on cherry-picked 71690968 which converted never-return/abstract/final-const to throw `CompileFatal`

## Verification

```bash
# All three issue repros now match Zend:
echo '<?php function f(): never { return 1; }' > /tmp/t.php
php bin/vm.php /tmp/t.php 2>&1
# → PHP Fatal error:  A never-returning function must not return in /tmp/t.php on line 1

echo '<?php abstract class A{abstract function f();}class B extends A{}' > /tmp/t.php
```

body: ### Fixed - **The health check reported on the wrong agent runtime.** It looked for a `claude` command on the system path, which measured nothing useful: neither supported runtime is a command on the path. Both are libraries the node loads directly, and the Claude one runs a program bundled inside that library rather than anything you could install yourself. So the check could say a runtime was fine when the node could not run it, and vice versa. It also only ever looked for Claude, even on a node whose stages were about to run on Pi because that is what the connected model provider needs, so the report could confirm a runtime the run never touched. The node now answers this with the same detection it uses to decide which runtimes it advertises, and it answers for whichever runtimes the workspace's connected providers actually need. author: experintellia
body:
## The problem

`verify-release-tag.yml` is the single gate every publishing workflow hangs off, and its own header was honest about its limit: it proved things about the *ref* and nothing about the *build*. A tag is only allowed on a commit that is an ancestor of `main` — but "merged" is not "tested". Post-merge CI runs for minutes after a merge lands, so a tag pushed in that window shipped a commit nobody had a green result for; so did a tag on a commit whose CI later went red.

The second gap is structural: a tag-push run executes the workflow files **at the tagged commit**, and both release workflows load the gate with `uses: ./.github/workflows/verify-release-tag.yml` from that same ref. Anyone who can push a `v*` tag to a commit of their choosing can push one where the gate — or the caller's `needs:` on it — has been weakened or deleted. `workflow_dispatch` against a chosen ref behaves the same way. **No change inside this repository can close that**; it needs GitHub-side rulesets and environment protections, which are not in version control and were documented nowhere.

## What this PR changes

**Gate (`verify-release-tag.yml`)** — one new step, in the one shared copy, so both callers inherit it. It queries the check-runs API for `$GITHUB_SHA` (the tag's commit, proven unmoved by the step above it) for each required check — `lint` and `test`, ci.yml's job names — with `filter=latest` so a re-run supersedes its predecessor's verdict rather than adding to it.

It fails closed on every path that is not an affirmative success:

| situation | API says | result |
|---|---|---|
| CI never ran on this commit | empty `check_runs` | `missing none` → fail |
| still queued / building | `queued` / `in_progress` | → fail |
| failed, cancelled, timed out, skipped | `completed` + a non-success conclusion | → fail |
| API unreadable (403 / 404 / network / bad JSON) | `gh api` exits non-zero | → fail, with a hint about `checks: read` |
| green | `completed success` | pass |

The header's "proves three things … and nothing about the build" list is now four, and gained a paragraph naming what the gate still cannot prove (its own integrity) with a pointer to the checklist below.

**Permissions.** Reading check runs needs `checks: read`, and a called workflow can only ever be granted permissions its caller holds — so `deploy-pages.yml`'s `verify-tag` job now grants it alongside `contents: read`.

**Docs (`RELEASING.md`)** — a new "Repository settings the release model depends on" section: an actionable admin checklist plus `gh api` one-liners to read back what is really configured.

## Requires a repo admin — this PR cannot enforce any of it

The settings half lives in GitHub, not in git. Merging this changes nothing about it. An admin has to:

1. **Tag ruleset for `v*`** (Settings → Rules → Rulesets): restrict creations, updates and deletions; bypass list = release maintainers only. This is what protects the gate from being edited by the same push that triggers it — without it everything else here is advisory.
2. **Branch ruleset for `main`**: PR required, ≥1 approval, dismiss stale approvals on push, require approval of the most recent reviewable push, required status checks `lint` + `test` (the same names the gate now demands), no force pushes or deletions, empty bypass list.
3. **`github-pages` environment**: keep the `v*` tag rule, and add **required reviewers** + prevent self-review — `deploy-pages.yml`'s header notes the tag rule exists today, but nothing puts a human in front of a prod deploy.
4. **A protected environment for the npm publish**: `publish-npm.yml` uses none at all today, so the trusted-publisher OIDC token is minted with no approval step. Create one with the same `v*` rule and reviewers, referenced from the job that holds `id-token: write`.

## Follow-up / overlap with the publish-npm restructure

`publish-npm.yml` and `.github/actions/build-web-app/action.yml` are being restructured in a separate PR and are **deliberately untouched here**. Two things belong to that PR or a follow-up:

- `publish-npm.yml`'s `verify-tag` job needs the same one-line `checks: read` grant `deploy-pages.yml` got. Until it has it, a `v*` tag push fails that workflow at validation ("requesting 'checks: read', but is only allowed 'checks: none'"). That is fail-closed, not a hole, but it does block npm releases — so land the one line in either PR before the next tag.
- Item 4 above (a protected environment on the publish job) is a change to that file too.

## Not executed

GitHub Actions cannot be run from here. What was verified: both changed workflows parse (PyYAML), and the new step's script was extracted from the YAML and run against stubbed check-run responses covering green / in-progress / missing / failure / skipped / API-error — green exits 0, the other five exit 1. Its first run against a real release tag is the actual proof.

body:
## TLDR

Problem this solves:

- Multipart array params only kept their last value
- `timestamp_granularities=["segment","word"]` returned words only

How it solves it:

- Iterate `form.multi_items()` instead of `dict(form)`
- Regression test covers both orders and singletons

## Relevant issues

Fixes #35937

## Linear ticket

## Pre-Submission checklist

- [x] I have added meaningful tests
- [x] My PR passes all CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, format, unit tests)
- [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem
- [ ] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review

## Delays in PR merge?

If you're seeing a delay in your PR being merged, ping the LiteLLM Team on [Slack (#pr-review)](https://join.slack.com/t/litellmossslack/shared_invite/zt-3o7nkuyfr-p_kbNJj8taRfXGgQI1~YyA).

## Screenshots / Proof of Fix

The report blamed `whisper_transformation.py`, but that isn't where it goes wrong. The OpenAI SDK already encodes the list correctly on the way out, the loss happens on the way in: `get_form_data` did `dict(form)` on a Starlette `FormData` multidict, and a plain `dict()` of a multidict keeps only the last value per key. The OpenAI SDK sends two separate `timestamp_granularities[]` parts, so the bracket-stripping loop below it only ever saw one of them and built a one-element list

```python
>>> from starlette.datastructures import FormData
>>> f = FormData([("timestamp_granularities[]", "segment"), ("timestamp_granularities[]", "word")])
>>> dict(f)
{'timestamp_granularities[]': 'word'}
```

Proof was captured against a proxy on localhost:4000 pointed at an upstream that logs the multipart parts it receives and echoes back segments and/or words accordingly, since this bug lives entirely in how the proxy reads the inbound form and never reaches the model. Both runs use the same audio file and the same four granularity combinations

Before, at 24dbd2b2db (parent of this PR's commit, fix reverted):

```
$ for g in "segment word" "word segment" "segment" "word"; do
    args=""; for x in $g; do args="$args -F timestamp_granularities[]=$x"; done
    echo "=== [$g] ==="
    curl -s http://localhost:4000/v1/audio/transcriptions -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-1234" \
      -F file=@audio.wav -F model=whisper-1 -F response_format=verbose_json $args \
      | python3 -c "import sys,json; r=json.load(sys.stdin); print('segments', len(r.get('segments') or []), '| words', len(r.get('words') or []))"
  done
=== [segment word] ===
segments 0 | words 2
=== [word segment] ===
segments 1 | words 0
=== [segment] ===
segments 1 | words 0
=== [word] ===
segments 0 | words 2

# what the upstream actually received
UPSTREAM RECEIVED timestamp_granularities: ['word']
UPSTREAM RECEIVED timestamp_granularities: ['segment']
UPSTREAM RECEIVED timestamp_granularities: ['segment']
UPSTREAM RECEIVED timestamp_granularities: ['word']
```

After, same commands at c1f005bbd4:

```
=== timestamp_granularities = [segment word] ===
segments 1 | words 2
=== timestamp_granularities = [word segment] ===
segments 1 | words 2
=== timestamp_granularities = [segment] ===
segments 1 | words 0
=== timestamp_granularities = [word] ===
segments 0 | words 2

# what the upstream actually received
UPSTREAM RECEIVED timestamp_granularities: ['segment', 'word']
UPSTREAM RECEIVED timestamp_granularities: ['word', 'segment']
UPSTREAM RECEIVED timestamp_granularities: ['segment']
UPSTREAM RECEIVED timestamp_granularities: ['word']
```

## Type

🐛 Bug Fix

## Changes

`get_form_data` now walks `form.multi_items()`, so every repeated part is appended rather than silently dropped. This applies to every `[]` form key, not just `timestamp_granularities`, so `include[]` on the newer transcription models gets the same fix

The existing `test_get_form_data` never caught this because its mock handed the function a plain Python dict literal with a duplicate `timestamp_granularities[]` key, which Python itself collapses before the code under test runs. Its own comment admitted "in a real MultiDict, both values would be present". That mock is now a real `FormData`, and a parametrized test asserts the exact list for `["segment","word"]`, `["word","segment"]`, `["segment"]`, and `["word"]`. Two other mocks that returned bare dicts from `request.form()` were switched to `FormData` for the same reason

### Final Attestation

- [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR

body:
Two bundled stories.

### `migration-context-run-surface-untested-end-to-end`

`MigrationContext#migrate`/`#up`/`#down` had no end-to-end coverage: the four
`migration.test.ts` cases that Rails writes against
`MigrationContext.new(MIGRATIONS_ROOT + "/valid")` ran a `Migrator` over
anonymous no-op migrations instead, so nothing proved the run surface executed
DDL. They now use the context over the vendored fixture migrations already
mirrored under `test-helpers/migrations/valid/`:

- `migration context with default schema migration` and `migrator versions` —
  migration_test.rb:86-100 and :106-120. `up` then `down`, asserting
  `currentVersion` / `needsMigration`, plus (in `migrator versions`) that
  `people.last_name` and the `reminders` table really appeared and were
  reversed, and that `schema_migrations` recorded `[1, 2, 3]`.
- `name collision across dbs` — migration_test.rb:122-128. Drops the per-test
  adapter swap it used to need; the migration and `Person` now ride the same
  canonical connection, as they do in Rails.
- `filtering migrations` — migration_test.rb:523-538, including the `down`
  half with the same name filter.

`migration-context.trails.test.ts` gains routing coverage for `#migrate`
(no target → up, lower target → down), which has no Rails test of its own —
upstream reaches it through `DatabaseTasks.migrate`.

Both files undo the DDL in `afterEach`, mirroring migration_test.rb's teardown.

### `burn-down-non-transactional-row-write-ratchet` (first slice, 44 → 42)

- `encryption/encryptable-record-api.test.ts` takes the
  `beforeAll(freshAdapter) + withTransactionalFixtures` shape its sibling
  `encryptable-record.test.ts` got in #5719 — it writes posts and books on the
  shared canonical connection, exactly the leak class that broke three lanes
  there.
- `support/handler-resolved-adapter.test.ts` takes `useTransactionalTests()`;
  its table stays laid in `beforeAll`, outside the per-test transaction.

I triaged all 44 rows. The remaining 42 are not wrap-convergeable: 24+ are
`adapters/*` files that build and close a throwaway `:memory:` / per-test
PostgreSQL adapter around every case, several drop their own tables in
`afterEach` (which is what Rails' `Migration::TestHelper` does too), and about a
dozen are textual false positives (`AliasTracker.create`, `SchemaDumper.create`,
`Object.create`, `DatabaseTasks.create(config)`, a GCM cipher's `.update`).
`support/setup-adapter-suite.test.ts` is already transactional via
`setupAdapterSuite`, which the per-file textual check cannot see. That analysis
is filed as `0064/retire-non-transactional-ratchet-non-wrappable-classes`
rather than resolved by widening anything here.

Closes-story: burn-down-non-transactional-row-write-ratchet
Closes-story: migration-context-run-surface-untested-end-to-end

## Problem

`MarkdownRenderer` statically imports optional peer dependencies (`marked`, `highlight.js`, `isomorphic-dompurify`). When a consumer app hasn't installed these packages, the import crashes at module load time — even if `MarkdownRenderer` is never actually rendered.

## Solution

Convert the static imports to dynamic `import()` calls inside `onMount`. The component now:

- Loads `marked`, `marked-highlight`, `highlight.js`, and `isomorphic-dompurify` asynchronously on mount
- Falls back to escaped-text rendering if any dependency is missing
- Properly cleans up via the `onMount` return function

author: dzakh
body:
## Summary

Simplifies chain-id field name validation by reserving both `chainId` and `chain_id` spellings unconditionally on per-chain entities, rather than checking which spelling each storage backend produces. This ensures the reserved name never depends on where an entity is stored.

## Key Changes

- **Validation logic**: `validate_chain_id_column_names` → `validate_chain_id_field_names` now checks GraphQL field names directly against `RESERVED_CHAIN_ID_FIELD_NAMES` (`["chainId", "chain_id"]`) instead of deriving reserved names per backend's `column_name_format`
- **Error messages**: Updated to say "using a name reserved for the chain id" instead of "collide with the chain-id column", and clarified that cross-chain entities get "no chain id" appended
- **Public config JSON**: 
  - `defaultCrossChain` now omitted when `true` (the default), so projects predating per-chain entities produce identical JSON and don't trigger reindex
  - `crossChain` per entity now omitted when it matches the resolved default, reducing diff noise
- **Test coverage**: Added three new test cases:
  - Both spellings reserved regardless of storage backend configuration
  - Derived fields (`@derivedFrom`) that claim the chain-id name are rejected
  - Public config JSON omits default values to maintain backward compatibility
- **Code generation**: Updated TypeScript type definition to use `TestIndexerEntityRow` for proper chain-id field inclusion in per-chain entity changes

## Implementation Details

The key insight is that both `chainId` (GraphQL surface) and `chain_id` (potential database column) must be reserved on the user's schema, independent of backend configuration. This prevents a field name from being valid or invalid based on storage backend choice—a user-facing concern that shouldn't depend on deployment details.

The public config JSON changes ensure that projects created before per-chain entities were introduced continue producing the same JSON output, preventing unnecessary reindex requests when the compatibility check diffs against stored state.

### Context

During organization onboarding, the UI launches one manual scan request per provider. On trial accounts, the first request creates an active scan and the subscription gate rejects the remaining requests, so only one provider is scanned.

This change makes organization onboarding use the bulk scan API so the subscription gate evaluates the organization scan once.

### Description

- Launch AWS and GCP organization scans with one `POST /api/v1/scans/bulk` request.
- Send the organization ID using the JSON:API organization relationship.
- Use the returned scan collection to report the launched scan count.
- Preserve the existing per-provider daily schedule flow and concurrency limit.
- Preserve schedule-only onboarding and standalone provider scans.
- Update unit and integration tests for the bulk request and organization onboarding.

This requires Cloud API support for `POST /api/v1/scans/bulk`.

### Steps to review

1. Onboard an AWS or GCP organization and select an initial scan.
2. Verify the UI sends one `POST /api/v1/scans/bulk` request with the organization ID.
3. Verify one scan is created for every provider linked to the organization.
4. Verify daily scheduling still creates schedules for each provider.
5. Verify schedule-only onboarding does not launch a bulk scan.
6. Verify bulk scan failures keep the manual flow open and display the API error.

## Summary

- add a genuinely rootless aih policy generate path that emits a portable, self-contained Policy Workbench without reading repository config, markers, AIH_ROOT, policy state, or a run ledger
- provide a compact schema/catalog-driven authoring matrix for AIH MCP and hooks, plus clearly report-only ECC or Superpowers agent, skill, and command curation
- preserve pending custom candidates, full safely escaped approval/evidence inspection, signed clarification, and exact external-curation provenance without implying runtime effectiveness
- keep all fourteen hard blockers non-waivable, custom MCP non-activatable, and GStack absent from supported operational surfaces

## Safety and contract

- browser import, mutation, validation, and download enforce the runtime policy grammar, including HTTPS registry/index origins and root-level refinement parity
- signed approvals bind clarification and remain subject to external authority, expiry, revocation, identity, evidence, target, ownership, and projector checks
- external framework curation is typed report metadata only; AIH does not install, project, or enforce ECC or Superpowers assets
- imported authority data is untrusted, escaped, preserved for preflight inspection only, and never labelled verified or effective

## Verification

- npm run verify: 303 test files passed; 5,256 tests passed; 4 files and 25 tests skipped
- typecheck, build, generated-schema, self-hosting, artifact, and published-package checks passed
- hostile temporary-root regression proves legacy GStack config, malformed repo policy, --root, and AIH_ROOT cannot affect generation and no ledger is written
- independent contract/schema, security/round-trip, and UI/accessibility reviews passed after corrective iterations
- isolated Chrome evidence at 1440, 768, 375, and 360 shows no horizontal overflow, no external network or console errors, at least 24px targets, one live region, keyboard tooltip and field-error recovery, safe receipt disclosures, and locked curation framework edits

## Known evidence limits

- formal visual regression is inconclusive because there is no approved prior visual baseline
- axe is inconclusive because the repository has no axe runner; semantic, accessibility-tree, keyboard, contrast, reflow, and live-region checks were performed directly

SemVer: minor. No release or version publish is included.

author: aeonsynergies
body:
## Summary
- Adds complete backend structure with Express, tRPC router, Prisma schema for all models, Socket.io for real-time, JWT auth with multi-account support, and frontend API client wired up.

## Before starting: two things that didn't match the request
- **`CLAUDE.md` still doesn't exist anywhere in this repo** (confirmed again — this is the third time it's been referenced but absent). Task 2 asked to "match exactly the data model in CLAUDE.md"; with no such file, I checked with the user, who asked me to derive the Prisma schema from the frontend's `src/types/index.ts` and Phase 1 mock data instead.
- **Phase 1 (PR #1 itself) was not actually merged** when this phase started — still open, CI green, no conflicts. Per the user, I continued building Phase 2 on the same branch/PR rather than merging first.

## Backend structure (`backend/`)
- `prisma/schema.prisma` — the 11 requested models (`User`, `WorkspaceMember`, `Workspace`, `Contact`, `Conversation`, `ConversationMember`, `Message`, `Attachment`, `Reaction`, `Integration`, `AuditLog`) plus two additions: **`Session`** (backs refresh-token rotation + multi-account) and **`Notification`** (backs the frontend's `NotificationsPanel`, which has no corresponding model in the requested 11).
- `src/modules/{workspace,members,contacts,conversations,messages,notifications,sms,integrations,audit}/` — each a `router.ts` (tRPC) + `service.ts` (real Prisma queries), merged into one `appRouter` in `src/trpc/router.ts`.
- `src/modules/auth/` — **plain Express REST**, not tRPC (`POST /auth/login|refresh|logout`), per the literal paths requested — it has to work before a client holds a token to authenticate a tRPC call with. Refresh tokens are JWTs carrying a session id cross-checked against a `Session` row, so refresh can actually revoke-and-rotate, and a user can hold several concurrently-valid sessions (multi-account).
- `src/lib/{prisma,redis,socket,bullmq}.ts` as requested, plus `s3.ts` and `email.ts` (needed since `@aws-sdk/client-s3` and `resend` were in the dependency list but had no designated home).
- File uploads (`multer` + S3) and Twilio's inbound-SMS webhook don't fit tRPC's JSON procedures, so they're dedicated Express routes (`messages/attachments.ts`, `sms/webhook.ts`) mounted directly in `server.ts` alongside `/trpc`.
- BullMQ is wired through `notifications/service.ts` (enqueues a job) → `notifications/worker.ts` (sends via Resend). Twilio/Resend/S3 calls are real SDK calls gated on env vars — they throw a clear error until real credentials are configured, rather than faking success, since there's no live Twilio/Resend/Postgres/Redis in this environment to test against.

## Frontend wiring
- `src/lib/auth.ts` is now a real client for the REST auth routes (localStorage-persisted session, `login`/`refreshSession`/`logout`) — this changes its exported shape from the Phase 1 stub.
- `src/lib/api.ts` is a real tRPC client (`createTRPCProxyClient`), type-imported from `backend/src/trpc/router.ts` (type-only import — no backend code is bundled into the frontend).
- `src/lib/socket.ts` is a real `socket.io-client` connection authenticated with the stored access token.
- Added `@trpc/client` and `socket.io-client` to the frontend's `package.json`.
- **Not done**: the UI components still render Phase 1's local mock data/state, and `hooks/useSocket.ts` + `hooks/usePresence.ts` remain Phase 1's inert stubs. Swapping the UI over to live data is follow-up work beyond "wire up api.ts and socket.ts clients."
- Settings → API keys/Webhooks (`ApiKeys.tsx`) has no backing model, since `ApiKey`/`Webhook` aren't in the requested 11 models — `integrations/service.ts` only covers connected-apps (`Integration`).

## Verification
- `pnpm typecheck` (`tsc --noEmit`) in `backend/` — passes, 0 errors
- `npx prisma validate` — schema is valid
- `pnpm build` (backend, emits to `dist/`) — succeeds
- Frontend `pnpm tsc --noEmit`, `pnpm lint`, `pnpm build` — all still pass after wiring in the new clients/dependencies
- **Not verified**: runtime behavior against a live Postgres/Redis/Twilio/Resend — none are available in this environment. This is compile-time/schema verification only; migrations have not been run.

## Test plan
- [x] `backend`: `pnpm install && pnpm typecheck` passes
- [x] `backend`: `npx prisma validate` passes
- [x] `backend`: `pnpm build` succeeds
- [x] frontend: `pnpm tsc --noEmit` passes
- [x] frontend: `pnpm lint` passes
- [x] frontend: `pnpm build` succeeds
- [ ] Run `prisma migrate dev` against a real Postgres instance and confirm the schema applies cleanly
- [ ] Smoke-test `/auth/login` → `/trpc` round trip against a running backend

## Summary
- Gateway inherits the DAB default `ANSIBLE_BASE_ALLOW_TEAM_ORG_MEMBER = False`, while Controller overrides it to `True` (`awx/settings/defaults.py:1111`).

author: hieunguyenzzz
body:
Follow-up to #36. Every field on `/[lang]/lets-connect` is now mandatory, but nothing on the page said so — couples only found out by pressing **Send**. This adds a `*` marker to all 14 labels.

## Change

`src/app/[lang]/lets-connect/LetsConnectForm.tsx` only:

- New `RequiredMark` component — a small `*` in `text-text-accent`, `aria-hidden` because each input already carries `required`, which assistive tech announces on its own.
- `Field` renders the marker when its `required` prop is set, so the marker can never drift out of sync with actual validation.
- Same marker on the notes label and on the two checkbox-group headings (`extraEvents`, `referralSource`), which are mandatory as a group.
- The `data-tina-field` moved from each label/heading element onto a `<span>` wrapping just the copy. This keeps the marker **outside** the Tina-editable region, so editors never have to type or preserve the asterisk themselves and can't accidentally delete it.

No content (`content/*.mdx`) touched — labels are unchanged.

Deliberately **not** added: a "* indicates required" legend. That would be new hardcoded copy, and it would show up in English on `/vi`; the bare asterisk is language-neutral. Say the word if you'd like the legend as a Tina field instead.

## Verification

Dev server in an isolated worktree with `DATABASE_URL` / `ERP_INQUIRY_*` / `ZOHO_*` blanked.

- `yarn typecheck` clean; `eslint` clean on the changed file; production `docker build` exit 0.
- `/en` and `/vi` both render exactly **14 markers** — 11 inputs + notes + both group headings — matching the 14 fields that report `:invalid` on an empty submit, so no field is marked without being enforced and none is enforced without a marker.
- `/vi` still renders 23 `required` inputs, unchanged by the refactor.
- Empty submit still blocked client-side with all 14 fields invalid.
- Screenshots checked at 1280px: marker reads as a subtle olive asterisk, no layout shift.

author: vaibhavdhir-ai
body:
## What this PR is

Analytics Agent can now compare a certified legacy metric with its rebuilt redesign-table pair, and Reporting PMs are being asked to validate those values before cutover. Appendix A did not explain that role boundary. This adds a copyable compare → recheck → approve-or-stop workflow while keeping legacy as the source of truth and promotion owner-controlled. This PR stacks on #142 because both changes touch the Analytics Agent card; I can rebase and force-push it to `master` if one independent PR is easier to review.

## Evidence

- [`self-serve-analytics` #1926](https://github.com/razorpay/self-serve-analytics/pull/1926), merged 5 August 2026, ships the registered legacy/redesign pair, `compare redesign`, explicit `use redesign` opt-in, and owner-run promotion contract.
- [The vendored Analytics Agent engine on `claude-plugins` master](https://github.com/razorpay/claude-plugins/blob/master/plugins/analytics-agent/ssa/.claude/skills/self-serve-analytics/SKILL.md) keeps legacy as the silent default, refuses unregistered pairs, marks deltas above 1% as failures, and requires snapshot-lag rechecks.
- [`#analytics-self-serve`, 5 August 2026](https://razorpay.slack.com/archives/C0A98PQTJH4/p1785925293599689) asks a Reporting PM to run `compare redesign` or `use redesign` and confirm that the values match before approval.

## What changed

- `appendices/A-tool-atlas/README.md` — adds the PM-facing validation loop, copyable evidence card, mismatch/freshness stop conditions, and the boundary between validation and production promotion.

## Why this and not something else

Automatic serial/parallel agent scheduling has a strong problem signal but no stable PM/designer-facing implementation contract, and open #151 already changes the adjacent orchestration lesson. A new Fable 5 route has one current support answer but no rollout, default, persistence, or fallback policy. The Analytics Agent workflow wins because its engine contract is merged, bundled in the current plugin, and already being assigned to a PM for live validation.

## Validation

- `git diff --check` — passed.
- Targeted `gray-matter` parse — passed; the touched chapter has one `updated` key set to `2026-08-05`.
- Content assertions for the registered-pair gate, `compare redesign`, `use redesign`, and both evidence links — passed.
- Full hub build reaches generation but is blocked by the pre-existing duplicate `updated` key in `belts/03-green/a-craft/G02-context-windows.md`; that file is inherited from #142 and untouched here.

body:
## Problems

1. **Disconnect button did nothing**: `disconnect_calendar` built the full OAuth provider (requires client id + secret) just to delete a keychain token — any config problem made disconnect fail silently-ish (error only in the small status line).

body:
TÂCHE : trouver pourquoi Loms ne peut pas se connecter, en vérifiant au lieu de déduire.
BRANCHE : `claude/integrer-backend-chatgpt`
RESPONSABLE : Claude — intègre `agent/payment-control-backend-v1` (ChatGPT)

---

## 1. La cause, vérifiée

`window._inviterCompte` appelait **directement** la fonction SQL `prepare_account_invitation`. Sa dernière ligne :

```sql
revoke all on function public.prepare_account_invitation(...)
  from public, anon, authenticated;
grant execute ... to service_role;
```

**Elle est refusée au navigateur, par construction** — et c'est voulu : préparer une invitation, c'est ouvrir un accès ; la clé qui peut le faire ne descend pas dans un téléphone.

La bonne porte est l'Edge Function **`invite-school-account`**, déjà présente dans `supabase/functions/`. C'est ce que ChatGPT avait écrit dans `AUTH_EMAIL_RECOVERY_DECISION` ; je ne l'avais pas suivi.

**Conséquence exacte :** chaque invitation partie de l'application était refusée. Le compte se créait — `save_school_user_profile` est bien ouvert à `authenticated` — mais **aucun courriel ne partait**. La Direction voyait le nom dans la liste et attendait un message qui n'existait pas.

Et sans invitation, **aucune identité Auth ne peut naître** : `private.handle_new_auth_user()` refuse avec `42501` — *« ce compte SchoolSafe ne possède pas une invitation valide »*. Une adresse enregistrée dans `public.users` ne suffit donc pas à se connecter.

Contrat vérifié ligne à ligne : la fonction attend `{app_user_id, email}`, rend `{ok:true, code:'ACCOUNT_INVITED'}`, et `https://medygoo.github.io` est dans ses origines autorisées **comme dans ses redirections**.

## 2. Vingt-neuf migrations de ChatGPT n'étaient pas dans le dépôt

`agent/payment-control-backend-v1` n'a jamais été intégrée. **C'est mon rôle** et je ne l'avais pas fait. Elle contient notamment :

| | |
|---|---|
| `…091650_repair_account_invitation_linkage_contract` | le déclencheur qui **rattache l'identité Auth au profil** |
| `…200317_fix_school_user_profile_auth_permission` | |
| `…090600_harden_payment_authorship_receipts` | l'auteur des reçus |
| `…091101_enforce_scanner_orientation_contract_v2` | le contrat scanner v2 |

**Cinq RPC que le frontend appelle** n'étaient définies nulle part dans le dépôt : `get_parent_fee_summary`, `get_cashier_student_fee_detail`, `record_payment_transaction`, `reverse_payment_transaction`, `check_gate_access_status`. Elles le sont maintenant.

La fusion est **purement additive** — 55 fichiers, aucun conflit, `dist/` intact.

## 3. Ce qui reste à signaler à ChatGPT

`get_safe_settings()` est décrite dans `coordination/RPC_REGISTRE.md` et appelée au démarrage par le frontend, mais **son SQL n'existe dans aucune branche**. Elle est probablement déployée sans avoir été déposée.

## 4. Tests

`npm run audit` — les 9 audits passent. `audit-schema` — aucun écart sur 49 tables.

## 5. Retour arrière

`git revert` du commit applicatif ; la fusion de la branche de ChatGPT se défait séparément.

author: blublinsky
body:
## Description

Summary
When RHOKP takes longer than the retry window to start, the app-server permanently loses product documentation RAG with no recovery short of a pod restart. This PR fixes the root cause and simplifies the startup sequence.

**Root Cause**
solr_hybrid_search was a @cached_property — once it resolved to None (Solr unreachable), it stayed None forever
Index loading ran on a background thread, racing with request handling — a request could arrive before initialization completed

**Changes**

Removed background threading.Thread for index loading — load_index() now runs synchronously before start_uvicorn(). Eliminates race conditions between initialization and request handling. The readiness probe budget (8 min) accommodates the startup delay.
ols/utils/config.py

Changed solr_hybrid_search from @cached_property to @property with manual caching. On failure, returns None without caching — the next request re-attempts initialization. After 3 failed attempts, gives up permanently with an error log. On success, caches the result for the lifetime of the process.
ols/src/rag_index/solr_support.py

Increased _SOLR_STARTUP_RETRIES from 24 to 36 (120s → 180s) to better align with RHOKP's startup probe budget (6 min).
tests/unit/query_helpers/test_docs_summarizer.py

Updated test to use the new caching attributes instead of __dict__ manipulation.

**Result**
RHOKP starting after the app-server is tolerated without a pod restart
No race between background thread and request handling
Bounded retry: 3 attempts × 180s = 9 minutes max before permanent give-up with clear error log

author: messias-olivindo
mastacontrola
body:
Fixes the HTTP 500 on **FOG Configuration → Kernel Update → Install**, reported on [forum topic 18211](https://forums.fogproject.org/topic/18211/) by two users independently.

### Cause

d36f94637 ported the *consumer* half of GH-850 to this branch: `FOGPage`'s Secure Boot helpers derive their paths from `FOG_BASE_DIR` instead of `/opt/fog` literals. The producer half — the installer-generated `commons/fogpaths.php` that actually defines it — stayed on `working-1.6`. So the constant is used five times here and defined nowhere.

On PHP 8 an undefined constant is a fatal `Error`, not a PHP 7 warning that degrades to the bareword string, so both entry points take the request down:

- `fogconfigurationpage::kernelUpdatePost()`, on clicking Install
- `FOGPage::secureBootSign()`, on the tftp upload step

Both reporters bisected to the same window — 1.5.10.2144 fine, 1.5.10.2191 broken. d36f94637 is 2179.

`working-1.6` is unaffected: `init.php:91` and `system.class.php:100` both define it.

### Fix

Ports the producer half rather than hardcoding `/opt/fog` back in. `$fogprogramdir` has always been settable in `.fogsettings` on this branch (`lib/common/config.sh:35`), it simply never reached PHP — hardcoding would leave the same trap armed for the next path derived from it.

- `lib/common/functions.sh` — `installFOGWebUI` writes `commons/fogpaths.php` from `$fogprogramdir`
- `packages/web/commons/init.php` — loads it before the autoloader, guarded on `is_readable`
- `packages/web/lib/fog/system.class.php` — guarded `/opt/fog` fallback for installs predating the file
- `.gitignore` — the generated file, alongside `config.class.php`

**Deliberately not ported:** GH-850's other parts — the `/opt/fog` literal sweep through `functions.sh` and the service classes (f8cbb7a92), and making the base path settable out-of-band via `/etc/fog/fog.conf` plus unit-file retargeting (5af14546d). Those are installer changes to the patches line, far wider than this regression, and every one of those literals works today.

### Verified

Booted the real `Initiator` against three trees:

| tree | result |
|---|---|
| `origin/dev-branch` as shipped (2208) | `Uncaught Error: Undefined constant "FOG_BASE_DIR"` |
| with this change, no `fogpaths.php` | `/opt/fog/bin/fog-sign-kernel`, `/opt/fog/secureboot-staging` |
| with an installer-written file, `/srv/fogserver` | `/srv/fogserver/bin/fog-sign-kernel`, `/srv/fogserver/secureboot-staging` |

Shell generator exercised separately for a default and a trailing-slash custom path (`${fogprogramdir%/}` strips it). `bash -n` and `php -l` clean.

author: fxeliott
body:
Suite de #597. La reservation etait le bon mecanisme, le budget en pixels etait faux — et c'est le hit-test post-deploiement qui l'a dit, pas une relecture.

## Mesure sur le build deploye, 375x667, `elementFromPoint` au centre de chaque cible

| Page | Cible | Apres #597 |
|---|---|---|
| `/` | « Se connecter » | OK |
| `/` | « Demander un acces » | atteignable, mais finit **6 px** dans la bande de la banniere |
| `/login` | « Se connecter » (submit) | OK (etait OCCLUDED) |
| `/login` | « Mot de passe oublie ? » | OK, et 130x24 (etait 114x17) |
| `/login` | « Faire une demande » | **encore OCCLUDED, de 27 px** |

Le hit-test passait deja sur 6 cibles sur 7. Il en restait une, et un chevauchement residuel de 6 px sur une autre — sous le contrat « aucun chevauchement, jamais », ce n'est pas fini.

## Deux causes, mesurees et non deduites

**1. La banniere fait 87 px, pas les ~68 px estimes.** A 375 px sa colonne de texte fait 204 px, et « Aucun tracker, aucune analytics tierce. » s'y enroule sur **deux** lignes. Chaque ligne de cette banniere coute ~19 px de contenu a **toutes** les pages. La phrase tient desormais sur une ligne ; le detail vit sur la page confidentialite qu'elle reference deja.

**2. Reduire le `padding-block` des coquilles d'auth ne touchait pas le vrai mou.** Ces pages empilent leur contenu dans un `<section>` en colonne a `gap-6` : trois intervalles de 24 px, c'est la que sont les pixels. Resserres a 16 px — sous `sm` uniquement, et uniquement tant qu'un ilot occupe le bas. A la fermeture de la banniere, la page reprend exactement son rythme d'origine.

## Ce que je retiens

Avoir estime un budget de pixels a partir du markup plutot que de le mesurer. Les chiffres de cette PR sont lus sur la page qui tourne.

## Barriere qualite

`lint` OK · `type-check` OK · `test` 6249 verts · `build` OK · `prettier --check` OK sur les 2 fichiers.

Verification post-merge : re-jouer le meme hit-test sur les 5 pages publiques.

author: nandanito
body:
Closes #108. Second slice of Phase 3 (epic #104), first half of T2.

Adds the **`artifact-only`** collaboration mode: the callee does the task in its own space, and what crosses back is the **references-only manifest** of the workspace artifacts it produced — paths, kinds, sizes, existence. Never its narration, never its memory, never the file bytes.

## The decision this encodes

The design note left a genuine fork in §4's one-line description ("files/diffs B produced"): do the file **contents** cross, or only a **manifest**? Worth being explicit that **the note does not settle it** — D2's *"the stricter modes exist for when even text shouldn't flow"* is satisfied by both readings (under a contents-crossing design the callee's *narration* still doesn't flow), and §4's "least-to-most curated" reads as "narrower in kind" as easily as "smaller in payload".

It was decided on engineering grounds:

1. **T5 forward-compatibility — the deciding argument.** §4 frames the modes as a dial on *"how much of B does **A** get back"* — A, not the operator's terminal. Under D4 the initiator is a human today, so contents crossing looks harmless: the operator already has access to both agents. **T5 (agent-initiated delegation) makes the caller an agent**, and the payload then lands *inside A's context mid-run*. Callee-authored file contents would become a prompt-injection channel between two agents the phase exists to keep apart — installed in the slice where it looked innocuous. A payload contract has to be designed for the agent↔agent case.
2. **The scrub is best-effort by our own published description.** `redactForTrace` is pattern-based over secret *value* shapes and built for bounded snippets. Stretching it across arbitrary-length file contents and calling the result screened would overstate it. A manifest needs no such stretch — the observation stream is already bounded and already redacted.

**Byte delivery is deferred, not cancelled.** The honest gap is that A cannot *dereference* a manifest (the files are in the callee's workspace; A's tools are workspace-confined). Materializing one is a **write into A**, with overwrite risk, so it belongs behind **A's own destructive-action gate** — a follow-up slice, and the natural completion of this mode. Until then the operator reads the file directly; they own the machine.

## Core

- **`artifact-manifest.ts`** — a pure `ObservedEffect[] → ArtifactRef[]` reducer: the *second* projection of the same stream `world-fact-harvest.ts` already reduces. State-changing effects only (a manifest of what the callee **read** would be precisely the leak this mode prevents), last-wins per subject, agent-chosen paths redacted at the boundary, bounded and defensive against malformed observations.
- **`ExecuteRunResult.artifacts?`** mirroring the established `harvest?` pattern, computed at all four exits — pause exits included, since an observation lives only in the invocation that produced it.
- **`performExchange` extracted** — one shared connection-check + both-logs audit + run-as-callee, so the invariants cannot drift between modes. Modes differ **only** in their projection.
- **`performArtifactExchange` → `ArtifactExchangeResult`**, a type with nowhere to put the callee's text: invariant 2 becomes a property of the **type**, not of a caller remembering not to read a field. Enforced at the kernel boundary, not the surface — a surface filter would leave the text one field access away for the next surface.
  - It returns **`runId`, not the `Run` row**: `Run.output` carries the callee's final text (`types.ts:247`), so handing back the row would have leaked exactly what the mode withholds.
  - **No `error` text** crosses either (free-form callee-side text); the caller learns `failed` from `status` and the operator is pointed at the callee's own log.
- `CONNECTION_MODES` grows to `["handoff", "artifact-only"]` — still only modes with a real implementation, so the write boundary can never persist a half-built mode.

## CLI

- **`asterism artifact <from> <to> "<task>"`** — its own verb (D9). A pair can hold several active mode-connections simultaneously (the partial unique index is per-`(from, to, mode)` — visible in the smoke test below), and the task is read **verbatim** to preserve flag-shaped tasks; a `--mode` flag would fight both. Shared arg parsing + prelude extracted from `cmdHandoff`, so `artifact` inherits the Codex-R1 dash-task protection.
- Mode-accurate copy: `connect` now names the verb the channel actually enables, and the connections legend is mode-neutral.

```
$ asterism connect writer helper --mode artifact-only
Connected writer → helper (artifact-only). Use it with: asterism artifact writer helper "<task>"

$ asterism artifact writer helper "draft the market section"
helper produced 1 artifact:
  drafts/market-section.md   4.2 KB

Only these references crossed — not helper's words, memory, or the file contents.
The files are in helper's own workspace.
```

## Tests (+42; 1161 → 1203)

- **`artifact.test.ts`** — the five §2 invariants for this mode, including: a `handoff` connection does **not** authorize it (and vice versa); the `Run` row never crosses; a secret-shaped *path* is redacted while a secret in file *contents* never crosses at all; a pure read contributes nothing; a withheld or paused action yields **no** artifact.
- **`artifact-manifest.test.ts`** — the pure reducer, incl. malformed-observation and fact-flood defenses.
- **`artifact-acceptance.test.ts`** — the §9 demo end-to-end through `runCli`.
- Moved the "unimplemented mode" assertions from `artifact-only` to `read-summary`.

## Gates

Suite **1203 pass / 0 fail** · `tsc -b` clean · `verify:node` 15/15 · `verify:deno` 15/15 · smoke-tested through the real `bin.js`.

## Not in this slice

`read-summary` (T2b — a *pull* that runs nothing; how its summary is generated is deliberately still open), `artifact fetch` (gated byte materialization), and the T1 follow-ups (HTTP parity, revoke).

author: tiptop33
body:
Implémente les écrans 1 à 6 de « Wireframes HERACLES.dc », l'espace référent, et ferme l'inscription libre.

**L'instance d'essai tourne : https://essai.oaf-heracles.cloud** — vrai HTTPS, vrais courriels, base vide. La chaîne complète a été parcourue de bout en bout : premier administrateur créé, invitation émise, courriel reçu, compte référent ouvert avec le bon rôle.

## Ce que ça change pour les gens

**On n'entre plus qu'invité.** N'importe qui pouvait ouvrir `/inscription`, se déclarer référent et créer un compte. Pour une application qui porte les dossiers de 107 personnes vulnérables, c'était la mauvaise porte. Désormais un administrateur — et lui seul — invite, dans une loge précise, avec un rôle précis.

**Un référent travaille sur ses candidats.** Liste, fiche complète, modification. Il voit qui est suivi, qui attend un premier contact, quelle part de chaque fiche est renseignée. Et il ne voit **que** les siens : pas par filtre d'affichage, la base refuse.

**Un administrateur invite depuis un écran**, plus depuis la console.

## Les écrans

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 1 · Connexion | « Rester connecté », mot de passe oublié, Google (en attente d'identifiants OAuth) |
| 2 · Mot de passe oublié | message identique que le compte existe ou non |
| 3 · Nouveau mot de passe | jauge, trois règles dont « différent des 3 derniers » |
| 5 · Invitation reçue | qui invite, quelle loge, quel rôle — accepter ou refuser |
| 6 · Création du compte | profil, CGU, mot de passe |
| Espace référent | liste, fiche, saisie |
| Administration | émettre une invitation, voir qui attend |

L'écran 4 (double authentification) n'est pas fait : le code part par SMS, il faut choisir un fournisseur.

## Sécurité — ce qui est prouvé, pas affirmé

Cinq migrations, chacune avec son test. La suite pose la question à la base plutôt qu'à une page, en devenant tour à tour chaque personne.

- Un référent voit les candidats dont il est référent **ou** parrain, jamais les autres. Un parrain voit ses filleuls. Une personne connectée sans fiche ne voit rien.
- Personne ne peut créer, supprimer ni s'attribuer un dossier — le rattachement est figé par déclencheur.
- Le jeton d'une invitation n'est pas conservé, seulement son empreinte. Elle expire en sept jours, ne sert qu'une fois, et ne vaut que pour l'adresse à laquelle elle est partie.
- « Seul un administrateur peut inviter » est vérifié deux fois : dans la route pour répondre proprement, dans la base qui refuse quoi qu'il arrive.
- Les trois derniers mots de passe sont mémorisés en empreintes bcrypt, dans une table sans policy ni grant.

## Défauts trouvés en faisant tourner le produit

**Aucune table n'était lisible.** Les migrations ne posaient aucun `GRANT`, en comptant sur des privilèges par défaut qui, pour les tables créées par `postgres`, ne donnent pas `SELECT`. L'application ne lisait donc rien : la connexion réussissait, puis la lecture du profil échouait en silence et renvoyait tout le monde vers le mauvais espace. Le lot 1 en souffrait déjà ; le harnais de test, qui grantait tout, le masquait. Corrigé par `0007`, plus serré que le réglage d'origine de Supabase.

**Le mot de passe finissait dans l'adresse.** Avant la fin de l'hydratation, un formulaire sans `method` part en GET : le mot de passe s'écrivait dans l'URL, donc dans l'historique et les journaux. Connexion et inscription fonctionnent maintenant **sans JavaScript** — ce qui est aussi la meilleure garantie qu'elles fonctionnent pendant qu'il charge.

**Un contrôle échouait dans le mauvais sens.** Quand la vérification des anciens mots de passe ne pouvait pas s'exécuter, elle laissait passer. Elle refuse désormais.

**Et un quatrième, côté poste de travail** : le README faisait créer le `.env` à la racine, alors que Next ne lit le sien que dans son propre dossier. Personne ne pouvait démarrer l'application en local.

## Défauts trouvés en la mettant en ligne

Rien de tout cela n'était visible en développement. C'est l'argument de l'instance d'essai.

**Studio était atteignable depuis Internet.** En lisant la configuration de Kong pour écrire les règles du reverse-proxy, on découvre qu'il sert **Studio sur `/`** — l'administration complète de la base. La configuration interdisait `/studio` et `/project`, deux chemins qui ne mènent nulle part. On passe à une liste blanche : `/auth/v1`, `/rest/v1`, `/storage/v1`, et rien d'autre n'existe de l'extérieur.

**Toutes les redirections menaient à `0.0.0.0:3003`.** Derrière un reverse-proxy, `requete.url` porte l'adresse d'écoute interne — la seule que le serveur voie. En développement c'est justement celle du navigateur, d'où l'invisibilité. En ligne, plus rien ne fonctionnait dès qu'une page en renvoyait vers une autre : le lien de courriel, la connexion, la déconnexion.

**La clé `service_role` n'était pas transmise au conteneur.** L'écran « Choisissez un mot de passe » levait, Next renvoyait du HTML là où le navigateur attendait du JSON, et l'écran annonçait une panne de réseau pour une variable manquante. Les deux routes concernées rendent maintenant leurs exceptions lisibles.

**Le port de l'application était en dur.** 3002 dans la composition, alors que l'essai annonçait 3003 : les deux instances se seraient disputé le port le jour où la production démarre.

**Le `.env` de Supabase se bâtissait sur notre modèle.** Sa composition lit une trentaine de variables, la liste change de version en version, et une variable absente arrive **vide** — un booléen vide fait tomber le service qui l'attend. Sans service d'authentification, pas de schéma `auth` ; sans schéma `auth`, aucune migration. Il part désormais du modèle de Supabase lui-même, dont on ne remplace que les secrets, les adresses, et ce qu'il laisse ouvert.

## Vérifier

```bash
cd apps/web && npm run lint && npm test && npm run build
PGHOST=localhost PGPORT=54332 PGUSER=postgres ./supabase/tests/executer.sh
```

59 tests unitaires, et l'ensemble des contrôles SQL des migrations 0001, 0002, 0006 à 0010.

Depuis l'extérieur, sur l'instance d'essai :

```
essai.oaf-heracles.cloud/connexion              200, HTTP/2, HSTS un an
api-essai.oaf-heracles.cloud/                   404 — Studio hors d'atteinte
api-essai.oaf-heracles.cloud/rest/v1/candidat   401 sans clé
```

## Mise en ligne

`infra/essai/deployer.sh` monte une instance d'essai en une commande, isolée de la future production et de MyCollabus : dossier, projet Docker, préfixe de conteneurs, ports, volumes. Le seul port publié est celui de Kong, sur `127.0.0.1`.

Le script s'adapte à la façade déjà en place sur la machine — Nginx s'il est seul, Traefik s'il tient déjà le port 80, auquel cas HERACLES se déclare par les étiquettes de ses conteneurs plutôt qu'en modifiant une configuration dont dépendent les autres sites.

`docs/deploiement.md` couvre la production de bout en bout, et note les deux pièges qui ont coûté le plus de temps : l'ordre entre certbot et la configuration qui réclame le certificat, et le mot de passe d'application exigé par Gmail.

author: dgprivate
body:
### Description of change

UniFi OS hands out per-device Protect permissions in a second, newer form that this library
does not parse. Alongside the classic `<model>:<nodes>:<obj ids>` strings, a user's
`allPermissions` can contain:

```
granular:camera:access:<camera id>
granular:camera:livestream:<camera id>
granular:camera:livestream:audio:<camera id>
granular:camera:playback:<camera id>
granular:camera:playback:audio:<camera id>
granular:camera:playback:download:<camera id>
granular:camera:settings:edit:<camera id>
```

`Permission.unifi_dict_to_dict()` passes `parts[0]` straight to `ModelType`. Because
`ModelType` is an `UnknownValuesEnumMixin`, `ModelType("granular")` does not raise — it
resolves to `ModelType.UNKNOWN` and logs at debug level. The permission is therefore
constructed, stored, and then never matches in `User.can()`, which short-circuits on
`if model is not perm.model`. Every granular grant is silently discarded.

**Current behaviour:** a user whose only write grant is
`granular:camera:settings:edit:<id>` gets `camera.can_write(user) is False`, so
`_save_device_changes()` raises `NotAuthorized: Do not have write permission for obj: <id>`
before any request is sent. The server accepts the same write — verified against a UNVR4 on
Protect 7.1.87 by driving `PATCH /proxy/protect/api/cameras/<id>` with
`{"speakerSettings": {"volume": N}}` as that exact user: HTTP 200, and the value round-trips
on a subsequent GET.

Downstream this surfaces in the Home Assistant `unifiprotect` integration as devices that
stay read-only (`sensor`/`binary_sensor` mirrors instead of `number`/`switch`/`select`) even
though the console was configured to allow editing that one camera.

**New behaviour:** `granular:` permissions are mapped onto the existing
`ModelType` / `PermissionNode` pair:

| granular capability | node |
| --- | --- |
| `access` | `read` |
| `livestream`, `livestream:audio` | `readlive` |
| `playback`, `playback:audio`, `playback:download` | `readmedia` |
| `settings:edit` | `write` |

The trailing segment is the object id, and `*` keeps `obj_ids` unset so the grant applies to
every object of that model, matching the classic form. An unrecognised capability maps to
`PermissionNode.UNKNOWN` and a string too short to carry an object id maps to
`ModelType.UNKNOWN`; both stay inert rather than raising, so a future firmware adding
capabilities cannot break bootstrap parsing.

Verified with `pytest` (2040 passed) and by re-running the new cases against the unpatched
parser, where three of them fail.

### Pull-Request Checklist

- [x] Code is up-to-date with the `main` branch
- [x] This pull request follows the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/uilibs/uiprotect/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md).
- [ ] This pull request links relevant issues as `Fixes #0000` — N/A, no open issue found
- [x] There are new or updated unit tests validating the change
- [ ] Documentation has been updated to reflect this change — N/A, no user-facing API change
- [x] The pull request title follows the [conventional commit spec](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/), such as "fix(api): prevent racing of requests" (PRs are squash-merged, so the title becomes the commit on `main`).

### Motivation

- When no documents have breached their review dates, the recipients still need visibility into upcoming reviews so they can prepare. 
- The change aims to provide a short, prioritized list of the next documents due for review and include it in the Outlook draft.

### Description

- Compute an `upcoming_df` from `doc_df` by selecting rows with `Next Planned Review Date` >= today, sort ascending, and limit to the next 10 items. 
- Generate a human-friendly `Review Alert` label per row (e.g., `REVIEW DUE TODAY`, `REVIEW IN 1 DAY`, `REVIEW IN X DAYS`) and set an `Alert Color`. 
- Build an HTML table with document link, responsible person, review cycle, remarks, status, review dates, and alert, and embed it into the Outlook mail body when no breached reviews are found by changing `mail.HTMLBody` to an f-string that includes the table.

author: kyawmintun08
body:
## Scope

Stages the first secure, persistent Broker–Customer chat foundation for the JACC Web/PWA/Android app.

This is a **stacked Draft PR on top of the Phase 2 branch**. It does not change the current production launcher, Apps Script deployment, Railway configuration, Supabase production schema or live website.

Tracks #17.

## Included

- Private Supabase chat schema linked to canonical `jacc_service_requests`.
- One persistent thread per request with current Customer and assigned Broker.
- Idempotent text messages using `(thread_id, sender_id, client_message_id)`.
- Read receipts, unread counts and audited close-chat flow.
- Service-role-only RPCs; direct browser table access remains denied.
- Staged Railway `aiohttp` API that verifies the Phase 2 Apps Script `verifyToken` membership/device session on every request.
- Explicit origin allowlist, bounded JSON/message/reason/pagination inputs and per-process rate limiting.
- Browser/PWA/Flutter client that uses the existing Phase 2 v4 session and never receives Supabase credentials.
- CI compilation, JavaScript syntax check, migration safety checks and API-boundary tests.

## Security model

- Browser sends the existing session token, member ID, installation ID and app type to Railway over HTTPS.
- Railway verifies the session with Apps Script and maps the numeric member ID to `jacc_profiles.telegram_user_id`.
- Railway alone uses the Supabase service role.
- Database RPCs re-check request participation.
- Customer/current Broker can send; Admin/lead Broker can audit but cannot silently send as a participant.
- Normal logs must not include message bodies, tokens, passwords, device IDs or service keys.

## Initial transport

Authenticated REST plus bounded polling. Direct Supabase Realtime is intentionally deferred because the current app uses Apps Script v4 membership sessions rather than Supabase Auth JWTs.

## Not included yet

- No production launcher import.
- No database migration execution.
- No root `index.html` integration.
- No attachments, voice/video, typing state or presence.
- No Telegram-message mirroring yet.
- No Phase 2 merge/deployment as a side effect.

## Required before any production activation

1. Phase 2 membership/device-session release must pass live acceptance.
2. Review and apply `phase3/sql/001_app_chat.sql` in a controlled migration window.
3. Register the Railway routes behind explicit allowed origins.
4. Integrate the panel into the generated Phase 2 website/app.
5. Pilot with one real Customer and the currently assigned Broker.
6. Prove third-party, expired, suspended and device-mismatch access fails closed.
7. Restart Railway and verify history/read state survives.
8. Keep Telegram proxy chat as fallback.
9. Obtain explicit owner approval before Ready/Merge or deployment.

## Release status

**STAGED ONLY — KEEP DRAFT.**

author: yonatangross
body:
Five commits: two reported bugs, four documentation claims that pointed at things which do not exist, and the first two of the security test files that could not fail.

Closes #3083
Closes #3283

## The two reported bugs

**#3083 `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}`** was reported as "never set". Verifying it turned up something worse: it is not a Claude Code placeholder at all. The plugins reference documents exactly three substitutions (`CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT`, `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA`, `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR`); this one appears zero times. It was invented here and grew to 442 references across 68 skills, partly because `scripts/eval/conformance-check.mjs` recommended it. Confirmed present in the installed 9.6.1 artifact, so every user has it.

The bash case is the nastier of the two failure modes: the shell expands an unset variable to empty, so `python3 ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/x.py` runs as `python3 /scripts/x.py`, a plausible-looking absolute path that simply is not there. 442 references now 0.

**#3283 label enforcer** denied compound `gh issue create` commands. A PreToolUse deny aborts before execution, so denying the second half of `cat > issue.md <<'EOF' ... && gh issue create ...` also discards the heredoc that already ran. The retry then failed for an unrelated reason (missing file), which made the block misleading rather than merely strict.

A sweep found five bash-facing hooks that deny without splitting compound commands first, but only one is a defect. The distinction is why each denies: `agent-browser-safety`, `git-validator`, `network-egress-guard` and `compound-cmd-validator` deny for SAFETY, where losing earlier work beats the hazard. `gh-label-enforcer` denies for POLICY, and a missing label is a nit. The fix is scoped to the policy hook: a simple `gh issue create` still denies, a compound one advises.

## Four documentation references to things that do not exist

Each verified missing at HEAD before being touched. The worst was CONTRIBUTING.md "Adding New Hooks", which described a bash system (top-level `hooks/`, `../_lib/common.sh`, registration in `.claude/settings.json`) that no longer exists. A contributor following it would produce a hook that never runs, which is the #959 dead-hook class this repo warns about elsewhere.

## 26 security test functions that could not fail

`test-path-traversal.sh` and `test-command-injection.sh` between them had 16 of 18 functions that could not fail. Each called a shell hook path deleted in the TypeScript migration, so `run_hook` returned 127, the `if [[ $HOOK_EXIT_CODE -eq 0 ]]` branch never ran, and the function hit an unconditional `return 0`. The suite passed BECAUSE the hooks were gone.

Both are rewritten against the real hooks' measured contracts, 30 assertions total, with `assert_hook_registered` aborting the run if a key stops resolving so a rename cannot make the allow-cases pass against a dead hook.

Two findings worth flagging:

- The **ME-001 symlink defence had zero coverage**. `file-guard.ts:1-8` claims it resolves symlinks before pattern-matching (CWE-59). It works, a symlink named `harmless-name.txt` pointing at `.env` is denied on its target, but that was documentation rather than a tested behaviour until now.
- The dangerous-command blocker has **three tiers, not two**. `rm -rf ./node_modules` returns `ask`, and the first draft asserted `allow`. The hook was right (`:73` documents ASK as "dangerous but sometimes legitimate"), so the assertion changed, not the hook. Tuning it the other way would have documented a weaker contract than the code provides.

The 19 old command-injection fixtures were deliberately NOT retargeted. They assert that subshells, backticks and `${IFS}` expansion get blocked, which was `bash-defaults`' threat model, and `bash-defaults` was removed on purpose (e844b4b25). Measured: those fixtures produce 2 denies from `dangerous-command-blocker`, 1 from `compound-command-validator`, 0 from `network-egress-guard`. Retargeting them would have manufactured ~17 failures and pressured someone into making the hook over-block.

## Not covered here

21 of the 47 known blind security test functions remain, in `test-additional-security.sh`, `test-input-validation.sh` and `test-symlink-attacks.sh`. Each needs the same measure-the-real-contract-first work and is being handled separately.

## Verification

- security suite 18/18
- placeholder gate green
- build drift 0/1242
- each converted file confirmed able to fail: a deliberately wrong expectation exits 1, a typo'd hook key exits 1, the restored file exits 0


## Interactive Playground

Mutation probe over the 26 converted assertions. Toggle `Break the hook on purpose` and watch which assertions go red. Before this PR the same mutation changed nothing, which is the entire finding.

**[Open Playground](https://htmlpreview.github.io/?https://github.com/yonatangross/orchestkit/blob/fix/claude-skill-dir-placeholder/docs/fix--claude-skill-dir-placeholder/playground.html)**

Source: `docs/fix--claude-skill-dir-placeholder/playground.html`
